items.reason: Verdicts 152, 162 and 163 settle it: 'runtime on a parameter checks it while the program runs' (152), 'runtime goes before a class type too' (162), 'runtime goes on a variable too' (163), and LT-48 (p07 704-721) and the §X.4 row (p10 315) carry them. Part I was never brought in line. p01 13-15: 'nothing about ownership, views or aliasing is checked while the program runs'. PHIL-8 (p01 67-70) lists the run-time checks and has no `runtime` entry. The I.4 row 'One name changes a place, or any number read it' (p01 147) says 'Checked while running: never'. I.6 (p01 217-218) lists 'an aliasing or exclusivity check while the program runs' as a non-goal. The front matter (p00 33-36, 'replaces ... every check of exclusive access made while the program runs') is just as stale. PHIL-15 is already true, since its list includes 'a type-id compare'.
items.lead_fix_text: p01 13-15 (I.1): 'nothing about ownership, views or aliasing is checked while the program runs, except where a line asks for it: a value marked `runtime` (`[LT-48]`) and `assert_disjoint` (`[DSJ-5]`)'. PHIL-8 (p01 70): add to the list 'the kind of a value marked `runtime`, at a line one of its kinds would make unsafe (`[LT-48]`)'. I.4 row p01 147, 'Checked while running' cell: 'where a parameter, variable or field says `runtime` and its kind is known only while running: one type-id compare at each line it guards (`[LT-48]`)', mechanism 'the view rules; zero cost, or one compare where a line says `runtime`'. I.6 p01 217-218: 'an aliasing or exclusivity check the program did not ask for (`[BRW-1]`; the checks it may ask for are `runtime`, `[LT-48]`, and `assert_disjoint`, `[DSJ-5]`)'. p00 35-36: '... and every check of exclusive access the program did not ask for'. Part VII's own 'nothing is checked while the program runs' sentences (p07 8, 254) are for the Part VII reviewer.

items.reason: No rule classifies the `runtime` check. EFF-9 lists RuntimeCheck(Aliasing) as only the compare of `assert_disjoint`/`check_disjoint`, 'the one run-time alias check there is' (p10 69-70). EFF-12 says `@no_alias_checks` 'forbids only RuntimeCheck(Aliasing), the run-time compare of assert_disjoint or check_disjoint' (p10 196-198). DSJ-6 repeats 'the one run-time alias check' (p09 513). The Panic(Explicit) row (p10 16) names `assert_disjoint` and `cast x as T` but not `runtime`. So whether a `@no_alias_checks` or `@nopanic(explicit)` function may take a `runtime` parameter is undecided, and the two nearest rules point different ways: `assert_disjoint` is both Aliasing and Explicit, while a bounds check is implicit. No verdict covers contracts and `runtime`.
items.title: May a @no_alias_checks or @nopanic(explicit) function use a runtime check?
items.problem: An audio mixer's inner loop is marked `@no_alias_checks` and `@nopanic(explicit)`, and one of its parameters says `runtime`, so a line in it may stop the program while it runs when two names turn out to look at the same list. The contracts' rules name `assert_disjoint` as the only alias check that runs, and say nothing about the `runtime` word. So the specification does not say whether this function compiles under either contract.
items.spec_today: EFF-9 (p10 69-70): "`Aliasing` covers the compare of `assert_disjoint` and `check_disjoint` (`[DSJ-1]`), the one run-time alias check there is". EFF-12 (p10 196-198): "`@no_alias_checks` permits `RuntimeCheck(Bounds)`, `(Arithmetic)` and `(Stale)`; it forbids only `RuntimeCheck(Aliasing)`, the run-time compare of `assert_disjoint` or `check_disjoint`". EFF-16 (p10 225-227): "`@nopanic(explicit)` forbids only the panics the programmer writes and allocation failure. Arithmetic, bounds, aliasing and stale checks ... are `RuntimeCheck` kinds and are allowed under it". Effect table (p10 16): "`Panic(Explicit)` | `panic`, `assert*` (`assert_disjoint` included), `unwrap`, `expect`, `todo`, `unreachable`, `cast x as T`". LT-48 (p07 706-708): "the function checks the kind at the line that would be unsafe, and stops the program there if it is that kind".

options.summary: As `assert_disjoint`: an alias check the programmer asked for, refused under both contracts
options.outcome: Under `@no_alias_checks` the `runtime` word is refused (E4030, 'compares the kind of `m` while running'). Under `@nopanic(explicit)` it is refused too (E4040). Without the two contracts it compiles, prints for a Fixed and stops at the push for a PassThrough. Where every kind that reaches `m` is known when compiling, nothing is compared and both contracts accept it.

options.summary: As a bounds check: an alias check the compiler adds, refused only under @no_alias_checks
options.outcome: With `@no_alias_checks` it is refused (E4030). With only `@nopanic(explicit)` it compiles, and its stop counts as a check like an index out of bounds, not as a panic the programmer wrote.

options.summary: As `cast s as Circle`: a kind compare the programmer wrote, refused only under @nopanic(explicit)
options.outcome: With only `@no_alias_checks` it compiles, since the check counts as a kind test and not an alias check. With `@nopanic(explicit)` it is refused (E4040).

recommendation.reason: The nearest existing rule is `assert_disjoint`, a check the program asks for that stops when two names look at the same memory. It counts as both an alias check and a panic the programmer wrote, and `runtime` is exactly that. A written `@no_alias_checks` then means what it says, with no alias check left running in the function.
recommendation.checklist: 5, 6 (nearest rule `assert_disjoint`), 11 (same idea classified the same way), 15 (a written contract means only what it says), 8

items.reason: The pattern grammar produces list patterns (p03 496: `"[" [pattern {"," pattern}] ["," ".." [IDENT]] "]"`), and only a match arm can begin a line with one. GRM-40 (p03 135-137) and verdict 155 make 'every line that begins with `[` anywhere else' E0100. The verdict was put to the owner with a stray expression line (`[10, 20].len()`) and a bracket above an enum, not with a match arm. No rule anywhere gives list patterns a meaning (grep: no slice or list pattern in any rule or example), and nothing says what `..rest` binds. Taken literally, verdict 155 refuses every top-level list-pattern arm, so whether such a `match` compiles is the owner's call. The verdict cannot be widened or narrowed without him.
items.title: May a match arm's pattern be a list pattern, a line starting with [?
items.problem: A command parser matches the words of a line against list patterns: `["quit"]` for one word, `["go", dir]` for two. Each arm's line then begins with `[`, and the rule for type-parameter lines refuses every line that begins with `[` and is not directly above a function, struct or class. The pattern grammar offers list patterns, but no rule says whether such an arm compiles or what `..rest` would name.
items.example:
enum Command:
    Quit
    Go(String)
    Unknown

fn parse_cmd(words: Span[StrView]) -> Command:
    match words:
        ["quit"]:                          # exactly one word, "quit"
            return Command.Quit
        ["go", dir]:                        # two words; `dir` looks at the second
            return Command.Go(String(dir))
        _:
            return Command.Unknown

fn main():
    line = "go north"
    words = line.split(" ").collect()
    println(parse_cmd(words.as_span()))   # prints Go("north")?
items.spec_today: GRM-40 (p03 134-137): "a bracket line not directly above one of them is `E0100`: a blank line or a comment line between `[T]` and its `fn` is `E0100` too, and so is every line that begins with `[` anywhere else, one that begins with a list included (`[10, 20].len()` on a line of its own; `n = [10, 20].len()` is the way)". Patterns (p03 496): "| \"[\" [pattern {\",\" pattern}] [\",\" \"..\" [IDENT]] \"]\"". GRM-10 (p03 382-383): "A `match` whose arms use `pattern: block` is a statement; one whose arms use `pattern => expression` is an expression."

options.summary: Inside a match, a line starting with [ is an arm's pattern
options.code:
match words:
    ["quit"]:
        return Command.Quit
    ["go", dir]:
        return Command.Go(String(dir))
    ["say", ..rest]:                 # `rest` looks at the words after "say"
        return Command.Unknown
    _:
        return Command.Unknown
options.outcome: Compiles and prints Go("north"). The rule for stray `[` lines still covers every line where an item or a statement begins (`[10, 20].len()` on its own line stays E0100). A list pattern's names are read-only views like other pattern names, and `..rest` names a Span of the remaining elements.

options.summary: Keep the rule as written: list patterns only inside another pattern
options.code:
match words.len():
    1:
        if words[0] == "quit":
            return Command.Quit
        return Command.Unknown
    2:
        if words[0] == "go":
            return Command.Go(String(words[1]))
        return Command.Unknown
    _:
        return Command.Unknown
options.outcome: `["quit"]:` as an arm is E0100 ('a `[...]` line gives type parameters ...'). A list pattern may still be written nested, as in `Some(["quit"]):`.

options.summary: Remove list patterns from the language
options.code:
match words.len():
    1:
        if words[0] == "quit":
            return Command.Quit
        return Command.Unknown
    _:
        return Command.Unknown
options.outcome: A `[` in pattern position is E0100 everywhere, nested included, and the grammar loses the list pattern.

recommendation.reason: The rule's purpose holds: a stray `[` line where an item or statement starts gets one clear message. But no type-parameter line or statement can stand in a match's arm list, so refusing a correct parser there is a side effect nobody chose. The list pattern's meaning must then be written: names are views by the pattern default, and `..rest` is a Span.
recommendation.checklist: 1, 2 (correct program accepted), 7, 13 (no hidden refusal from an unrelated rule), 6

Verdict 159: 'A constructor's argument takes no word'. GRM-15 (p03 394-396) requires `owns` 'before an argument for an `owns` parameter, whatever is given', with neither exception. FN-2a (p05 115-121) also has 'whatever is given' and carries only 159 (p05 131-132, 'a constructor's argument take no word'). No rule text carries 160: it appears only in examples (p05 97, p07 151, p16 503) and the changelog (p26 2396-2397). As the rules read, the owner's own line `setup(shares mut game)` is E3028.
items.decided_by: Verdicts 159 and 160 (JOB.md 1217-1227); checklist item 16 for the sibling words.
items.lead_fix_text: GRM-15 (p03 394-396), after 'whatever is given (...)', add: 'except a value made in the call with a word that makes an owner or a link, which says what is given and takes no `owns` before it (`setup(shares mut game)` for `fn setup(owns game: shares mut Game)`, `ROSTER.push(weakref this)`), and a constructor's argument, which takes no word and works as `=` does (`Words(names=xs)`, `[FN-2a]`)'. Write the same exception into FN-2a (p05 117-118) and OWN-9 (p07 91-93). The verdict names `shares`/`shares mut` and `weakref`. By checklist 16, the same holds for `thread_shared x` and `sharedref mut x` made in the call, since 'the word that makes the value says what is given' is the verdict's own reason. The phase-3 critic should confirm that this is not a widening.

items.reason: Verdict 159 was decided on a struct's memberwise constructor (`Words(names=xs)`): 'A constructor's argument takes no word: it works as `=` does (verdict 147 does not reach a constructor)'. FN-2a (p05 131-132) and OWN-9 (p07 93-94) say it of every constructor. CLS-2 (p05 313) and STR-6 (p05 253) call a written `fn init(...)` 'the constructor'. But a written init has a first line with its own parameter words, and FN-2a and GRM-15 require `owns` before an argument for an `owns` parameter. Neither rule says which wins for `Emitter(...)` when `init(owns name: String)` exists. With a plain init parameter, the 'as `=`' reading would hand over a value the init only reads, against FN-2 (p05 112: 'A parameter with no word reads'). I.5 (p01 195) writes `Emitter("fountain")` for `init(owns name: String)`, so it depends on the answer.
items.title: Does a call of a class's own init say owns before an owns parameter's argument?
items.problem: A class writes its own `init` with an `owns` parameter, and the program builds an object with `Emitter(title)`. Every function call says `owns` before an argument its `owns` parameter takes over, while a constructor's argument takes no word and works as `=` does. A written `init` is both, so the specification says two things for this line, and nothing for an `init` whose parameter only reads.
items.example:
class Emitter:
    name: String
    rate: f32 = 100.0

    fn init(owns name: String):          # this init takes the name over
        this.name = name

class Label:
    text: String

    fn init(text: String):               # this init only reads what it is given
        this.text = copy of text

fn main():
    title = String("fountain")
    fountain = Emitter(title)            # no word, as for a struct's constructor?
    caption = String("smoke")
    sign = Label(caption)                # does `caption` end here, as `=` would end it?
    println(fountain.name)
    println(sign.text)
    println(caption)
items.spec_today: FN-2a (p05 115-118): "A call says `ref mut` before an argument the callee may change, and `owns` before one it takes over ... `take(owns xs)` for `fn take(owns xs: Array[int]):`, whatever is given"; FN-2a (p05 131-132): "`return a` and a constructor's argument take no word: they hand a value over as `=` does (`[OWN-9]`)". OWN-9 (p07 93-94): "and so does a constructor's argument, as `=` does: `w = Words(names=xs)` hands `xs` over". CLS-2 (p05 313): "`fn init(…)` is the constructor". FN-2 (p05 112): "A parameter with no word reads." I.5 (p01 176, 195): "fn init(owns name: String):" ... "fountain = Emitter(\"fountain\")".

options.summary: A written init is called like any function, with its parameters' words
options.code:
fountain = Emitter(owns title)       # init says `owns name`
sign = Label(caption)                # init only reads `text`
w = Words(names=xs)                  # a struct with no init: as `=`, no word
options.outcome: Compiles. `title` ends at the call, and `caption` stays the program's, so `println(caption)` prints smoke. `Emitter(title)` is E3028 ('say so at the call: `Emitter(owns title)`'). The overview's line becomes `Emitter(owns "fountain")`. A constructor made from the fields with no init keeps no word, as decided.

options.summary: No owns at any constructor call; the init's parameter word decides what happens
options.code:
fountain = Emitter(title)            # handed over: init says `owns name`
sign = Label(caption)                # lent: init only reads `text`
options.outcome: Compiles. `title` ends at the call and `caption` stays, so `println(caption)` prints smoke. `Emitter(owns title)` is refused ('remove `owns`'). A `ref mut` parameter of an init is still written `ref mut` at the call, as at every call.

options.summary: Every constructor argument works as `=`, whatever the init's first line says
options.code:
fountain = Emitter(title)
sign = Label(caption)
options.outcome: `title` and `caption` both end at their calls, although `Label`'s init only reads `text`, so `println(caption)` is E3040 ('`caption` was handed to `Label`').

recommendation.reason: A written init has a first line with words, like any function, and the rule that the call repeats the parameter's word (`take(owns xs)`) was chosen so that each line shows what happens to each name. A constructor made from the fields has no first line to repeat, which is why its argument works as `=`.
recommendation.checklist: 5 (one word, one meaning at every call), 6 (the exception holds only where there is no first line to repeat), 11, 15, 2

items.reason: TYP-27 (p04 57-59): 'Written as a type, `()` is `void`: a tuple type has two or more elements (ODR-071)'. Verdict 115 also calls '`(A,)`, a tuple `[TYP-27]` refuses', which the owner accepted as the reason to drop one-element tuples for variadic generics. Part III still produces them: GRM-29 (p03 243-244, 'or of one expression followed by a comma, is a tuple'), GRM-38 (p03 464, '`(e,)` a tuple'), tuple_type (p03 178, `(int,)`) and tuple_lit (p03 358). The grammar text is stale against TYP-27's settled decision. The only reading consistent with TYP-27 and PHIL-12 is that these forms are refused.
items.decided_by: TYP-27 / ODR-071 (p04 57-59, p26 359), and the reason the owner was given in verdict 115 (JOB.md 945-950).
items.lead_fix_text: GRM-29 (p03 243-244): 'An `expr_list` of two or more expressions is a tuple: `a, b = b, a` swaps, and `return x, y` returns a tuple. One expression followed by a comma (`return pos,`, `x = e,`) is `E0100`, whose help removes the comma, since a tuple has two or more elements (`[TYP-27]`).' GRM-38 (p03 464): '`(e)` without `for` is a parenthesised expression, and `(e,)` is `E0100` as above'. Grammar: `tuple_type := "(" ")" | "(" type "," type {"," type} [","] ")"` and `tuple_lit := "(" ")" | "(" expression "," expression {"," expression} [","] ")"`. Treat a one-target `target_list` with a trailing comma (`a, = f()`) the same way.

items.reason: How long the temporary lives is settled, so that part is refuted: EXP-4 (p06 20-23) says a temporary in a `while` condition that names what it holds 'lives to the end of that block only'. Ownership is not settled. GRM-44 (p03 271-272) and BRW-14 (p07 222-225) make a plain opened name a read-only view that keeps its place. BRW-12 (p07 200-202) says 'A call whose result is a new value the callee made ... hands that value to the name, which owns it'. CTL-1 (p06 132-133) hands a temporary given to `for` over with no word. `match` needs `owns` before its scrutinee to take it (GRM-15 p03 392-394). GRM-15 lists no `owns` before an `exists as` value, `opened_name`'s words (p03 220) have no `owns`, and `while Some(job) = jobs.pop():` is E0115 (GRM-19). No rule or example opens a temporary (grep 'exists as': only links and map lookups). So whether `done.push(owns job)` compiles is undecided, and the nearest rules disagree.
items.title: Does a name opened from pop()'s result own the popped value?
items.problem: A job server drains its queue with `while jobs.pop() exists as job:` and moves each finished job into another list. The name `exists as` gives is a read-only view, but a name given a value a call just made owns it, and a `for` over such a value takes it over. The specification does not say which holds for this name, or whether `owns` may be written before the value as `match owns` allows, so it is undecided whether `done.push(owns job)` compiles.
items.spec_today: GRM-44 (p03 271-272): "The name is declared there with its words, as a pattern name is (`[GRM-13]`): plain `p` is a read-only view and never changes (`E3023`)". BRW-14 (p07 222-225): "a name opened with `exists as` ... stand for what the caller, the loop, the opening or the test gave, and keep it for their whole scope". BRW-12 (p07 200-202): "A call whose result is a new value the callee made (a list it built, a list of views included) hands that value to the name, which owns it". CTL-1 (p06 132-133): "`for x in owns e:`, or a value `e` (a temporary) whose type is `IntoIterator`: hands `e` over, and each element to the loop's name". GRM-15 (p03 392-394): "before the scrutinee of a `match`, where the default is a view, so that the loop or the branches take the value over (`for x in owns xs:`, `match owns e:`)". EXP-4 (p06 20-23): "unless the condition names what it holds (`exists as`, ...) ... it lives to the end of that block only".

options.summary: Write `owns` before the value, as `match owns` does
options.outcome: Compiles and prints 2: `job` owns each popped Job. Without `owns`, `job` is a read-only view and `done.push(owns job)` is refused with this line as its help.

options.summary: A value a call made is handed to the opened name with no word, as with `=` and `for`
options.outcome: Compiles as written and prints 2: `job` owns what the Option held. A place that is opened (`if this.target exists as t:`, a map lookup, a link) stays a read-only view, as today.

options.summary: An opened name is always a view; to keep the value, copy it or use match
options.code:
while true:
    match owns jobs.pop():
        Some(job):
            job.run()
            done.push(owns job)
        None:
            break
options.outcome: `while jobs.pop() exists as job:` with `done.push(owns job)` is refused (the name only looks at the popped Job), with this `match owns` form, or `done.push(owns copy of job)`, as the help.

recommendation.reason: The language already gives a name the value a call made, with no word, at `=` (`j = jobs.pop()`) and at `for` over a temporary. The opened name is the same thing, a name for a value nothing else holds, so one rule covers all three.
recommendation.checklist: 5, 6 (nearest rules: a name given a call's new value owns it; `for` over a temporary), 2 (the queue drain compiles), 13 (no second spelling just for headers)

items.reason: `copy of` is allowed on a name after `exists as` (name_word, p03 220; BRW-14 p07 228-229, 'The one exception is a name opened `exists as copy of v`'), and on captures (p03 330). Loop names and pattern names, which GRM-42 (p03 419-421) treats as the same kind of list, have only `ref`/`ref mut` (`primary_pattern`, p03 497). No reason is given. The match form of the same map lookup (`Some(copy of v):`) cannot say what the `exists as` form says. Verdicts 66 and 67 decided `exists as copy of v` only, and nothing settles loops or patterns. Lambda parameters stay out, since FN-2 (p05 112) says 'There is no by-copy mode' for parameters.
items.title: May a loop name or a match pattern name say copy of, as exists as does?
items.problem: A combat preview wants a copy of each enemy to change, and writes `for copy of e in enemies:`, as it may write `if scores.get(name) exists as copy of v:`. Names after `exists as` may say `copy of`, but loop names and pattern names, which follow the same rules for their words, may not. The specification gives no reason, so it is unclear whether the loop is meant to be refused.
items.example:
struct Enemy:
    name: String
    hp: int

fn preview_hits(enemies: Array[Enemy], dmg: int) -> Array[Enemy]:
    preview: Array[Enemy] = []
    for copy of e in enemies:       # a copy of each enemy, the program's own
        e.hp -= dmg                 # changes the copy; `enemies` stays as it was
        preview.push(owns e)
    return preview

fn main():
    enemies = [Enemy(name=String("orc"), hp=30)]
    after = preview_hits(enemies, 10)
    println(f"{enemies[0].hp} {after[0].hp}")   # 30 20
items.spec_today: Grammar (p03 219-220): "opened_name := [name_word] IDENT ...", "name_word := \"ref\" [\"mut\"] | \"copy\" \"of\""; patterns (p03 497): "| \"ref\" [\"mut\"] IDENT". BRW-14 (p07 228-229): "The one exception is a name opened `exists as copy of v`, a copy of your own, which may be changed". GRM-42 (p03 419-421): "In a list of names declared without types of their own (a capture list, a loop's names, a pattern's names, the names after `exists as`, a lambda's parameters written without types) each word belongs to the one name after it".

options.summary: `copy of` on loop names and pattern names too, each a changeable copy of the program's own
options.code:
for copy of e in enemies:
    e.hp -= dmg
    preview.push(owns e)

match scores.get(name):
    Some(copy of v):
        v += 1                     # the map is untouched
    None:
        pass
options.outcome: Both compile, and the program prints 30 20. Each `copy of` name is a copy made by the type's `Clone`, may be changed, and its cost is shown where it is written. Lambda and function parameters still have no copy mode.

options.summary: Keep it as today: only `exists as` takes `copy of`
options.code:
for e in enemies:
    mine = copy of e
    mine.hp -= dmg
    preview.push(owns mine)
options.outcome: `for copy of e in enemies:` and `Some(copy of v):` are E0100, whose help gives the two-line form.

recommendation.reason: The same idea, a named copy of the item being looked at, then has one spelling wherever the language declares names without types. The copy is still written on the line, so nothing is copied silently.
recommendation.checklist: 5, 11 (the same idea spelled one way), 16 (an existing spelling reaching every place the same thing happens), 4

items.reason: LT-48 (p07 705, 719-721) and the grammar give `runtime` to a parameter and a variable only (`param` p03 75, `var_decl` p03 204), not to `field_decl` (p03 85). E3021's help (p17a 132) offers only 'runtime on the parameter or the variable'. So a method whose unsafe line comes from a `dyn` field cannot have the check on the field itself. The finder's claim that it cannot be written at all is not shown: BRW-12 (p07 196-199) makes `r = this.renderer` a read-only view, not a hand-over. But whether a local of bare `dyn` type may view a field (TYP-45 p04 413-414 gives `dyn I` alone to parameters, while LT-48's own example gives it to a local) is itself unclear. The owner's verdict on variables gave as its reason that 'No function is needed only to carry the word', and that reason bears on fields.
items.title: May a field say runtime, so its methods' lines are checked while running?
items.problem: A scene object holds its renderer in a field whose kind is picked at startup, and a method draws into a scratch buffer and then grows that buffer. One kind of renderer gives back the buffer it was handed, so the growing line is unsafe for that kind only. The `runtime` word that turns this into a check while running may go on a parameter or a variable, not on a field, and the error's help names only those two.
items.example:
interface Renderer:
    fn draw(scratch: Array[u8]) -> Span[u8]

struct Gpu implements Renderer:
    pixels: Array[u8]
    fn draw(scratch: Array[u8]) -> Span[u8]:
        return this.pixels.as_span()       # a view of its own pixels

struct Software implements Renderer:
    unused: int
    fn draw(scratch: Array[u8]) -> Span[u8]:
        return scratch.as_span()           # a view of the buffer it was handed

class Scene:
    renderer: owns dyn Renderer            # which kind is known only while running
    scratch: Array[u8] = []

    fn render():
        frame = this.renderer.draw(this.scratch)
        this.scratch.push(owns 1)          # unsafe if the renderer is a Software
        println(frame)

fn main():
    r: owns dyn Renderer = owns Gpu(pixels=[0]) if input() == "gpu" else owns Software(unused=0)
    scene = Scene(renderer=r)
    scene.render()
items.spec_today: LT-48 (p07 705): "`runtime` before the `dyn` or class type of a parameter or a variable lets the function do what one of the kinds that may reach that value would make unsafe"; (p07 720-721): "`runtime` is a word only right after the `:` of a parameter or a variable, before its type". Grammar (p03 85): "field_decl := [\"let\"] IDENT \":\" type [\"from\" ...] [\"guarded\" \"by\" IDENT]". E3021 (p17a 132): "(help: `runtime` on the parameter or the variable)". TYP-45 (p04 413-414): "`dyn I` alone is a parameter's type, a read-only view of the value".

options.summary: `runtime` right after a field's colon, checking every method line that uses the field
options.code:
class Scene:
    renderer: runtime owns dyn Renderer
    scratch: Array[u8] = []

    fn render():
        frame = this.renderer.draw(this.scratch)
        this.scratch.push(owns 1)          # kind of `renderer` compared here
        println(frame)
options.outcome: Compiles. With Gpu it prints the frame, and with Software it stops at the push ('`this.scratch` changes while `frame` looks at it: `renderer` is a `Software` ...'). E3021's help names the field as a third place for the word.

options.summary: No `runtime` on fields; the method names the field in a local with the word
options.code:
fn render():
        r: runtime dyn Renderer = this.renderer   # a read-only view of the field
        frame = r.draw(this.scratch)
        this.scratch.push(owns 1)
        println(frame)
options.outcome: Compiles, with the same result as (a), and the field stays `renderer: owns dyn Renderer`. Without the local line, `render` is E3021, whose help gives this local line.

recommendation.reason: The reason for allowing the word on a variable, so that no extra code is written only to carry it, holds for a field. The word then stands right after the colon of every declaration that names a value: parameter, variable, field. A local made only to carry the word is a workaround for missing syntax.
recommendation.checklist: 12 (add the syntax rather than a workaround), 5, 6, 3 (one compare at each guarded line, as for a parameter)

The grammar cannot produce it. A lambda exists only at `expression` level (p03 323), `unary := value_word unary` (p03 345) reaches `power`/`postfix_expr`/`atom`, and `atom` (p03 355-357) has no lambda. items.reason: LEX-14 (p02 71-72) says `r#name` 'uses a keyword as a name', and the FFI table (p16 194) maps 'an identifier that is an Ember keyword' to `r#`. LEX-15 (p02 109-113) says `async`, `await`, `macro`, `owned` and `self` are 'lexed as keywords' but stand outside 'the complete reserved set' of 52 (p02 90), and 'any use' of `owned`/`self` is E1010. Whether `r#owned` or `r#self` is a use of the reserved word, or a raw identifier that lifts it, is not said. C headers do use `owned` and `self` as field names. The literal reading leans toward `r#` working, but the text supports both. Thin evidence, hence low confidence.
items.title: Can a C field named owned or self be reached as r#owned?
items.problem: A C header has a struct with a field called `owned`. Ember reads `owned`, `self`, `async`, `await` and `macro` as reserved words outside its list of keywords. The specification says `r#name` lets a keyword be used as a name, and also says any use of `owned` or `self` is an error, so it is unclear whether `b.r#owned` compiles.
items.spec_today: LEX-14 (p02 71-72): "A raw identifier `r#name` uses a keyword as a name (for imported C fields such as `type`)." LEX-15 (p02 109-113): "**Reserved for a future version** (lexed as keywords; using one as a name is `E0005` ...): `async`, `await`, `macro`. **Reserved and not words of Ember** (lexed as keywords so that no program uses them as names; any use is `E1010` ...): `owned` ... and `self`". FFI table (p16 194): "an identifier that is an Ember keyword | a raw identifier `r#type`".

options.summary: `r#` names any word Ember reads as a keyword, the reserved ones included
options.code:
if b.r#owned:
    println("the buffer frees its own data")
options.outcome: Compiles, and the importer names the C field `r#owned`. The bare word keeps its error: `owned` alone is E1010 ('write `owns`'), and `async` alone is E0005.

options.summary: `r#` only for the 52 keywords; the reserved words cannot be names at all
options.outcome: `b.r#owned` is E1010. The C field is reachable only through a C function written for it.

recommendation.reason: `r#` exists so that C names Ember reserves can still be reached. A field named `owned` or `self` in a C struct is no different from one named `type`, and refusing it would push a correct program into writing C.
recommendation.checklist: 2, 5 (one rule for every word the lexer reserves), 7

jobs.notes:
I checked all 16 J1 findings against the whole of Hardened_11 (the part files), JOB.md verdicts 1-163 and OWNER-DIRECTION.md, and added one new item (J1-17). Totals: 9 owner ODRs (J1-02, 05, 07, 09, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15), 8 lead fixes (J1-01, 03, 04, 06, 08, 12, 16, 17), none fully refuted. J1-09's lifetime half is refuted (EXP-4 p06 20-23 settles it), and only its ownership half goes to the owner.

For the phase-3 consistency critic:

(1) `runtime` reaches four items: J1-01 (Part I text), J1-02 (effect kind and contracts), J1-11 (fields) and J1-17 (placement before the type's words; lambda parameters). They fit together: J1-17 puts the word right after the colon, before the whole type, and J1-11 (a) applies the same placement to fields. Whatever the owner picks in J1-02 must also replace 'the one run-time alias check there is' in EFF-9 (p10 69-70), DSJ-6 (p09 513) and the E4030 row (p17a 157), and J1-01's lead fix should be worded to match. Part VII has its own stale 'nothing is checked while the program runs' sentences (p07 8, p07 254 in BRW-1), which belong to the Part VII reviewer.

(2) LT-48's and LT-1's example `p: dyn Picker = Mine(items=[9]) if ... else Yours(items=[9])` (also in verdict 152's own words) gives a local the bare `dyn` type. TYP-45 (p04 413-414) says '`dyn I` alone is a parameter's type, a read-only view'. Whether a bare-`dyn` local may hold a made value, or must be `owns dyn Picker = owns Mine(...)`, belongs to the TYP-45/OBJ-2 reviewer. J1-11 option (b) and J1-17's text depend on it.

(3) J1-06's lead fix extends verdict 160 from `shares`/`weakref` to `thread_shared` and `sharedref mut` made in the call, on checklist 16 and the verdict's own reason ('the word that makes the value says what is given'). If the critic reads that as widening, it becomes a one-line owner question.

(4) J1-07 (a) would change I.5's line to `Emitter(owns \"fountain\")`. CLS-2's E2108 help ('write `fn init(name: String):`', p05 328-329) gives an init whose `this.name = name` stores a read-only parameter in an owning field, which does not compile under any option. Wording it is the lead's job, but the help must give a line that compiles (checklist 9), and it depends on J1-07's answer.

(5) J1-09 (b) and J1-07 (a) do not conflict. J1-09 is about a name given a value a call made (no word, as with `=` and `for` over a temporary). J1-07 is about a call repeating its callee's parameter word. J1-09 (b) leaves `match` over a temporary as it is (GRM-15 requires `match owns`). That inconsistency between `match` and `for` over a temporary predates these items and is for the Part VI reviewer.

(6) J1-03 is routed to the lead on PHIL-12 alone, with no verdict behind it. If the critic holds that a contradiction between two rules is always the owner's, it becomes an ODR with options (a) E0104 or (b) a comment.

(7) J1-05 (a) would also require writing what list patterns mean, which no rule says today: names are read-only views under the pattern default, and `..rest` is a Span. The `primary_pattern` production cannot express `[..rest]` alone (it needs a leading comma).

jobs.name: Types (Part IV)

items.reason: OWN-8 (p07 167-171) says every Copy type has Clone 'so b = copy of a works', and verdict 68 says a Copy type always works with copy of, E2116 never given for it. The same rule (p07 182-183), TYP-36 (p04 694-695) and the E2116 row (p17a 85) then name StrView and Span[T], both always Copy by the marker table (p04 576), as E2116. A @derive(Copy) struct holding a StrView is a Copy struct (STR-3 says copy of works on every one) and a view type (TYP-36 refuses it). No verdict says what copy of gives before a view: verdict 10 says the copy word copies the thing itself, never a link; verdict 79 says a link inside a struct is copied as a link; verdict 93 has copy of t on a loop view of a String give a copy of the text. The rules leave the result of copy of w open: refused, a String, or another view.
items.title: What does `copy of` give before a text view, or a Copy struct holding one?
items.problem: A lexer's token holds a view into the source text and is marked Copy; the programmer writes `copy of tok` and `copy of w` for a StrView. One rule says every Copy type works with `copy of`; the same rule's list of refusals names StrView and Span, which are Copy, and refuses every struct holding a view. Nothing says whether the copy is a String of its own or another view of the same text.
items.example:
@derive(Copy)
struct Token:                            # a lexer's token: a view into the source text
    text: StrView
    line: int

fn main():
    src = String("let x = 1")
    tok = Token(text=src.as_str(), line=1)
    t2 = copy of tok                     # a Copy struct that holds a view: allowed?
    println(t2.text, t2.line)
    w = src.as_str()                     # a StrView, which is always Copy
    w2 = copy of w                       # a String of its own, another view, or refused?
    src.clear()                          # a reshape: ends every view into `src`
    println(w2)                          # fine if `w2` is a String; refused if it is a view
items.spec_today: OWN-8 (p07 167-171): "`copy of x` makes a copy of the thing itself, by its type's `Clone` ...: of a class object, a new object (`p2 = copy of player`); for a `shares` or `sharedref mut` link, a copy of its target. Every `Copy` type has `Clone` (`@derive(Copy)` gives it), so `b = copy of a` works for a `Point` marked only `Copy`." OWN-8 (p07 171-174): "A value that holds links is copied field by field ... each link is copied as a link to the same target." OWN-8 (p07 182-183): "* a value of a view type (`StrView`, `Span[T]`, a struct holding a `ref mut` field): "`w` is a view of `line`'s text; to make your own copy write `String(w)`"". TYP-36 (p04 693-695): "every `Copy` type is `Clone`; before what it cannot copy as itself (a `weakref` link, a value of a view type, a type with no `Clone`) it is `E2116`." Marker table (p04 576): Copy "always for scalars, `ref T`, `Span`, `StrView`, ...". STR-3 (p05 234-235): "it gives `Clone` too, so `copy of` works on every `Copy` struct". TYP-36 table (p04 710): `StrView` Clone ✓, Copy ✓.

options.summary: `copy of` before a view copies what it views (a StrView gives a String, a Span[T] an Array[T], a `ref T` a T); a view inside a struct is copied as one more view of the same place, as a link inside a struct is copied as one more link.
options.code:
t2 = copy of tok     # a new Token whose `text` views the same source text
w2 = copy of w       # a String of its own, as String(w) makes
options.outcome: Compiles. Prints `let x = 1 1`, then `let x = 1`: `w2` is its own text, untouched by `src.clear()`. `copy of` before a `ref mut` view or a `MutSpan`, or a struct holding one, stays E2116 (no second changing view can be made).

options.summary: A Copy view is copied bit for bit, as `=` copies it: `copy of w` is another StrView of the same text and `copy of tok` another Token; only views that are not Copy (`ref mut`, `MutSpan`) are E2116.
options.code:
t2 = copy of tok     # a Token, the same bits
w2 = copy of w       # another StrView of `src`'s text
options.outcome: Lines 9-12 compile and print `let x = 1 1`; `println(w2)` after `src.clear()` is refused (E3060: `w2` views `src`, which `clear` reshaped). For text of your own the programmer writes `String(w)`.

options.summary: As the refusal list says today: `copy of` before a StrView, a Span or any struct holding a view is E2116, Copy or not; the general sentence is narrowed to say so.
options.code:
t2 = tok             # `=` copies a Copy struct
w2 = String(w)       # text of your own
options.outcome: `copy of tok` and `copy of w` are E2116 ("`w` is a view of `src`'s text; to make your own copy write `String(w)`"); with the lines above the program compiles and prints the same as A.

recommendation.reason: It is the one reading that keeps every decision at once: the copy word copies the thing itself, never a link, before a bare link or view; a link or view inside a struct is copied as one more link; and every Copy type works with `copy of`. Nothing is refused that has a meaning, and the result is never a hidden second view.
recommendation.checklist: 1 (copy of means a copy of your own), 2 (correct programs accepted), 5 (copy of means one thing for links and views alike), 6 (the same rule as shares/sharedref mut links, bare and in fields), 11 (reuses the struct-field link rule already written)

items.decided_by: Verdict 163 (an owned interface value on a variable, shown as `Box[dyn Renderer]`), TYP-45's mapping of `Box[dyn I]` to `owns dyn I` (verdict 19's words in types) and `dyn I` alone only as a parameter's type, verdicts 74/85/97 (`owns` on the making line).

items.reason: TYP-21 (p04 745-746) says a type has an operator only by implementing its interface, and (p04 751-752) that String implements none of the operator interfaces, while TXT-11 (p15 163-164) gives String a `+` that 'takes `a` over' and a `+=`. So String's `+` is a path no interface declares, a String fails an `Add` bound while `a + b` on it compiles, and TYP-21's own desugaring (p04 741-742: 'both operands read in place') is broken by a `+` that takes its left side over with no `owns` written, which verdicts 84, 145 and 147 require of every hand-over. No verdict decides String's `+`.
items.title: Is String's `+` an ordinary `Add`, and does it take the left text over?
items.problem: A HUD builds labels with `label + "!"` and `label += "10"`, and a generic helper bounded by `Add` adds a suffix to any text type. Today String's `+` is built in, outside the operator interfaces every other type goes through, so the helper refuses a String; and `label + "!"` silently hands `label` over, so a later `println(label)` is refused though the line never says `owns`.
items.example:
[T: needs Add[StrView, Output = T]]
fn with_suffix(a: T, b: StrView) -> T:          # any type that `+` can extend with text
    return a + b

fn main():
    label = String("hp: ")
    label += "10"                                # appends in place
    shown = label + "!"                           # today: takes `label` over, with no word
    println(label)                               # today: E3040, `label` was handed over
    tagged = with_suffix(shown, "?")              # today: E2040, String implements no Add
    println(tagged)
items.spec_today: TYP-21 (p04 741-742): "Operators desugar to these interfaces for non-scalar operands; `a + b` calls `Add.add(a, b)` with both operands read in place." TYP-21 (p04 745-746): "A type has an operator only by implementing its interface (`[TYP-40]`); a method that merely shares the name is not one." TYP-21 (p04 751-752): "`bool`, `char` and `String` implement none of them (`String`'s `+` takes its left operand over, `[TXT-11]`)." TXT-11 (p15 163-164): "`a + b` for `a: String, b: StrView` takes `a` over and returns it extended; `s += t` appends. `StrView + StrView` is `E2040` whose help is an f-string."

options.summary: String implements `Add[StrView, Output = String]`, reading both sides and giving a new String (as Python and C++'s `std::string` `+` do), and `AddAssign[StrView]`, appending in place. Its `+` goes through the interfaces like every other type's.
options.code:
shown = label + "!"          # a new String; `label` stays
label += "10"                # appends in place, no new String
options.outcome: Compiles; prints `hp: 10`, then `hp: 10!?`. `with_suffix` accepts a String. Each `+` makes one new String (one allocation and copy); `+=` in a loop costs what C++'s `append` costs.

options.summary: String implements `Add` with its `add` taking its object over (Rust's way, no copy), and the line says so with the word every hand-over uses.
options.code:
shown = (owns label) + "!"   # `label` handed over and extended in place
label = String("hp: ")       # `label` must be given a value again before use
options.outcome: `shown = label + "!"` without `owns` is refused, its help giving `(owns label) + "!"`; `println(label)` after it is E3040. No copy is made. `with_suffix` must take `owns a: T`.

options.summary: Keep String's `+` built in, outside the operator interfaces, taking its left side over with no word.
options.code: shown = label + "!"          # `label` silently handed over
options.outcome: As today: `println(label)` after it is E3040 and `with_suffix(shown, "?")` is E2040.

recommendation.reason: It removes the only operator that bypasses its interface and the only hand-over not written with `owns`, and matches TYP-21's own 'both operands read in place'. `+=` keeps the fast in-place path; B is faster for long `+` chains but makes every label line read `(owns label) + ...`.
recommendation.checklist: 2 (correct generic code accepted), 4 (nothing handed over without a word), 5 (one operator rule for every type), 10 (Python's and C++'s meaning), 13 (no hidden built-in path)

items.reason: TYP-5 (p04 100-101) says the rules compose 'only where stated (widening after range erasure, and rule 11 after rules 1–4)'. So the Option wrap (rule 11) does not follow rule 8 (a value to `owns dyn I`), rule 10 (a function to a callable type), rule 12 (a known number widened) or rule 7 (reading through a view). `slot: Option[owns dyn Weapon] = owns Sword(...)` and `on_hit: Option[Handler] = log_hit` are refused while the same lines without Option compile. No spec example writes either (grep `Option[owns dyn`, `Option[fn`), and no verdict covers composition.
items.title: Does a value become `Some` after any other conversion, or only after four?
items.problem: A game slot holds an optional weapon and an optional hit callback. `weapon: owns dyn Weapon = owns Sword(edge=4)` and `on_hit: OnHit = log_hit` compile, but the same lines into `Option[...]` fields are refused, because wrapping in `Some` is allowed only after the first four conversions. The same holds for `cap: Option[u64] = n` after `n = 5`, which compiles without the Option.
items.example:
interface Weapon:
    fn damage() -> int

struct Sword implements Weapon:
    edge: int
    fn damage() -> int:
        return this.edge * 2

type OnHit = fn(int)

fn log_hit(dmg: int):
    println("hit for", dmg)

struct Slot:
    weapon: Option[owns dyn Weapon] = None
    on_hit: Option[OnHit] = None

fn main():
    s = Slot()
    s.weapon = owns Sword(edge=4)     # `owns Sword` to `owns dyn Weapon`, then to Option: refused today
    s.on_hit = log_hit                 # a function to `OnHit`, then to Option: refused today
    n = 5
    cap: Option[u64] = n               # a known number widened, then to Option: refused today
    if s.weapon exists as w:
        if s.on_hit exists as f:
            f(w.damage())
    println(cap)
items.spec_today: TYP-5 rule 11 (p04 89-91): "a value of type `T` to `Option[T]`, as `Some(value)`, where `T` is not itself an `Option`: one level only, so nothing becomes `Option[Option[T]]`". TYP-5 (p04 100-102): "Each rule composes with the others only where stated (widening after range erasure, and rule 11 after rules 1–4). Nothing converts implicitly to or from `bool` or `char`." Rules 8, 10, 12 (p04 84-86, 88, 92-97): a value to an interface keeping its word; a function to a callable type; a known whole number to another whole-number type.

options.summary: Wrapping in `Some` follows any one of the other conversions: whatever a plain `T` place accepts, an `Option[T]` place accepts as `Some` of it. Still one level only.
options.code:
s.weapon = owns Sword(edge=4)
s.on_hit = log_hit
cap: Option[u64] = n
options.outcome: Compiles; prints `hit for 8`, then `Some(5)`.

options.summary: As today: `Some` follows only the first four conversions; the other lines write `Some(...)`.
options.code:
s.weapon = Some(owns Sword(edge=4))
s.on_hit = Some(log_hit)
cap: Option[u64] = Some(n)
options.outcome: The unwrapped lines are E2020; with `Some(...)` written the program compiles and prints the same as A.

recommendation.reason: `x: T = v` and `x: Option[T] = v` then accept the same values, with no list of which conversion may come first; the one-level limit, the part that prevents surprises, stays.
recommendation.checklist: 2 (correct programs accepted), 5 (one rule for T and Option[T] places), 6 (no exception the rule's wording does not need), 7 (general over every conversion)

items.reason: THR-8 (p11 43-50) and the marker table (p04 577) list what is not Send (shares, shares mut, a weakref to one, thread-bound values) and which views are Send (`ref T`/`Span` when T is ThreadShared, `ref mut T`/`MutSpan` when T is Send), never `sharedref mut T`; THR-9 (p11 64-65) and the table (p04 578) leave it out of ThreadShared's list too. Inferred by components, a struct holding one would count as Send and ThreadShared. THR-13 (p11 149-151) only says what scoped tasks may do with a `sharedref mut` target and that an unscoped thread never holds one; verdict 3 says 'on two threads, only with a lock', and verdict 77 lets scoped tasks reduce through two links. Those cover tasks that use the caller's variables (THR-11 p11 388-389, no Send needed), not a link handed through a channel. The finder's fix (not Send) keeps verdict 77, since scoped tasks reach the link without Send.
items.title: May a struct holding a `sharedref mut` link be sent to another thread?
items.problem: A camera's `Watcher` holds a changeable link to the player that other holders share. The programmer sends a Watcher through a channel to a scoped task that changes `target.hp` while `main` changes `p.hp`. Neither the Send nor the ThreadShared list names this link, so whether the channel accepts a Watcher, and so whether this program races, is not decided.
items.example:
import std.thread
from std.sync import channel

class Player:
    hp: int = 10

struct Watcher:                                   # a camera's changeable link to the player
    target: sharedref mut Player

fn main():
    p = Player()
    tx, rx = channel[Watcher](capacity=1)         # is Watcher Send?
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): rx.recv().expect("gone").target.hp -= 1)   # the task writes p.hp
        tx.send(owns Watcher(target=sharedref mut p)).expect("gone")
        p.hp -= 2                                 # main writes p.hp while the task may too
    println(p.hp)
items.spec_today: Marker table (p04 577): Send "inferred: every component is `Send`, so nothing reachable from the value is a one-thread owner (`shares`, `shares mut`), a `weakref` link to one, or bound to its thread ...; `ref T` and `Span[T]` are when `T` is `ThreadShared`, `ref mut T` and `MutSpan[T]` when `T` is `Send`". THR-9 (p11 64-65): "`ref mut T`, `Cell`, `UnsafeCell`, raw pointers, `shares T`, `shares mut T`, and a `weakref` link to a value that is not `thread_shared` are not." THR-13 (p11 149-151): "a `sharedref mut` target: a scoped task changes it directly only where neither another task nor the parent may touch it before the join, or by a reduction (`E7007`); an unscoped thread never holds one (`E7015`)." LT-46 (p07 688-689): "on two threads it is changed only under a lock, through `Atomic`, or by a reduction from scoped tasks".

options.summary: A `sharedref mut` link is neither Send nor ThreadShared, as a `shares mut` owner is: it is never handed or sent to another thread. Scoped tasks still reach it by using the caller's variables, where the compiler sees what each task changes (two tasks doing `a.target.hp -= 1` and `b.target.hp -= 2` still add up).
options.code: tx, rx = channel[Watcher](capacity=1)   # refused
options.outcome: Refused (E7015: a `Watcher` holds `target`, a changeable link other names share on this thread; let the task use `w` where it is instead of sending it). No race is possible.

options.summary: A `sharedref mut T` link is Send when T is, as `ref mut T` is, and goes only to scoped tasks; never ThreadShared.
options.code: tx, rx = channel[Watcher](capacity=1)   # accepted
options.outcome: Compiles as written unless the compiler follows the link through the channel to see that the task changes `p.hp` while `main` does, which no rule says; without that, the task and `main` write `p.hp` at the same time (a data race).

recommendation.reason: `ref mut` may cross to a task because it is the only name for its place; a `sharedref mut` link never is, so it belongs with `shares mut`. A refuses a race when compiling and loses nothing the reductions need.
recommendation.checklist: 2 (refuses only what is wrong), 3 (decided when compiling), 6 (the nearest rule, `shares mut`'s), 8 (a forgotten lock is a refusal, not a race)

items.reason: Verdict 115 says 'a function or type takes any number of types' and names as uses a tuple's interfaces written once for every size, `zip` over any number of iterators, the ECS view, and `Event[int, String]` with handlers `fn(int, String)`; verdict 116 chose C++'s dots. TYP-47 (p04 495-510) defines a pack only on a function: its last parameter, `Cs...` among type arguments, `values...` in a call. It does not say a struct or class may take a pack, nor that `fn(Ts...)` or `(Ts...)` may be written, and the library's own `View[Cs...]` (p04 497, ECS-4 p12 223-225) and `zip` (p15 34) cannot be written by its rules. Packs on types are the owner's (verdict 115); what a tuple of a pack is when the pack holds one type or none is not decided anywhere: TYP-27 (p04 58-59) says a tuple type has two or more elements, and verdict 115 began from the complaint that one type became `(A,)`, a tuple TYP-27 refuses.
items.title: What is a tuple of a pack's types when the pack holds one type, or none?
items.problem: A CSV reader keeps one row as a struct with a field `cells: (Ts...)`, one cell per column type, and a game event keeps handlers of type `fn(Ts...)`. With two or more types the tuple is an ordinary tuple. With one type the language has no one-element tuple, and with none no empty one, so `Row[int]` has a field whose type is undecided. Both options let a struct, class or enum take a pack and spell it in a function type, a tuple, or once per type (`ref Pool[Cs]...`), as C++ does.
items.example:
[Ts...]
struct Row:                                    # one parsed CSV row, one cell per column type
    cells: (Ts...)                             # a tuple of the pack's types

[Ts...]
class Event:                                   # a game event handing several values to each handler
    handlers: Array[fn(Ts...)] = []            # a function type over the pack

    fn fire(values: Ts...):
        for h in this.handlers:
            h(values...)

fn on_hit(dmg: int, who: StrView):
    println(who, "takes", dmg)

fn main():
    hit = Event[int, StrView]()
    hit.handlers.push(owns on_hit)
    hit.fire(5, "orc")                         # prints: orc takes 5
    pair = Row[int, StrView](cells=(7, "ann"))  # two types: an ordinary tuple
    one = Row[int](cells=7)                    # one type: is `cells` the int 7, or a one-element tuple?
    println(pair.cells.1, one.cells)
items.spec_today: TYP-47 (p04 495-498): "`...` after a type parameter's name makes it a **pack**: any number of types, none included (`[Cs...]` above `fn view() -> View[Cs...]:`)." TYP-47 (p04 500-501): "`Cs...` among type arguments spells the pack's types out (`View[Cs...]`), `values...` among a call's arguments passes the values on". TYP-27 (p04 58-59): "Written as a type, `()` is `void`: a tuple type has two or more elements (ODR-071)." ECS-4 (p12 223-225): "A view takes any number of component types, with no limit (`reg.view[Position]()`, ...; variadic generics, `[TYP-47]`)". STD (p15 34): "`zip(a, b, …)` (any number of iterables, `[TYP-47]`; stops at the shortest)".

options.summary: A tuple of a pack holding one type is that type itself, and of none is `void`: a tuple always has two or more elements, as written tuples do. A tuple's interfaces are written once for every size from two up (`[A, B, Ts...]` above `extend (A, B, Ts...) implements Display:`).
options.code:
one = Row[int](cells=7)          # `cells` is an int
println(one.cells + 1)           # 8
options.outcome: Compiles; prints `ann 8` with the line above (`ann 7` as the example stands). `zip(xs)` of one list gives its items plainly, and `reg.view[Position]()` gives each Position with no tuple around it.

options.summary: A tuple of a pack is a tuple of any size, one and none included, distinct from the type itself and from `void`; a one-element tuple then needs a spelling of its own, which the language does not have today.
options.code:
one = Row[int](cells=(7,))       # a one-element tuple, a new spelling
println(one.cells.0 + 1)         # 8
options.outcome: Compiles only once `(7,)` is added to the language; `Row[int](cells=7)` is E2020. `zip(xs)` of one list gives one-element tuples.

recommendation.reason: It keeps the tuple rule that exists (two or more elements), adds no spelling, and gives exactly what the pack design was asked for: one component type with no tuple around it.
recommendation.checklist: 5 (a tuple means one thing everywhere), 11 (no new spelling of a tuple), 12 (no syntax missing), 13 (no special one-element tuple only packs make)

items.reason: TYP-22 (p04 785-789) makes an interface unusable as `dyn` only for a static method, a method returning `Self` by value, or a generic method; a method taking a `Self` parameter passes. Nothing says what `a.overlaps(b)` does when two `dyn` values are of different kinds. TYP-36 (p04 691-693) settles this for Eq only ('values of two different kinds are never equal', a method-table entry) and says nothing of Ord, so sorting an `Array[owns dyn Shape]` with `interface Shape: needs Ord:` is undecided too. No verdict.
items.title: Can an interface whose method takes another `Self` be used as `dyn`?
items.problem: A physics engine's `Collider` interface has `fn overlaps(other: Self) -> bool`, implemented by Circle and Aabb, each comparing with its own kind. A function taking two `dyn Collider` values then calls `a.overlaps(b)` with a Circle and an Aabb. The rules neither refuse the interface as `dyn` nor say what that call does.
items.example:
interface Collider:
    fn overlaps(other: Self) -> bool             # takes another value of the same kind

struct Circle implements Collider:
    x: float
    r: float
    fn overlaps(other: Circle) -> bool:
        d = this.x - other.x
        return d * d < (this.r + other.r) * (this.r + other.r)

struct Aabb implements Collider:
    min_x: float
    max_x: float
    fn overlaps(other: Aabb) -> bool:
        return this.min_x < other.max_x and other.min_x < this.max_x

fn check(a: dyn Collider, b: dyn Collider) -> bool:
    return a.overlaps(b)                         # a Circle may be handed an Aabb here

fn main():
    println(check(Circle(x=0.0, r=1.0), Aabb(min_x=0.5, max_x=2.0)))
items.spec_today: TYP-22 (p04 785-789): "An interface is usable as `dyn` only if every method has an object (none is a `static fn`), does not return `Self` by value (methods marked `where Self: needs Sized` excepted), and is not generic, except over a type parameter used only as the type of a parameter that views its value". TYP-36 (p04 691-693): "`owns dyn I` compares when `I` requires `Eq` (`interface Shape: needs Eq:`, a method-table entry as for `Clone`): values of two different kinds are never equal, and two of one kind compare their contents."

options.summary: A method with a `Self` parameter makes the interface unusable as `dyn` (E2050), as returning `Self` does; `where Self: needs Sized` on that method keeps the rest usable. Eq keeps its stated answer (two kinds are never equal, which is true); an interface requiring Ord is not usable as `dyn`, since no order between two kinds is true.
options.code:
interface Collider:
    fn overlaps(other: Self) -> bool where Self: needs Sized   # only for known kinds
options.outcome: As written, `check`'s `dyn Collider` is E2050 ("`overlaps` takes another `Self`, and two `dyn Collider` values may be of different kinds"). With the marked line it compiles; `a.overlaps(b)` on `dyn` values is refused, and the program calls it on known kinds or writes a method taking `other: dyn Collider`.

options.summary: Allowed; the call checks that both values are of one kind and stops the program otherwise, one compare of type indices.
options.code:
fn check(a: dyn Collider, b: dyn Collider) -> bool:
    return a.overlaps(b)
options.outcome: Compiles; stops: "`a.overlaps(b)` on line 17: `a` is a `Circle` and `b` an `Aabb`". A Circle with a Circle runs.

recommendation.reason: It decides the program when compiling, with the same rule already applied to a method returning `Self`; Eq stays the one case where an answer across kinds is true.
recommendation.checklist: 3 (compile time first), 6 (the nearest rule, returning Self; Eq's exception exists because its answer is true), 8 (no stop the programmer did not see coming)

items.reason: TYP-14 (p04 286-287) and TYP-5 rule 7 name only references and `owns T` as read through where a T is wanted. IV.11 (p04 854-855) strips one level of `shares`/`shares mut`/`thread_shared` for method calls only, IV.6a reads a field through one (`reader.hp`, p04 386), and RC-2a/RC-2b (p08 136-139) speak of passing a shared value to a plain parameter as a view, which assumes the read-through without stating it. TYP-36 (p04 688-692) and TYP-39 (p04 727-728) give `ref T` and `owns T` the interfaces of T; nothing gives them to shared owners, so `println(scores)`, `a == b` and a shared map key are undecided. Rust's `Rc` compares contents while C++'s `shared_ptr` compares addresses, so `==` has a real choice.
items.title: Does a shared owner read, print and compare as the value it owns?
items.problem: A leaderboard shares its score list with the HUD (`shares mut`). The programmer passes the shared list to a function that reads a list, prints it, and compares it with another list. The language lets a method call see through `shares mut`, but says nothing for an argument, for printing, or for `==`, and two languages answer `==` differently (Rust compares contents; C++ compares which value).
items.example:
fn total(scores: Array[int]) -> int:             # reads a list of scores
    return scores.iter().sum()

class Leaderboard:
    scores: shares mut Array[int]                # shared with the HUD

fn main():
    scores = shares mut [10, 20]
    board = Leaderboard(scores=shares mut scores)
    board.scores.push(owns 30)                   # a method call sees through `shares mut`
    println(total(scores))                       # an argument: read through to the list?
    println(scores)                              # printed as the list?
    others = shares mut [10, 20, 30]
    println(scores == others)                    # the lists compared, or which list?
items.spec_today: TYP-14 (p04 286-287): "A reference, and an `owns T`, is read through wherever a `T` is wanted — a field access, a method call, an operand, an argument to a plain parameter." IV.11 (p04 854-855): "Strip views from `recv`'s type `R` (`ref`, `ref mut`, `sharedref mut`), and one level of `owns`, `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared`." TYP-36 (p04 688-689): "A read-only view `ref T` implements `Eq`, `Ord`, `Hash`, `Display` and `Debug` as `T` does". TYP-36 (p04 691): "Two `owns` values compare with `==` when what they hold does". TYP-39 (p04 727-728): "An `owns T` and a `Cell[T]` show as the `T` they hold". RC-2a (p08 136-137): "Passing a shared value to a parameter that is not `owns` (`x: shares T` reads the caller's shared value for the call)."

options.summary: A `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` owner reads as the value it owns wherever that value is wanted, as an `owns T` does: an argument, an operand, and `Eq`, `Ord`, `Hash`, `Display` and `Debug` as the value's type has them. `is` still asks whether two owners own the same value; a class object's `==` stays identity, its own.
options.code:
println(total(scores))
println(scores)
println(scores == others)
println(scores is others)
options.outcome: Compiles; prints `60`, `[10, 20, 30]`, `true`, `false`.

options.summary: Read through for arguments and printing as in A, but `==` and hashing of two owners compare which value they own, as C++'s `shared_ptr` does.
options.code: println(scores == others)
options.outcome: Compiles; prints `60`, `[10, 20, 30]`, `false`. To compare the lists the programmer writes a function with two plain parameters; `==` and `is` then mean the same thing on owners.

recommendation.reason: The owner word says who owns the value, not what it is, so the value behaves the same under every owner word; `is` already exists for 'the same value', so `==` keeps one meaning.
recommendation.checklist: 5 (one meaning of == and of each owner word), 6 (the nearest rule, owns T's), 11 (`is` already spells identity), 13 (no owner word left on a side path)

items.reason: TYP-44 (p04 808-813) and DSP-6 (p08 306-312) give `cast s as Circle` on `owns dyn` and `shares dyn` values, and say a cast of a place is a place bound read-only or `ref mut`, never handed over. OWN-13 (p07 135-136) says a word before a value acts on the object it names, and the grammar (p03 316) puts `owns` and `cast … as` at one level, so `owns cast s as Circle` parses, but no rule says what it gives: the same block as an `owns Circle` (Rust's `Box::downcast`), a refusal, or something else. A cast of a temporary is not covered either. No verdict (25 and 27 decided the spelling only).
items.title: Can a downcast hand over the concrete value from an `owns dyn` value?
items.problem: A scene holds `Array[owns dyn Shape]`, and a pass keeps only the circles, as `Array[owns Circle]`. The language lets a downcast give a read-only or changing view of the Circle, but not take it over, so there is no line that moves the Circle out without copying it.
items.example:
interface Shape:
    fn area() -> float

struct Circle implements Shape:
    r: float
    fn area() -> float:
        return 3.14159 * this.r * this.r

struct Square implements Shape:
    side: float
    fn area() -> float:
        return this.side * this.side

fn keep_circles(owns shapes: Array[owns dyn Shape]) -> Array[owns Circle]:
    circles: Array[owns Circle] = []
    for s in owns shapes:                        # each shape handed over to `s`
        if s is Circle:
            circles.push(owns cast s as Circle)  # hand the Circle over in its own block?
    return circles

fn main():
    scene: Array[owns dyn Shape] = [owns Circle(r=1.0), owns Square(side=2.0)]
    kept = keep_circles(owns scene)
    println(kept.len())
items.spec_today: TYP-44 (p04 808-813): "`cast s as Circle` gives the `Circle`, on `owns dyn` and `shares dyn` values too, and stops the program when `s` is not one ... A cast of a place is a place: the name bound from it is read-only unless written `ref mut` (`pool = ref mut cast this.pools[k] as Pool[T]`)". DSP-6 (p08 306-309): the same. OWN-13 (p07 135-136): "Before a value, a word acts on the object the value names (for a link or an owner, on its target)".

options.summary: The words before a value act on a cast as on any value: `owns cast s as Circle` takes `s` over and gives its block as an `owns Circle`, with no copy and no new block; `shares cast s as Circle` on a `shares dyn Shape` is one more owner, typed `shares Circle`. A cast of a temporary gives the value, held as the temporary was.
options.code: circles.push(owns cast s as Circle)
options.outcome: Compiles; prints `1`. A wrong kind stops the program as any cast does (inside `if s is Circle:` it cannot).

options.summary: A cast only gives a view; to keep the Circle the program copies it.
options.code: circles.push(owns copy of cast s as Circle)   # Circle needs Clone
options.outcome: `owns cast s as Circle` is refused ("a cast gives a view of `s`'s Circle; to keep one write `owns copy of cast s as Circle`"); with the copy it compiles and prints `1`, at one new block and one copy per circle, and `s`'s block is freed.

recommendation.reason: The words before a value already mean the same before every value, a cast included, and A costs nothing where C++ and Rust cost nothing; B forces a copy only because the line has no meaning for the word.
recommendation.checklist: 5 (each word one meaning before every value), 7 (no ceiling: no copy forced), 11 (reuses `owns`/`shares` before a value), 12 (no case exempted for missing syntax)

items.reason: IV.5 (p04 340-342) declares two library functions named `ref_to_ptr`, differing only in the parameter's word and the result type. TYP-26 (p04 867-868) says there is no overloading and two functions of one name in one scope are E1030, with exceptions only for operator implementations and `extend` blocks of different types; neither covers this, so the library has an overload a program cannot write. The same idea is already spelled by the safe cast `r as *T` / `r as *mut T` (p04 342-344). ODR-075 (p26 363) kept the name before the redesign; no verdict.
items.title: How is a pointer made from a reference: one library name, two, or the cast?
items.problem: FFI code turns a reference into a raw pointer. The library offers two functions both named `ref_to_ptr`, one read-only and one changing, which the language forbids a program to declare. The safe cast `ref x as *T` already does the same thing.
items.example:
fn main():
    pos = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
    p = ref_to_ptr(pos)                     # a *Array[float]: the read-only function
    q = ref_to_ptr(ref mut pos)             # a *mut Array[float]: a second function of the same name
    r = ref pos as *Array[float]            # the safe cast already spells the same thing
    println(p == r)
items.spec_today: IV.5 (p04 340-344): "`ref_to_ptr(r: T) -> *T` and `ref_to_ptr(ref mut r: T) -> *mut T`, called `ref_to_ptr(x)` and `ref_to_ptr(ref mut x)`, keep the predecessor's name. An explicit `r as *T` is also safe when the pointee type is unchanged and the cast does not strengthen mutability: `ref T` to `*T`, or `ref mut T` to `*T` or `*mut T`." TYP-26 (p04 867-868): "There is no overloading: two functions of one name in one scope are `E1030`, except operator-interface implementations and `extend` blocks for different types."

options.summary: Two names, one function each.
options.code:
p = ref_to_ptr(pos)
q = ref_to_mut_ptr(ref mut pos)
options.outcome: Compiles; `ref_to_ptr(ref mut pos)` is refused, its help giving `ref_to_mut_ptr(ref mut pos)`.

options.summary: One spelling, the safe cast that exists; `ref_to_ptr` goes.
options.code:
p = ref pos as *Array[float]
q = ref mut pos as *mut Array[float]
options.outcome: Compiles; `ref_to_ptr(pos)` is E1010, its help giving `ref pos as *Array[float]`.

options.summary: Functions of one name may differ by a parameter's word, for programs too.
options.outcome: Compiles; the call's word picks the function. Overloading by word becomes part of the language.

recommendation.reason: The idea already has a spelling, the safe cast, so the second spelling goes and the library keeps no overload a program cannot write.
recommendation.checklist: 5 (said once), 11 (the existing spelling kept, the older one removed), 13 (no library-only path)

items.reason: TYP-43 (p04 586-588) limits the hand-written `unsafe extend T implements Send:` to 'a struct or enum of its own package that holds a raw pointer'; THR-8 (p11 54-55) says 'the author of a type that holds a raw pointer declares it' and calls a class object Send when its fields are (p11 48). A class wrapping a C handle is then never Send by TYP-43 and may be by THR-8, with no reason given for leaving classes out (a `shares` owner of the class stays one-thread whatever its fields are). No verdict.
items.title: May a class holding a raw pointer be vouched `Send` with `unsafe extend`?
items.problem: A renderer wraps a GPU texture handle, a raw pointer, in a class and hands the object to a loader thread. A struct holding the same pointer may be declared Send by the programmer, who vouches for it; one rule says only a struct or enum may, another says any type.
items.example:
import std.thread

class GpuTexture:                          # wraps a driver handle
    handle: *mut u8
    size: int

# SAFETY: the driver's texture handles may be used from any thread
unsafe extend GpuTexture implements Send:
    pass

fn main():
    tex = GpuTexture(handle=null[*mut u8](), size=0)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns tex: tex.size)   # needs GpuTexture to be Send
    println(h.join())
items.spec_today: TYP-43 (p04 586-588): "A program writes `Send` by hand, for a struct or enum of its own package that holds a raw pointer, only as `unsafe extend T implements Send:` with no members and a `# SAFETY:` note". THR-8 (p11 48): "class objects are `Send` when every component is". THR-8 (p11 54-55): "the author of a type that holds a raw pointer declares it with `unsafe extend T implements Send:` and a `# SAFETY:` note".

options.summary: A struct, enum or class of the program's own package may be vouched Send this way.
options.code:
unsafe extend GpuTexture implements Send:
    pass
options.outcome: Compiles; prints `0`.

options.summary: Only a struct or enum; a class holding a raw pointer is never Send, and the program wraps the pointer in a struct it vouches for.
options.code:
struct TexHandle:
    raw: *mut u8

# SAFETY: the driver's texture handles may be used from any thread
unsafe extend TexHandle implements Send:
    pass
options.outcome: `unsafe extend GpuTexture implements Send:` is refused; with `handle: TexHandle` in the class it compiles and prints `0`.

recommendation.reason: The vouching is about the pointer, not about the kind of type holding it; nothing true about classes needs the exception, and THR-8 already says 'a type'.
recommendation.checklist: 5 (one rule for every type), 6 (no exception without a reason), 11 (THR-8's wording kept)

items.title: May `as` convert a `bool` or a `char` to any integer type?
items.problem: A parser turns a digit character into its value with `c as int`, and a renderer packs flags with `visible as u8`. The conversion list gives only `char` to `u32` and nothing for `bool`, without saying the list is complete, so whether these lines compile is not written.
items.example:
fn digit_value(c: char) -> int:                  # a parser's digit
    return (c as int) - ('0' as int)             # char to int: allowed?

fn pack_flags(visible: bool, lit: bool) -> u8:   # a renderer's flag byte
    return (visible as u8) | ((lit as u8) << 1)  # bool to u8: allowed?

fn main():

options.code:
return (c as int) - ('0' as int)
return (visible as u8) | ((lit as u8) << 1)
options.outcome: Compiles; prints `7 1`.

options.summary: The list is complete: only `char → u32` and `u8 → char`; everything else with a bool or char is E2020.
options.code:
return ((c as u32) as int) - (('0' as u32) as int)
return (1 if visible else 0) | ((1 if lit else 0) << 1)

jobs.notes:
Patterns:
(1) Closed lists that drop a sibling: String in `using` (J2-02), `sharedref mut` in the Send/ThreadShared lists (J2-06), shared owners in read-through and the interface lines (J2-09), classes in TYP-43 (J2-12), conversions in TYP-5's composition and TYP-6 (J2-05, J2-14). Each recommendation states the rule by its property. Reviewers of Parts VII, VIII, IX and XI should check the same lists there.
(2) A library facility that the rules do not let a program write, i.e. a hidden path: String's `+` (J2-04), `ref_to_ptr`'s overload (J2-11), `View[Cs...]` and `zip` over packs on types (J2-07). Related, flagged but not filed: TYP-46 does not say how any type, std or a program's own, declares that it takes `using` (so even with J2-02 option A a game engine's own SlotMap cannot take one). The critic should decide whether that goes to the owner after J2-02.
(3) J2-06 departs from the finder's reasoning but keeps its fix. Scoped tasks reach a `sharedref mut` link by using the caller's variables (THR-11, p11 388-389), which needs no Send, so marking the link not Send keeps the reductions of verdict 77. If a Part XI checker finds that scoped-task use does require Send/ThreadShared, J2-06's option A must say the scoped path stays as THR-13 states it.
