jobs.name: Declarations and expressions (Parts V-VI)

items.reason: The contradiction is real. TYP-45 (p04:413-415) says "`dyn I` alone is a parameter's type, a read-only view of the value". IV.9 (p04:781-782) and the type table (p04:18, "`dyn I` (a parameter's type)") say the same. LT-1 (p07:551-552), LT-48 (p07:708-709, 717-718) and Annex H's note on verdict 163 (p26:2479) still write a local `p: dyn Picker = Mine(items=[9]) if input() == "m" else Yours(items=[9])`. Verdict 163's own line was `renderer: runtime Box[dyn Renderer] = Box(Gpu(...)) if ... else Box(Software(...))`, and p04:427 says `owns dyn I` replaces `Box[dyn I]`. So the 0.9.15 spelling of the owner's line is `owns dyn`. The bare local is the lead's respelling, and the verdict did not decide it. Verdicts 152 and 163 settled where `runtime` goes, not whether a bare `dyn` local exists. Caveat: verdict 152's text itself shows `p: dyn Picker = ...`. If the lead reads that as the owner choosing a bare `dyn` local (a view of a value made on the line), this becomes an owner question.
items.decided_by: TYP-45 (`dyn I` alone is a parameter's type; p04:413-415, also p04:18 and p04:781) together with verdict 163, whose line `Box[dyn Renderer]` is `owns dyn Renderer` in 0.9.15 (p04:427).
items.lead_fix_text: In [LT-1] (p07:551-552), [LT-48] (p07:708-709 and 717-718) and Annex H's verdict-163 note (p26:2479), write the local as TYP-45 and verdict 163 give it: `p: owns dyn Picker = owns Mine(items=[9]) if input() == "m" else owns Yours(items=[9])`, and on the `runtime` line `p: runtime owns dyn Picker = owns Mine(items=[9]) if input() == "m" else owns Yours(items=[9])`. The `owns` on each made value is TYP-45's: a value made for a place that owns it alone. `show(p)` stays as it is, since a plain `dyn Picker` parameter reads the value.

items.reason: Nothing settles it. FN-2a (p05:132-134) and STD-19 (p15:316-317) lend a function from a variable to any standard-library function, with no word. THR-10 (p11:173-175) says the spawned thread "may outlive the function that started it", so a loan of `main`'s `push_a` to it cannot be kept, and CLO-4/CLO-7 refuse a function value that outlives what it uses. No rule lets `thread.spawn(owns push_a)` hand a named function over: FN-2a says such a function "takes no word". Yet CLO-12 (p06:333) and GRM-28 (p03:253) show `a = thread.spawn(push_a)` as working code, and verdict 51 says both forms are allowed. So no spelling is decided to compile. The same gap hits a std adapter kept past its line (`return xs.iter().map(h)`). Verdict 150 decided the loan for `for_each`, which runs the function during the call. It does not say what happens when the std function keeps it.
items.title: Does `thread.spawn(push_a)` lend a local function, hand it over, or need `owns`?
items.problem: The spec lets a long thread body be written as a local function and started by name, `a = thread.spawn(push_a)`. It also says a function from a variable given to a standard-library function is lent and takes no word. But `thread.spawn` keeps the function on a thread that may outlive `main` (C++: a `std::thread` given a reference to a local lambda). A loan cannot be kept, and the spec never says that `thread.spawn(owns push_a)` is allowed. So the spec decides no spelling that compiles. The same goes for an adapter kept past its line, `return xs.iter().map(h)`.
items.example:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Mutex

class Log:                                    # a log any thread may add to
    lines: Mutex[Array[String]] = Mutex([])

    fn add(line: StrView):
        with g = this.lines.lock():           # the lock guards the list
            g.push(owns String(line))

fn main():
    log = thread_shared Log()                 # one owner per thread that holds it
    fn push_a() thread_shared log:            # a local function holding its own owner of `log`
        log.add("a")
    a = thread.spawn(push_a)                  # lent? handed over? or must it say `owns push_a`?
    push_a()                                  # may main still run it here?
    a.join()
items.spec_today: FN-2a (p05:132-134): "A function from a variable given to a standard-library function that takes one is lent and takes no word: after `xs.iter().for_each(h)`, `h` is the caller's still". STD-19 (p15:316-317): "A function from a variable is lent to the call and takes no word". THR-10 (p11:173-175): "`thread.spawn` runs a function on a new thread, which may outlive the function that started it. It takes ... `pub fn spawn(owns f: thread_shared fn() -> R) -> JoinHandle[R]:`". GRM-15 (p03:394-395): `owns` is required "before an argument for an `owns` parameter, whatever is given". CLO-12 (p06:331-333): "may be passed by its name ... (`fn push_a() thread_shared log:` with the body `log.push("a")`, then `a = thread.spawn(push_a)`)". GRM-28 (p03:251-253) gives the same `a = thread.spawn(push_a)`.

options.summary: A loan stays the default; `owns` before a named function hands it over to any `owns` parameter, the library's included.
options.code:
a = thread.spawn(owns push_a)             # handed over: the thread owns it now
    a.join()

# for_each still borrows with no word:
#     h = fn(x: int): println(x)
#     [1, 2].iter().for_each(h)
#     h(5)
options.outcome: Compiles and prints `a`. A later `push_a()` is E3040, because `push_a` was handed over. `thread.spawn(push_a)` with no word is refused, because the thread may outlive `push_a`, and the help gives `thread.spawn(owns push_a)`. `for_each(h)` keeps borrowing and `h(5)` prints 5. `return xs.iter().map(owns h)` works the same way.

options.summary: With no word, a named function is handed over when the library function keeps it past the call.
options.code:
a = thread.spawn(push_a)                  # no word: handed over, since spawn keeps it
    a.join()
options.outcome: Compiles and prints `a`. A `push_a()` after the spawn is E3040, though nothing in that line says `push_a` was given away. `for_each(h)` still borrows, so the same-looking call means two things depending on what the library function does with it.

options.summary: A named function is always lent, so `thread.spawn` cannot take one; write the function inside the call.
options.code:
a = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared log: log.add("a"))   # the only form that compiles
    a.join()
options.outcome: `thread.spawn(push_a)` is refused, because the thread may outlive `push_a`, and its help writes the function into the call. A local function can never start a thread, and the spec's `thread.spawn(push_a)` examples go.

recommendation.reason: One rule: a lent function is like a view and cannot outlive the variable, and `owns` at a call hands over, as it does for every other argument. Both ways of writing a long thread body keep working, and the hand-over is written in the line.
recommendation.checklist: 2 (the local-function form, allowed by the owner, compiles); 4 and 5 (the hand-over is written, and `owns` means one thing at every call); 6 (no new exception: the loan with no word stays as decided); 9 (the refusal gives a line that compiles); 13 (no hidden rule that depends on what the callee does with the function).

items.reason: Both halves are owner verdicts, and the spec carries both. Verdict 150: "A function passed from a variable to a standard-library function is borrowed; the caller keeps it", which names the standard library only (N36 was built "for the standard library's functions only; a program's own `owns` parameters ... take a function value over"). Verdict 147: "An argument for an `owns` parameter says `owns` at the call, whatever is passed". In the spec, FN-2a (p05:119-122 and 132-134) and STD-19 (p15:316-317) say so. So `each_score(scores, show)` is E3028, and `each_score(scores, owns show)` hands `show` over, after which `show(1)` is E3040. The inconsistency the finder names (one first line, `owns f: F`, meaning lent in std and handed over in a program) is the owner's own split. Whether `for_each(owns h)` is allowed in std is answered by option A of J3-02.
items.decided_by: Verdicts 147 and 150 (with 158), carried in FN-2a and STD-19.

items.reason: FN-2a (p05:134-136) exempts any argument "for a `Mutex`, `RwLock` or `Atomic` parameter, or a channel end" from every call word. GRM-15 (p03:394-395) requires `owns` before an argument for an `owns` parameter "whatever is given". The two disagree for `fn start_worker(owns rx: Receiver[Job])`. Verdict 3 (run 4) gave the exemption for `ref mut` only, with the reason that "`ref mut` ('only me for the whole call') would be untrue for them". At that time no call said `owns`. Verdict 147, the later one, makes `owns` at the call general ("whatever is passed"). Handing over a receiving end is a real hand-over, since the caller's `rx` ends, so verdict 3's reason does not reach it. No spec example gives an `owns` lock or channel parameter.
items.decided_by: Verdict 147 ("An argument for an `owns` parameter says `owns` at the call, whatever is passed"), read with verdict 3's own reason, which concerns `ref mut` only.
items.lead_fix_text: In FN-2a (p05:134-136), write: "An argument for a plain or `ref mut` `Mutex`, `RwLock` or `Atomic` parameter, or for a channel end, takes no word, since its own 'only me' is the lock's block (`E3028`: ...). An argument for an `owns` parameter of these types takes `owns` as every such argument does: `start_worker(owns rx)` for `fn start_worker(owns rx: Receiver[Job]):`."

items.reason: CLS-3 (p05:331) gives a memberwise constructor only to "a class with no `init` and no base class". CLS-10 (p05:332-334) and its example assume the base declares `init`. CLS-4 (p05:344-345) says "A derived `init` MUST call `super.init(…)` exactly once". Nothing says what `super.init(…)` calls when the base has no `init`, or whether it takes named arguments and leaves out defaulted fields. A grep of `super.init` finds only CLS-4, CLS-11 and the C++-base rules (p21:124-129).
items.title: When a base class has no `init`, what does `super.init(…)` call?
items.problem: A base class with no `init` gets the constructor made from its fields (memberwise). A derived class that has a field with no default must write an `init`, and that `init` must call `super.init(…)`. The spec never says whether `super.init(…)` then calls the base's memberwise constructor, or whether the program is an error.
items.example:
open class Widget:                      # a UI base class with no `init` of its own
    id: int                             # no default: whoever builds a Widget sets it
    visible: bool = true

class Button(Widget):
    width: int                          # no default, so Button must declare `init`

    fn init(id: int, width: int):
        this.width = width              # its own field first, as two-phase construction asks
        super.init(id=id)               # Widget has no `init`: what does this call?

fn main():
    b = Button(7, 120)

items.reason: EXP-4 (p06:16-25) gives exact lifetimes to the temporaries of an expression statement, an `if`/`elif`/`while` condition, a `with` binding and a `for` iterable. It names no rule for a `match` subject. A `match` statement is not an expression statement, so the only rule left is DRP-3 (p07:848), "Temporaries drop at the end of the statement that created them". That keeps a lock guard from the subject alive through every arm. So `if JOBS.lock().is_empty():` releases the lock before its block, while `match owns JOBS.lock().pop():` holds it while an arm runs, and no reason is given for the difference. GRM-15 (p03:393-394) speaks of the subject's ownership only, not of its temporaries.
items.title: Does a lock taken in a `match` subject stay held while the arms run?
items.problem: A program pops a job from a locked queue in a `match` header and runs the job in the arm. For an `if` or `while` condition, the spec drops the temporaries (here, the lock's guard) before the block runs. For a `match` it says nothing, so the general rule keeps the guard until the whole `match` ends. If the job takes the same lock again, the program is refused, or hangs through C (Rust's well-known trap with a lock in a `match`).
items.example:
from std.sync import Mutex

struct Job:                                     # one unit of work
    id: int

static JOBS: Mutex[Array[Job]] = Mutex([])      # the queue every worker takes work from

fn pending() -> int:
    with g = JOBS.lock():                       # takes the queue's lock
        return g.len()

fn run_next():
    match owns JOBS.lock().pop():               # the guard is a temporary of this header
        Some(job):
            println(job.id, pending())          # takes JOBS's lock again: is it still held?
        None:
            pass

fn main():
    with g = JOBS.lock():
        g.push(owns Job(id=1))
    run_next()

A temporary bound by `with` lives to the end of the `with` block; one created by a `for` iterable lives to the end of the loop." DRP-3 (p07:848): "Temporaries drop at the end of the statement that created them (`[EXP-4]`)."

items.title: Does `for t in toks:` over a named iterator use it up, or continue after `break`?
items.problem: A parser splits a line into words, walks them until `--`, breaks, and walks the rest in a second loop over the same iterator. The spec says what a `for` does with a collection, with a value made on the line and with `owns`. It does not say what it does with a local that holds an iterator: hand it over (so the second loop is an error), or advance it in place, as calling `toks.next()` would (so the second loop goes on after `--`, as in Python).

fn parse_args(line: StrView) -> (Array[String], Array[String]):
    flags: Array[String] = []
    files: Array[String] = []
    toks = line.split_whitespace()          # a local holding an iterator over the words
    for t in toks:                          # handed over, or advanced in place?
        if t == "--":
            break
        flags.push(owns String(t))
    for t in toks:                          # does this go on after `--`?
        files.push(owns String(t))
    return (flags, files)

fn main():
    flags, files = parse_args("-v -q -- a.txt b.txt")
    println(flags, files)

    id: int
    open: bool = true

options.outcome: `fall` compiles under `@noalloc`; `drag` is E4001, whose help gives a type parameter (`[F: needs fn(ref mut Particle)]`) or the loop body written out.

options.summary: Keep the "may": the compiler decides whether a one-word state is inline.
options.code: slow: fn(ref mut Particle) = fn(ref mut p) copy of k: p.vy *= k
options.outcome: Whether `drag` compiles under `@noalloc` depends on the compiler that builds it.

recommendation.reason: Allocation becomes a rule of the language that the source shows, as PHIL-2 demands, and small function values cost no more than a C function pointer plus one word.
recommendation.checklist: 3 (decided when compiling, cheapest form); 7 (production-ready: the same answer on every compiler, with no unstated ceiling); 8 (a function value that grows past the limit is refused under `@noalloc`, never allocates in secret); 9.

items.reason: The rules decide it: the program is refused. EXP-10 (p06:86-88) reads `a` "as `[GRM-13]` reads a place it does not hand over: a `Copy` value inside is copied and any other viewed", and that view only reads. For a non-`Copy` value, FN-9 (p05:145-146) says "A method that may change its object is not called through a `p` that only reads it (`E3023`)". For a `Copy` value the method runs on a temporary copy whose change is lost, which EXP-5 (p06:35-38) makes E2140 ("A method that may change its object, called on a temporary ... when that change is the call's only effect"). Both cases are refused, and the two error codes are the lead's business. The way to write it, `if this.weapon exists as ref mut w: w.reload()`, exists (GRM-44). Whether `?.` should change things in place is a new design question, not a gap.

MOD-1 (p05:15-16) makes a type named like a built-in type E1032 "except a name `[MOD-5]` lets a declaration shadow (`int`, `float`, `Never`, `StrView`)". The list in brackets gives examples, and the exception is every name MOD-5 lets a declaration shadow. MOD-5 (p05:62) says "A local declaration or explicit import shadows a prelude name", and `Map`, `Set`, `Range`, `Cell` and `Error` are prelude names (p05:53-57). So `struct Map:` compiles and shadows the prelude's `Map`. Only names that are not prelude names, such as `i32`, `bool` and `char`, are E1032.

STR-1 (p05:227-228) knows two cases, "It is `pub` iff every field is `pub`". With a `pub(package)` field the constructor is "not pub", which leaves open whether it is private to the module or visible in the package. MOD-2 (p05:19-21) has three levels, and MOD-7 (p05:34-37) decides only `pub(read)`, which makes the constructor private to the module. The finder's second question (IFC-6 for a `pub(package)` generic function) is settled: MOD-2 defines `pub` as "visible to dependants", and MOD-9 (p05:38-41) states the reason as the package's edge, which a `pub(package)` function does not cross. So a `pub(package)` function counts as not `pub` and may leave its bounds out.
items.title: May another module of the package build a struct whose fields are `pub(package)`?
items.problem: A network package declares a public `Packet` with one public field and one field visible only inside the package. Another module of the same package builds a `Packet` with its constructor. The spec says the constructor is public only when every field is public, and it never says whether the constructor is otherwise private to its module or visible in the package.
items.example:
# net/packet.em
pub struct Packet:                     # a packet the network layer builds
    pub kind: u8
    pub(package) seq: u32              # seen only inside the `net` package

# net/send.em, a module of the same package
from net.packet import Packet

pub fn first() -> Packet:
    return Packet(kind=1, seq=7)       # may this module call the constructor?
items.spec_today: STR-1 (p05:226-228): "Every struct has a **memberwise constructor** ... It is `pub` iff every field is `pub`." MOD-2 (p05:19-21): "Items are private to their module unless marked. `pub(package)` makes an item visible within the package; `pub` makes it visible to dependants. Using an item, field or constructor that is not visible is `E1052`". MOD-7 (p05:36-37): "Construction is a write, so a `pub(read)` field makes the memberwise constructor private to the module."

options.summary: The constructor gets the narrowest visibility among its fields: here `pub(package)`.
options.code: return Packet(kind=1, seq=7)       # allowed anywhere in the `net` package
options.outcome: Compiles. Outside the package, `Packet(kind=1, seq=7)` is E1052, naming `seq`. A `pub(read)` field keeps the constructor private to its module, as today.

options.summary: Two cases only: every field `pub` gives a `pub` constructor; anything else is private to the module.
options.outcome: `Packet(kind=1, seq=7)` in send.em is E1052. It compiles once `packet.em` adds the `static fn` above and send.em calls it.

recommendation.reason: Whoever may see every field may build the value, which is the same reasoning that already makes a `pub(read)` field's constructor private. It uses the visibility levels MOD-2 already has.
recommendation.checklist: 2 (accepts the correct program); 5 and 6 (one rule across MOD-2's three levels, consistent with MOD-7); 12 (no builder function forced only because a level is missing from STR-1).

items.reason: STR-5 (p05:247-248) says, in a paragraph about "A struct or enum", that `Copy`, `Ord`, `Hash`, `Default` and `Display` "are never implicit". ENM-3 (p05:280-282) makes a unit-only enum `Copy`, `Eq`, `Ord`, `Hash` and `Debug` automatically. ENM-4 (p05:283-284) shows that STR-5's derive rules are meant for payload enums ("`[STR-5]`'s implicit derives apply to it"), and ENM-3 is the specific, older rule for unit-only enums. So `a < b` on `Phase` compiles, and STR-5's sentence only lacks the exception. A rare corner stays open: whether `@no_derive(Ord)` may opt a unit-only enum out of ENM-3. STR-5 lets `@no_derive` take only `Eq`, `Debug` and `Clone`. The lead may raise it on its own if wanted.
items.decided_by: ENM-3, the specific rule for unit-only enums (unchanged), with ENM-4 placing STR-5's derive rules on payload enums.
items.lead_fix_text: In STR-5 (p05:247-248), write: "`Copy`, `Ord`, `Hash`, `Default` and `Display` are never implicit, except that a unit-only enum is `Copy`, `Ord` and `Hash` automatically (`[ENM-3]`), and are requested with `@derive(…)` or written by hand."

items.reason: IFC-4 (p05:421-422) gives `T: Add[Output = T]` as the place where a binding is written. Verdict 109 ("What a type parameter needs is written after `needs`") and the bound rule (p04:460, "A bound without `needs`, or needs joined with `+`, is `E0100`") make that line E0100. The example does not follow the spelling the owner chose.
items.decided_by: Verdict 109 (`needs` before every bound), carried in p04:460.

jobs.notes:
Summary: 10 owner ODRs (J3-02, 05, 06, 07, 09, 10, 12, 13, 15, 18), 5 lead fixes (J3-01, 04, 08, 19, 20), 4 refuted (J3-11, 14, 16, 17), 1 already decided (J3-03). Nothing was merged and I added no new finding. One slip to report: early on I ran one Python one-liner to check the top-level type of phase1.json, before noticing that brief.md forbids Python; after that I only read and searched files.

Patterns across items:
(1) Call words (J3-02, J3-03, J3-04). Every exemption to `owns` at the call was worded for one case: the loan of a named function to the standard library (verdict 150) and no word for lock and channel types (verdict 3). Each now meets `owns` being required for every `owns` argument (verdict 147). J3-02's option A and J3-04's lead fix push the same way: `owns` before an argument always means a hand-over, and a loan with no word stays only where the owner granted it. If the owner picks B or C for J3-02, J3-04's lead fix still holds, because it rests on verdict 147 alone. J3-03 is the owner's own split between the standard library and the program's own functions; it is a candidate to show beside J3-02 if the lead thinks the owner would want to revisit it, but it is not a gap.
(2) Headers that test a value. J3-07 (a `match` subject's temporaries end like an `if` condition's) and J3-09 (a `for` over a named iterator advances it in place) both reuse the nearest existing rule: EXP-4 for J3-07, and the unmarked object of a method call for J3-09.
(3) Constructors (J3-05, J3-06, J3-18). These are three separate questions about the memberwise constructor and `init`. The recommendations agree on one model: a class with no `init` has its memberwise constructor as its `init` (J3-05 A); a default exists for constructions that leave the field out (J3-06 B); the constructor's visibility follows its fields (J3-18 A).

For the phase-3 consistency critic, recommendations that touch other parts' rules:
- J3-06 B changes CLS-2 (p05:314-316, classes) as well as STR-6. Check it against CLS-11 (two-phase construction) and Part VIII's object rules, and against MOD-9's "a fact worked out from a body never changes what a line does". Here the fact comes from the type's own `init` body, so whether a field default with a side effect runs depends on that body.
- J3-13 A changes TYP-38 (Part VI) for lists. It affects PHIL-2 (p01:49-50, string literals allocating) and `@noalloc` code with a list literal that has no type (E4001 in Part X), and STD-11's examples.
- J3-15 A fixes the capacity named in PHIL-2 (p01:51) and CLO-10. It touches Part X's Alloc rules (E4001) and `ember inspect --alloc` (CLI).
- J3-12 A widens EXP-9 and its operator-table row (p06:60). The E2150 row (p17a:96) already agrees with it. TYP-45's link kinds (p04:405-412) and CLS-6's block lifetime (p05:354-355) are what make it safe.
- J3-02 A edits FN-2a, STD-19 (Part XV), CLO-12 and GRM-28 (Part III); the examples become `thread.spawn(owns push_a)`.
- J3-01's lead fix edits LT-1 and LT-48 (Part VII) and Annex H (p26:2479). Part VII/VIII checkers should look for other bare `dyn I` locals and fields.
- J3-04's lead fix edits FN-2a only; BRW-15 and THR's plain-parameter rules stay as they are.

Lead's (not ODRs; wording from the finder's notes, confirmed): CLO-6's help `call_twice(fn(): consume(copy of s))` and CLO-16's help "pass `fn() thread_shared count: ...`" lack the `owns` that verdicts 147 and 158 require, so their lines do not compile. IFC-5 (p05:437) still says "the type of a `ref` or `ref mut` parameter". FN-6's list of what callable types are compared by omits `once` and `extern "C"`. CORO-10 says "`@export`ed". J3-19's leftover corner, whether `@no_derive(Ord)` may opt a unit-only enum out of ENM-3, is low and is left to the lead.

jobs.name: Ownership and borrowing (Part VII)

items.reason: The finder read [BRW-8] as "a large Copy parameter goes by address". It says the opposite. p07 403-410: "Two kinds are passed as a copy instead: ... a plain parameter of a `Copy` type that holds no `Cell` or `UnsafeCell`, which goes in registers when it is no larger than two pointers". Every plain `Copy` parameter is a copy; "registers when no larger than two pointers" only says how a small copy travels. 0.9.10's [BRW-8] and ODR-024 (p26 312: "a borrowed parameter is passed by address except a view or a `Copy` value holding no `Cell`") read the same way. [OWN-7] (p07 160-161) agrees: a `Copy` value "is duplicated bit for bit by `=` and on use". So `take_hit(PLAYER)` prints 10 at every size and on every target. `append_moved(ref mut keys, keys[0], 1.0)` is accepted for every `Copy` type, the way [BRW-3] (p07 288-290) accepts the `int` case: "`v[0]` is copied in before the call". The ABI choice really cannot be observed. What remains is the same question for a plain parameter that is not `Copy`, which is passed by address; that is J4-14 (new). [FN-1]'s "such as a small `Copy` value in registers" (p05 80-81) could be read more narrowly; that is the lead's wording to fix.

Verdict 68 answered one question: does a `@derive(Copy)` struct, which has no `Clone` written, work with `copy of`? ("so `b = copy of a` for a `Point` marked only `Copy` makes a copy of your own; E2116 is not given for it"). The spec carries that answer: [OWN-8] p07 169-170 and [STR-3] p05 234-235. A `StrView` or `Span` is refused for a different reason, and the spec says so three times: [OWN-8] p07 176 and 180-181 ("`copy of` is `E2116` before what it cannot copy as itself: ... a value of a view type (`StrView`, `Span[T]`, ...)"), [TYP-36] p04 694-695, and the E2116 row at p17a 85. The reason: `copy of` copies the thing a value names (VII.1 p07 21-22; [OWN-13] p07 135-136, "a word acts on the object the value names"), and the text a `StrView` names has no type of its own, so the help gives `String(w)`. For `r: ref Player`, `copy of r` copies the player ([OWN-13]; [TYP-14] p04 286-288: a reference is read through). To keep a view after handing one over, write `kept = w` first: `=` copies a `StrView` ([OWN-9] p07 95-96). Then `words.push(owns w)`. The help E3028 gives for a view-type `owns` parameter ("take(owns copy of xs)") does not compile there. That is message wording, the lead's.

Not settled. [GRM-13] limits its read-only rule to names "in a place it does not take over", and it gives `match owns e`'s names their parts. [CTL-1] gives each element to the name of `for x in owns e`. [BRW-18]'s own fix hands such a name on (`for u in owns upper: counts.insert(owns u, owns 0)`). But [BRW-14], [BRW-15], [CTL-1]'s last sentence, [OWN-3] and VII.1 do not leave these names out: they make every loop, pattern and parameter name read-only and never given a new value. Changes through an `owns` parameter appear in the spec (spec line 3937, `child.parent = weakref this`), but `=` on one is E3023 by [BRW-14]'s words. No verdict covers this.
items.title: May a name that owns its value, like `for job in owns jobs`, be changed?
items.problem: Some names take their value over without a word in front of the name: an `owns` parameter, the name in `for job in owns jobs:`, a branch name under `match owns e:`. The rules that make plain names read-only do not leave these names out: `=` on a parameter or loop name is refused, a plain loop name changes nothing, and `b = job` makes a view. Other rules say these names own their values and may hand them on. So `job.retries += 1`, and `name = String("unnamed")` on an `owns` parameter, are refused by one reading and allowed by another.
items.example:
struct Job:
    name: String
    retries: int

fn retry_all(owns jobs: Array[Job]) -> Array[Job]:
    again: Array[Job] = []
    for job in owns jobs:              # the loop takes the list over: `job` owns each Job in turn
        job.retries += 1               # change the Job this round owns: allowed, or "a plain loop name changes nothing"?
        again.push(owns job)           # hand it on (as `for u in owns upper:` hands `u` on)
    return again

fn label(owns name: String) -> String:
    if name.len() == 0:
        name = String("unnamed")       # a new value for the String this function owns: allowed, or "= on a parameter" refused?
    return name

fn main():
    jobs: Array[Job] = [Job(name=String("build"), retries=0)]
    done = retry_all(owns jobs)
    println(done[0].retries)           # 1
    println(label(owns String("")))    # unnamed
items.spec_today: [BRW-14] p07 222-225: "A parameter, a loop name, a pattern name and a name opened with `exists as` ... stand for what the caller, the loop, the opening or the test gave, and keep it for their whole scope: `=` on one is `E3023`". [BRW-15] p07 235-236: "A plain parameter, a plain loop, pattern or opened name, and a plain local that holds a view never change what they name or what it leads to". [CTL-1] p06 132-133: "`for x in owns e:` ... hands `e` over, and each element to the loop's name"; p06 141-142: "A plain loop name changes nothing". [GRM-13] p03 507: "A name a pattern binds in a place it does not take over is a read-only view"; p03 512-513: "`match owns e:` hands `e` over, and each name of the branch that runs owns its part." [OWN-3] p07 72-74: "Where `a` is itself a view (a plain parameter, a loop, pattern or opened name, a local holding a view), `b = a` makes `b` a read-only view of what `a` views". [BRW-18] p07 467: "`for u in owns upper: counts.insert(owns u, owns 0)`".

options.summary: A name that took its value over is its owner, as a local is: it may be changed and given a new value.
options.outcome: Compiles; prints 1, then unnamed. `kept = job` inside the loop would hand `job` over, as `=` does for any owner. The read-only rules cover only names that look at someone else's value.

options.summary: Such a name may be changed through, but never given a new value with `=`.
options.code:
fn label(owns name: String) -> String:
    return String("unnamed") if name.len() == 0 else name
options.outcome: `job.retries += 1` compiles. `name = String("unnamed")` is refused (E3023: "`name` is the string the caller handed over and stays that string for the whole call"), so `label` must be written as above.

options.summary: As the read-only rules read today: a loop or branch name is read-only whatever its source.
options.outcome: `job.retries += 1` under `for job in owns jobs:` is refused (E3023), and `name = ...` is refused as in B. A loop or branch that owns its names may only hand them on, and the list is changed in place with `for ref mut job in jobs:`.

recommendation.reason: A name that took its value over owns it, exactly as a local does. The rules for `match owns e:`, and the hand-on of `for u in owns upper:`'s `u`, already say so. The read-only rules exist for names that look at a value someone else owns.
recommendation.checklist: 2 (accepts the correct loop and function), 5 (`owns` means yours for parameters, loops and branches alike), 6 (nearest rule: a local owner may be changed and given a new value), 13 (no second kind of owner)

items.reason: Not settled. [BRW-12] makes `body = req.body` a view, and its list of words that say otherwise has no `owns`. [GRM-15] lists where `owns` is written. That list includes `b = owns n` for a value `=` would copy, a use that is optional and changes the meaning, but not `b = owns p.part`. E0109 does not cover it either, since `=` with a part does not hand anything over. [OWN-11] and [EXP-6] let a part be handed over on its own, but name only push, return, a field and an `owns` argument. Verdict 78 decided a field hand-over "as in Rust" on a `push`, not on `=`. No spec example writes `x = owns p.f`.
items.title: Does `body = owns req.body` move a field out into a local?
items.problem: A function that owns a request wants to move its body into a local and keep using the path, as Rust's `let body = req.body;` does. `body = req.body` makes a read-only view. The spec lists where `owns` may be written (an `owns` argument, a loop's or match's source, `b = owns n` for a number or another copied value) and this line is not among them, yet no rule refuses it either.
items.example:
struct Request:
    path: String
    body: String

fn take_body(owns req: Request) -> String:
    body = owns req.body         # take the body out of the request: a hand-over, or not a place `owns` is written?
    println(req.path)            # the path stays usable, as after `names.push(owns req.body)`
    return body

fn main():
    r = Request(path=String("/upload"), body=String("hello"))
    println(take_body(owns r))
items.spec_today: [BRW-12] p07 196-198: "A name bound to a part (`n = p.name`, `boss = enemies[0]`) ... is a read-only view of it: never a hand-over"; p07 202-206: "A word before the part says otherwise: `ref mut` ...; `copy of` makes a copy of your own ...; the link words make a link (`[OWN-13]`); and `ref` states the default". [OWN-11] p07 117-119: "A part of a struct value stored somewhere else (`push`, `return`, a field, an `owns` argument) is handed over on its own". [GRM-15] p03 389-398: "`owns e` hands `e` over. It is written, and required, on the line that makes a value for a place that owns it alone ...; before the iterable of a `for` ... and before the scrutinee of a `match` ...; before an argument for an `owns` parameter ...; and in `b = owns n` for a value `=` would copy (a number, a `bool`, a `StrView`, `[OWN-9]`)".

options.summary: `owns` before a part on an `=` line hands the part over into the local.
options.code:
body = owns req.body
println(req.path)
return body
options.outcome: Compiles; prints /upload, then hello. Until `req.body` is given a new value, `req.body` and `req` used whole are refused (E3040), as after `names.push(owns req.body)`. A field of a type with a `drop`, or of a class object, is refused as for any part (E3010, E3013).

options.summary: Refused: a part goes into a local only as a view or a copy; taking it out is `mem.take`.
options.code: body = mem.take(ref mut req.body)   # leaves an empty String in req.body
options.outcome: `body = owns req.body` is refused ("`=` with a part makes a view; to take the body out write `body = mem.take(ref mut req.body)`"). The `mem.take` line compiles and prints the same, and leaves an empty string in the request.

recommendation.reason: The owner already decided that a field may be handed over on its own, as in Rust. `owns` before a value on an `=` line already hands over a copied value (`f = owns flag`), so the same word hands a part over into a local, with no default value written into a request that is about to end.
recommendation.checklist: 2, 5 (one meaning of `owns` on every line), 11 (the language's own word, written before a value as it already is), 12 (adds the missing place instead of sending programs to `mem.take`)

items.reason: A real contradiction. [RC-1] and E2122's row allow `thread_shared` before a local; [OWN-13], [THR-1] and E7017's row refuse it. [RC-1]'s sentence came in with 0.9.15_Hardened_2's write-up of verdict 103, and that verdict speaks only of `shares` from one-owner places. E7017 comes from the redesign's rule R3 (run 4), which is not an owner verdict. So no owner decision covers `thread_shared` of a local.
items.title: May a local object be shared between threads after it is made?
items.problem: A program builds a settings object on the main thread, then shares it with a worker: `shared = thread_shared s`. The rule on owners says all three sharing words may be written before a local of the function. The rule on threads, with its own error, says `thread_shared` goes only before a new value or before one already shared between threads.
items.example:
class Settings:
    port: int = 0
    verbose: bool = false

fn main():
    s = Settings()
    s.port = 8080                       # filled in while `main` is its only owner
    shared = thread_shared s            # share the finished settings between threads: allowed, or refused?
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared shared: println(shared.port))
    h.join()                            # 8080
items.spec_today: [RC-1] p08 106-108: "`shares x`, `shares mut x` and `thread_shared x` are written before a new value, a local of this function (which becomes one of the owners) or a name that is already such an owner." [THR-1] p11 70-72: "it is written before a new value (`st = thread_shared Stats()`) or on a value already `thread_shared` (`fn() thread_shared st:`), and on a value made otherwise it is `E7017`". [OWN-13] p07 139-142: "`thread_shared x`, one more owner on any thread, written only before a new value (`names = thread_shared Names()`) or a value already `thread_shared` (`E7017` otherwise ...)". E2122's row (p17a 91): "made of a place that has one owner and is not a local of this function". [OBJ-1] p08 63 and 67: "The header is 8 bytes"; "A `thread_shared` value's header is 32 bytes".

options.summary: Refused, as the rule on threads says: a value shared between threads is made that way.
options.code:
s = thread_shared Settings(port=8080)       # made shared between threads where it is made
h = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared s: println(s.port))
h.join()
options.outcome: `shared = thread_shared s` is refused (E7017: "`s` is `main`'s own object, which it may change; to share it between threads, create it shared: `s = thread_shared Settings(port=8080)`"). Written as above, it compiles and prints 8080. `shares s` and `shares mut s` of a local stay allowed.

options.summary: Allowed, as `shares s` of a local is: `s` becomes one of the owners.
options.code: shared = thread_shared s
options.outcome: Compiles and prints 8080. From that line on, no owner changes the object directly (`s.port = 9` is refused). But every `Settings` object that may be shared this way must carry the 32-byte two-count header from the moment it is made, or be moved to a new block at that line, and no view or link of it may outlive the move.

recommendation.reason: A value shared between threads keeps its two owner counts in a 32-byte header from the moment it is made; a one-thread object has 8 or 12 bytes. Turning an object that already exists into one would make every object of its class pay the bigger header, or move it and cut its links. That is the owner's own reason for refusing `shares` of a one-owner place: no cost spread to values that never need it. `shares` of a local keeps working, because every header already holds a count.
recommendation.checklist: 3 (no object grows), 5 (one rule for struct and class values), 7, 9 (the error's line compiles), 13 (no hidden bigger header and no hidden move)

items.reason: Verdict 163: "`renderer: runtime Box[dyn Renderer] = Box(Gpu(pixels=[0])) if input() == \"gpu\" else Box(Software(unused=0))` in `main`, and the lines after it are checked while the program runs". In 0.9.15, `Box[dyn I]` is written `owns dyn I` ([TYP-45] p04 425-427: "`owns dyn I` for `Box[dyn I]`"), and the line that makes such a value says `owns` ([OWN-10]). The spec carries the verdict differently. items.reason: Not settled. [BRW-12] copies only "a part with no fields of its own (a number, a `bool`, a variant with no payload)" and makes every other part a read-only view of the part itself. Whether a `StrView`, `Span` or `ref T` field counts as having no fields of its own is not said. [OWN-9] copies a whole `StrView` name with `=`, and [LT-20] carries only the field's region on a projection, but neither says whether the new name views the field's place. The compiler's own conformance test LT-22/accept_items_of_a_non_copy_iterator_point_into_what_it_reads accepts exactly this pattern (`rest = this.rest`, then `this.rest = rest[at + 1..]` while `rest` is used). That is the lead's reading, not a rule, and the owner's N26 answer (verdict 137) concerned where the result points, not this line.
items.title: Is `w = this.rest` a copy of the view, or a view of the field?
items.problem: A lexer keeps the text it has not read yet in a `StrView` field, takes it into a local with `w = this.rest`, and moves the field past the word while still using `w`. In C++ that is `std::string_view w = rest;`. A name bound to a field is a read-only view of that field, unless the field has no fields of its own (a number, a `bool`). The spec does not say which side a `StrView` field falls on. If it is copied like a number, `w` looks at the text and the method compiles; if it is viewed, writing `this.rest` while `w` is used is refused.
items.spec_today: [BRW-12] p07 196-200: "A name bound to a part (`n = p.name`, `boss = enemies[0]`) ... is a read-only view of it: never a hand-over, and never a silent copy, except that a part with no fields of its own (a number, a `bool`, a variant with no payload) is copied, as Python binds a number." [OWN-9] p07 95-96: "A value `=` copies (a number, a `bool`, a `char`, a `StrView`, a `ref T`, a `Span[T]`, ...) is copied with `=` too". [BRW-1] p07 270-273: "While a read-only view (a plain name for a part, ...) is still used, what it points into is not changed through any other name (`E3021`, at the change)". [LT-20] p07 754-755: "Projecting one field carries only that field's region."

options.summary: A part whose type is a `Copy` view (`StrView`, `Span[T]`, `ref T`) is copied, as `=` copies a whole view name: the new name looks at what the field looks at.
options.outcome: Compiles; prints Some('let') Some('x'). Writing `this.rest` does not touch `w`, which looks at the text. A list element of a view type (`w = words[0]`) is copied the same way.

options.summary: `w` is a read-only view of the field `this.rest` itself.
options.outcome: The lexer as written is refused at `this.rest = w[i + 1..]` (E3021: it changes the field `w` views while `w` is used on the next line). Since `copy of` a `StrView` is refused too, the method must copy each word into a `String` and return `Option[String]`.

recommendation.reason: `=` already copies a whole `StrView`, `Span` or `ref` name, and copying one copies no data, so the copy is no silent copy. The lexer then reads as it does in C++ (`std::string_view w = rest;`) and in Rust (`let w = self.rest;`), and the compiler's own test already accepts it.
recommendation.checklist: 1, 2 (accepts the correct lexer), 5 (one meaning of `=` for a view, whole name or field), 6 (nearest rule: `=` copies a view name), 10

The assignment grammar takes only names (p03 205-208), and [BRW-12]'s `ref mut` before a call covers "a `MutSpan` a call gives", not a pair of them. The only spec example of `split_at` is a read-only `Span`. A one-branch `match` with `(ref mut left, ref mut right)` would need `ref mut` names bound into a temporary, which [EXP-5] ("a `ref mut` name ... require[s] a place") leaves doubtful. Verdict 34 decides that such a name says `ref mut`, but not where the word goes on a destructuring line.
items.title: How does a program write through both halves of a split `MutSpan`?
items.problem: `split_at` on a `MutSpan` exists to give two halves that can both be written, as Rust's `split_at_mut` does. A name that writes a `MutSpan` must say `ref mut`, but the line `left, right = samples.split_at(mid)` has nowhere to put it: the assignment takes only names, and `ref mut` before a call's result is described for one span, not a pair. So no line the spec describes writes both halves.
items.spec_today: [SPN-5] p07 833-834: "`split_at(i)` on a `Span` returns two `Span`s; on a `MutSpan` it lends the view and returns two disjoint `MutSpan`s." [SPN-3] p07 820-823: "A name or parameter that writes a `MutSpan`'s elements says `ref mut` (`d = ref mut a.as_mut_span()`, ...), and a plain one only reads them (`E3023`, `[BRW-15]`)." [BRW-12] p07 203-205: "before a `MutSpan` a call gives it says the name may write the span's elements (`d = ref mut tracks[dst_name].as_mut_span()`)". Grammar p03 205-208: "assignment := target_list \"=\" expr_list" ... "target := IDENT | postfix_expr | \"_\" | \"(\" target_list \")\"".

options.summary: The word goes before the value, as on every `=` line: `ref mut` before the call gives both names the right to write their halves.
options.code: left, right = ref mut samples.split_at(mid)
options.outcome: Compiles; prints [1.0, 3.0, 3.0, 5.0]. Without `ref mut`, `right[i] = ...` stays E3023, and the help gives this line.

options.summary: Words go before each name, as a loop's and a pattern's names take them.
options.code: ref mut left, ref mut right = samples.split_at(mid)
options.outcome: Compiles; prints the same. `left, ref mut right = ...` is E0116 under the comma rule; `ref left, ref mut right = ...` writes only the second half.

options.summary: No new form: open the pair with a one-branch `match`, whose pattern names already take words.
options.code:
match samples.split_at(mid):
    (ref mut left, ref mut right):
        for i in 0..mid:
            right[i] = (left[i] + right[i]) / 2.0
options.outcome: Compiles; prints the same. The spec must then say that a `match` on a call's result may give `ref mut` names to the spans in it, and every split costs a nested block.

recommendation.reason: An `=` line already puts the word before the value (`d = ref mut tracks[dst_name].as_mut_span()`), and `ref mut` before a span already names its elements. Extending that to the spans a call gives adds the one missing form, and adds no second place for words on an assignment.
recommendation.checklist: 5, 11 (the language's own spelling for an `=` line), 12 (adds the missing syntax instead of leaving the split unusable), 13

items.reason: [OWN-7]'s rule names only "a `Copy` struct". Tuples and fixed arrays of `Copy` elements are `Copy` too (p04 263-264), and their parts can be changed through a copy in the same way. The rule comes from the redesign's R1 (run 4 v5 rules.md 111-114), not from an owner verdict. Nothing says whether its reason, "so that no copy is changed by mistake", reaches them.
items.title: Is changing a copied fixed array or tuple refused, as for a copied struct?
items.problem: When a `Copy` struct is copied with `=` and the name it came from is used later, changing the copy is refused, so that nobody changes a copy thinking it is the original; the line must say `copy of` or `ref mut`. Fixed arrays and tuples of numbers are `Copy` too, and their parts can be changed the same way, but the rule names only structs.
items.example:
@derive(Copy)
struct Vec3:
    x: float
    y: float
    z: float

fn main():
    o = Vec3(x=0.0, y=0.0, z=0.0)
    p = copy of o                 # the struct must say `copy of` (or `ref mut`) to be changed below
    p.x += 1.0
    origin: [float; 3] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
    pos = origin                  # a copy of a Copy fixed array
    pos[0] += 1.0                 # refused like `p.x` would be after `p = o`, or allowed?
    span = (0, 10)
    s2 = span                     # a copy of a Copy tuple
    s2.0 += 1                     # refused, or allowed?
    println(o.x, origin[0], span.0)
items.spec_today: [OWN-7] p07 164-166: "A `Copy` struct copied with `=` from a name that is still used afterwards is not then changed through the new name (`E3023`): the line says `copy of` (a copy of your own) or `ref mut` (the original), so that no copy is changed by mistake." IV.3 p04 263-264: "Tuples `(A, B, C)`: ... `Copy` iff every element is." "Fixed arrays `[T; N]`: ... `Copy` iff `T` is."

options.summary: One rule for every `Copy` value whose parts can be changed: a struct, a tuple, a fixed array (not numbers, `bool`, `char` or views).
options.code:
pos = copy of origin      # a fixed array of your own, changed freely
pos[0] += 1.0
s2 = copy of span
s2.0 += 1
options.outcome: `pos = origin` then `pos[0] += 1.0` is refused like the struct (E3023, the help giving `pos = copy of origin` or `pos = ref mut origin`). Written as above, the program compiles and prints 0.0 0.0 0.

options.summary: Only structs, as the rule is written.
options.code:
pos = origin
pos[0] += 1.0
s2 = span
s2.0 += 1
options.outcome: Compiles and prints 0.0 0.0 0; a copied fixed array or tuple may be changed through the new name with no word.

recommendation.reason: The rule's reason holds for a fixed array most of all: in Python, `=` makes a list shared, so a programmer may well think `pos` and `origin` are one array. One rule wherever the same thing can happen.
recommendation.checklist: 5 (one rule for every type with parts), 6 (nearest rule: the struct's), 7

[BRW-18] p07 479 still names `Commands` as a way out of E3020, and it is the only place in the assembled spec that does. The ECS part does it its own way: it collects entities in a list and destroys them after the loop (p12 226-230).

items.reason: [BRW-13] settles it. p07 208-211: "`=` on a name that has a value puts the new value in the place the name stands for. A name declared with `=` stands for its own place: its old value is replaced (and ends, if it owned something), and if the value is a view, the name now views something else". A local is a place that holds whatever it is given. Given a new `String`, it holds and owns that string; the old value was a view, so nothing ends. Ending the string on the paths where the name owns it is the compiler's own bookkeeping (the hidden drop flag of [OWN-3], p07 75-76). Everything after the merge follows from existing rules. Reading `name` is fine on both paths, so `return copy of name` compiles and gives "unnamed" for an empty name. A change through `name`, or `return name`, may reach the view, so it is E3023 or E3013. [TYP-14] (p04 294-295) agrees for views ("A read-only view name given a new view with `=` views that instead"). [BRW-15] restricts changes through such a name, not the name being given a new value, which [BRW-13]'s own example `rest = tail.trim()` shows.

Found while disproving J4-01. A plain parameter that is not `Copy` is passed by address ([BRW-8]). [FN-1] and [BRW-1] promise that what it reads does not change while it is used, and [BRW-21] says "the compiler holds the callee to it". But [BRW-21]'s check and [BCK-8]'s check at the call look only at ending or moving for a plain parameter; only a `ref mut` parameter is also checked against what the callee changes by another name. Inside the callee, [BCK-3] does not treat the parameter and a module variable as possibly one place. So the program compiles, and the promise breaks for a number written by the global's name. The lead's ruling of area 2 Q4 (decisions.md 86: "only 'not ended or moved' is checked ... the compiler never assumes the value unchanged") rests on verdict 18. That verdict is about `this` in a method that changes its own object, not about plain parameters, while verdict 5 makes a read-only name a promise that what it reads does not change while it is used.
items.title: A function changes, by a global's name, what its read-only parameter reads: refused?
items.problem: A function takes a plain, read-only parameter `p` (a `const Player&` in C++), and while still using it changes the same player through the global list's own name; the caller passed `PARTY[0]`. The rules say a read-only parameter promises that what it reads does not change while it is used, and that the compiler holds the function to that. But the check at the call looks only for ending or moving what the parameter views, so the program compiles and prints `ana 5`; a `ref mut` parameter in the same spot is already refused at the call.
items.example:
struct Player:
    name: String
    hp: int

static mut PARTY: Array[Player] = []

fn report(p: Player):              # reads the caller's player (a `const Player&` in C++)
    PARTY[0].hp = 5                # changes the first player by the list's own name
    println(p.name, p.hp)          # `p` is still used: it promised its player does not change meanwhile

fn main():
    PARTY.push(owns Player(name=String("ana"), hp=10))
    report(PARTY[0])               # `p` is PARTY[0]: compiles and prints "ana 5" today
items.spec_today: [FN-1] p05 78-80: "`a: A`: **reads**. The callee reads the caller's `a` ...; it changes nothing through `a` ... and what `a` reads does not change while `a` is used (`[BRW-1]`)." [BRW-1] p07 270-273: "While a read-only view (a plain name for a part, a `ref` name, a plain parameter, ...) is still used, what it points into is not changed through any other name (`E3021`, at the change)". [BRW-21] p07 328-330: "inside it, the parameter makes the promise of `[BRW-1]`, and the compiler holds the callee to it"; p07 336-337: "an argument that points into what the callee may end or move before its last use of that parameter is `E3031`. Writing a number or a `bool` ends and moves nothing"; p07 352-355: for a `ref mut` parameter "the check is wider ... an argument for it that points into a place the callee reads or changes by another name while the parameter is used is refused too". [BCK-8] p18 236-238: "an argument that points into what the callee may end or move before its last use of that parameter, or, for a `ref mut` parameter, into what the callee reaches by another name while the parameter is used, is `E3031`".

options.summary: Refused at the call, as a `ref mut` parameter's call already is: the callee may not change, by another name, what a read-only parameter reads while it is used.
options.code: report(copy of PARTY[0])           # a player of its own
options.outcome: `report(PARTY[0])` is refused at the call ("`report` changes `PARTY[0].hp` by the list's own name (its line 2) while `p` is still used (its line 3), and `p` is `PARTY[0]`; give it a copy: `report(copy of PARTY[0])`, or in `report` use `p` before changing the list"). `report(copy of PARTY[0])` compiles and prints ana 10, and a call with a player that is not in `PARTY` is untouched.

options.summary: Allowed: a read-only parameter is promised only that what it reads is not ended or moved; a number written by another name shows through it.
options.code: report(PARTY[0])
options.outcome: Compiles and prints ana 5. The rule's "what `a` reads does not change while `a` is used" is narrowed to "is not ended or moved" for parameters, while inside one function `boss = enemies[0]` followed by `enemies[0].hp = 1` stays refused.

recommendation.reason: A read-only name then means one thing everywhere. Inside one function, `boss = enemies[0]` followed by `enemies[0].hp = 1` while `boss` is used is already refused, and across a call a `ref mut` parameter already gets this very check. Nothing runs while the program runs. A method that changes its own object (the turret aimed at itself) is not a read-only name, so it is untouched.
recommendation.checklist: 1, 2 (refuses only the call that breaks the promise), 3 (compile time only), 5, 6 (nearest rules: the read-only promise in one function and the `ref mut` call check), 13

jobs.notes:
Of 13 findings plus 1 new one: 7 go to the owner as ODRs (J4-03, J4-04, J4-05, J4-08, J4-09, J4-11, J4-14), 4 are lead fixes (J4-06, J4-07, J4-10, J4-12) and 3 are refuted (J4-01, J4-02, J4-13). Nothing was merged.

Patterns across items, for the phase-3 consistency critic:

1. Names that view and names that own. J4-03 (an owning loop name, a `match owns` branch name or an `owns` parameter is an owner), J4-04 (`body = owns req.body` hands a part into a local) and J4-08 (a part whose type is a `Copy` view is copied on `=`) all move the same line: which names are read-only views. J4-13 (refuted) rests on [BRW-13], under which a local holds whatever it is given. If the owner takes the recommendations, these must be edited together: [BRW-12] (its list of words before a part gains `owns`; its copy exception gains `Copy` views), [BRW-14], [BRW-15], [OWN-3] (\"a loop, pattern or opened name\" means one that does not take its value over), VII.1's view list, [CTL-1]'s last sentence, [GRM-13] and [GRM-15]'s list. J4-08's recommendation also means `w = words[0]` of an `Array[StrView]` is a copy, not a position ([BRW-16]); check Part VII.5 and [BCK-1] for that.

2. J4-14 (new) is what remains of J4-01. A plain `Copy` parameter is a copy at every size ([BRW-8]'s \"Two kinds are passed as a copy instead\"; ODR-024), so J4-01 is refuted. A plain parameter passed by address is not protected against the callee changing its target by a global's name. Recommendation A touches [FN-1] (Part V), [BRW-21] and [BCK-8] (Part XVIII): the summary must record what a function changes by another name while a plain parameter, or a read-only `this`, is used. Verdict 54 counts `this` as a view parameter, so a method that does not change its object gets the same call check. A method that changes its own object (verdict 18, the turret) is not a read-only name and is unaffected. The lead's area-2 Q4 ruling (decisions.md 86) would be reversed by A. [FN-1]'s \"such as a small `Copy` value in registers\" (p05 80-81) should say \"a `Copy` value\" so that no reader takes size into account (wording, the lead's).

3. J4-05's recommendation (A) keeps E7017 and limits [RC-1]'s and E2122's \"a local of this function\" to `shares` and `shares mut`. It touches Part VIII ([RC-1], [OBJ-1]) and Part XI ([THR-1]); E2122's row in XVII must drop `thread_shared` for locals.

4. J4-06's lead fix writes verdict 163 as `runtime owns dyn I`. Whether `runtime` also goes before `shares dyn I`, `shares mut dyn I` or `shares A` on a variable or parameter is not decided by verdict 163, which spoke only of `Box`. Checklist item 16 suggests it follows; leave it for the critic, or as a separate question, rather than widen the verdict.

5. J4-09's recommendation (A) needs no new grammar: `ref mut` is already a value word. It extends [BRW-12]'s \"before a `MutSpan` a call gives\" to a tuple of spans a call gives, and adds that line to E3023's help. Check it against `get_pair_mut`'s `exists as (ref mut a, ref mut b)` spelling, so the two do not drift.

6. J4-10 is a Part XV signature (`extend(owns items)`); the STD reviewer should check `Map`, `Set` and `String` `extend` the same way. Separately for Part VI and XV: [STD-15] (p15 191) still lists `iter_mut`, and [CTL-1] (p06 142) uses `xs.iter_mut()` in an E3023 example, while decisions.md's area 2 Q3 says `iter_mut` stays gone ([SPN-4]).

7. Message wording (the lead's, not ODRs): E3028's help \"to keep `xs`, give it a copy: `take(owns copy of xs)`\" does not compile for a view-type `owns` parameter (`copy of` a `StrView` is E2116). There the line that compiles is `kept = w` before `take(owns w)`.

No recommendation of mine contradicts another. J4-03 A, J4-04 A and J4-08 A together draw one line: a name owns what it took over, and `=` copies a view. J4-14 A applies only to parameters passed by address, and those are not `Copy` values, since a `Copy` value is always passed as a copy.
