items.reason: The finding holds as written. At `b.next = Some(shares mut a)`, the stored value is `a`, which was made in the function. The only owner stored into it since is `b`, also made in the function, with nothing stored into it before this line. So [WK-7] proof (1) (p08 473-475) passes and the line that closes the loop is accepted. Proof (2) fails, because an owner of `b` was stored into `a.next`. The proof is unsound as worded, and decisions.md section 6's [WK-7] row calls both proofs sound. Verdict 99 settles the program in its own words: `make_pair` doing `a.next = Some(shares mut b)` then `b.next = Some(shares mut a)` "is refused at the line that closes the loop". The wording is wrong, not the language.
items.decided_by: Verdict 99 (make_pair's closing line is refused). The proofs' wording is the lead's (decisions.md section 6, [WK-7]).
items.lead_fix_text: [WK-7] (p08 473-475), proof (1): add the holder condition, so it reads: "(1) the stored value was made in this function, on the line or earlier, and since then no owner has been stored into it or into anything it owns but values that themselves meet (1), and the holder is none of these values (the stored value, and what was stored into it or into what it owns before this line): nothing the stored value reaches is the holder". Then [WK-6]'s make_pair is E3032 at `b.next = Some(shares mut a)`, because the holder `b` was stored into `a`. The top-down tree (`root.children.push(shares mut child)`) still meets (1). Correct decisions.md section 6's [WK-7] row to match.

items.reason: No rule ties a `weakref` link to the instance its target was made in. [ALC-1], [TYP-46] and [LT-4] bind only "a value made in an instance, and every value that holds one". [WK-11] says a link "holds one weak count", not the value. [OBJ-3] keeps the block, which sits in the arena's memory, until the weak count reaches 0. [ALC-1] (1) frees all of an arena's memory at once. [ALC-5] guards a reset only "while a value made in it lives". Grepping `weakref` with arena, instance and manager finds nothing more. [PHIL-10] demands an answer (no use-after-free), but more than one safe answer exists, so the choice is the owner's.
items.title: Can a weakref link to an arena-made object outlive the arena?
items.problem: A level loader makes the boss `using` a level arena, and the camera follows it with a `weakref` link. The link keeps the boss's memory block, but the arena frees all its memory when it ends. Once the level is gone, the camera's link points into freed memory: in C++ terms, a `weak_ptr` whose control block lived in a `std::pmr` arena that was released. The specification ties to an arena's life only the values made in it and the values that hold one. A link does not hold its target, so nothing says whether the camera line compiles, or what opening the link does later.
items.example:
class Enemy:
    hp: int

class Camera:
    target: weakref Enemy = None             # follows an enemy without keeping it alive

fn load_level(ref mut cam: Camera):
    level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)   # the level's memory, freed when load_level returns
    boss = Enemy(hp=500) using level         # the boss's block is taken from `level`
    cam.target = weakref boss                # the link's weak count keeps the boss's block
    println(boss.hp)
    # here boss ends (its block kept by the link), then `level` ends and frees all of its memory

fn main():
    cam = Camera()
    load_level(ref mut cam)
    if cam.target exists as e:               # tests the boss's header, in memory the arena gave back
        println(e.hp)
    else:
        println("gone")
items.spec_today: p09-memory.md 199-200 [ALC-1]: "a value made in an instance, and every value that holds one, lives no longer than that instance (`E3063`, `[LT-4]`)". p09-memory.md 207-208 [ALC-1]: "all of it is freed together when the instance is cleared or ends". p08-classes.md 331 [WK-11]: "Every `weakref` link holds one weak count on its target". p08-classes.md 85 [OBJ-3]: "the block is freed when the weak count reaches 0". p09-memory.md 242-243 [ALC-5]: "While a value made in a memory manager's instance lives, the instance is changed only by what allocates from it and gives blocks back to it".

options.summary: The link counts as holding the boss, so it lives no longer than the arena, like the values made in it.
options.code:
class Enemy:
    hp: int

class Camera:
    target: weakref Enemy = None

fn load_level(ref mut cam: Camera, ref mut level: Arena):   # the caller keeps the arena
    boss = Enemy(hp=500) using level
    cam.target = weakref boss
    println(boss.hp)

fn main():
    level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)   # made before cam, so it ends after cam
    cam = Camera()
    load_level(ref mut cam, ref mut level)
    if cam.target exists as e:               # the boss ended with load_level; its block is still in `level`
        println(e.hp)
    else:
        println("gone")
options.outcome: The example is E3063 at `cam.target = weakref boss`: `cam` outlives `level`, so make the arena in the caller. This version compiles and prints 500, then gone. `level.reset()` while `cam` still holds the link is E3021, just as a reset under a live value is.

options.summary: A `weakref` link may only name an object from the built-in memory manager.
options.outcome: Every `cam.target = weakref boss` with a boss made `using` an arena is refused: "a `weakref` link needs an object from the built-in memory manager; make the boss without `using`". This version prints 500, then gone. A camera can never follow an arena-made enemy, even while the arena lives.

recommendation.reason: It applies the rule the specification already has for values that hold an arena-made value to the one holder that rule misses. It is checked when compiling, nothing runs, and the common layout of a level arena with links into it keeps working.
recommendation.checklist: 2 (accepts the level-arena program, refuses only the dangling one), 3 (decided when compiling, nothing runs), 6 (the nearest rule: what holds a value made in an instance lives no longer than the instance), 7 (every link, every manager)

items.reason: [EXC-3] (p08 247-250) says paths into one class family may reach one object, yet it lists "different classes" as proof that they differ. [BRW-17] (p07 435-436) and [BCK-3] (p18 179-181) say "values of one type ... unless ... different types", and [SIMD-3] gives an alias fact to "different types". A path typed `Unit` and a path typed `Player` are different types of one family, and an upcast is implicit (conversion 8). Read literally, the text lets the reshape free the text that `s` views. No rule defines "type" to include derived classes or implementers (grep 'derives from', 'class family'). That literal reading breaks [PHIL-10] (p01 125-131: a Safe program "cannot perform ... a use-after-free"). Verdicts 5 and 82 decide by what a name reads, not by its static type. So writing in the reading that includes subtypes is a lead fix. Merged with J5-04, which is the same notion in the rules about ending objects.
items.decided_by: [PHIL-10] (no use-after-free in Safe Ember), [EXC-3]'s own class-family rule, verdict 5 ("what it reads does not change while it is in use") and verdict 82 (a name opened from a link is not used across a call "that may destroy what it reads").
items.lead_fix_text: Write the subtype rule once, in §VIII.3 beside [EXC-3] (or in [BCK-3]), and point the other rules at it: "An object of type T is an object whose class is T or derives from T; for `dyn I`, an object of any type implementing I. A place owns one when its type can hold one: a place of T or of a base class of T, an `owns dyn I`, `shares dyn I`, `shares mut dyn I` or `thread_shared` place for an I that T implements, and an `Option`, a list or a function value's state holding such a place. Two paths are proved apart by their types only when neither type can hold an object of the other (sibling classes, unrelated types); a base class and a class derived from it, or a `dyn I` and a class implementing I, may be one object." Then: in [EXC-3] (p08 250), "different classes" becomes "classes neither of which derives from the other". In [BRW-17] (p07 435-436), [BCK-3] (p18 179-181) and [SIMD-3] (Part XII, "the two have different types"), "different types" becomes "types neither of which can hold an object of the other". [RC-5] point 1 (p08 196-198), [WK-17] condition 2 (p08 387-389), [BCK-7] (p18 217) and [DRP-8] read "an object of that type" / "of its type" by this definition. J5-03's example is then E3060 at `println(s)`, and J5-04's at `println(t.hp)`.

items.reason: This is the same question as J5-03: whether "an object of that type" or "of its type" counts derived classes, base-class places and `dyn` places. It is merged into J5-03, whose lead fix covers [RC-5] point 1, [WK-17] condition 2, [BCK-7] and [DRP-8]. Verdict 82 ("not used across a call that may destroy what it reads") decides by the object that is read, so clearing an `Array[Unit]` that owns the player ends the view `t`.

[TYP-46] (p04 433-434) and [ALC-1] allow `using` after `thread_shared`. [OBJ-1] (p08 69-71) reads the making thread only from the header of the runtime's memory chunk (verdict 101, fix 1), and a manager's block has no such header. After a hand-over ([RC-4] point 4), the last owner, and with it `drop` and the manager's `deallocate`, may run on another thread. [LT-4]'s instance word is a kept `sharedref mut` link, which may be changed on two threads only under a lock ([LT-46]). No rule refuses this or says how it runs (grep 'memory chunk', 'making thread': OBJ-1 only). Whether it compiles is the owner's question.
items.title: May a `thread_shared` value take its memory from an arena or other manager?
items.problem: The list of types that `using` may follow names `thread_shared`, so on paper `stats = thread_shared Stats() using level` is allowed. But a `thread_shared` value finds the thread that made it from the header of the runtime's own memory chunk, and a block from an arena has no such header. Once the value is handed to another thread, its last owner, and so the arena's give-back, may run on that thread, while an `Arena` is a one-thread struct. The specification says neither whether this compiles nor how it runs.
items.example:
from std.sync import Atomic
import std.thread

class Stats:
    hits: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)

fn main():
    level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)               # a one-thread arena
    stats = thread_shared Stats() using level             # the list of types `using` may follow names `thread_shared`
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn() owns stats: stats.hits.fetch_add(1))   # the owner goes to a task on another thread
    println("done")                                       # the last owner ended on that thread, giving the block back to `level` there
items.spec_today: p04-types.md 433-434 [TYP-46]: "It may follow an `owns`, `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` type, a class type, or an `Array`, a `Map` or a `Set`". p08-classes.md 69-71 [OBJ-1]: "Which thread made a value is read from the header of the memory chunk its block came from, written once when the chunk is made, never from the value." p08-classes.md 176-178 [RC-4] point 4: "from then on every thread, the making thread included, counts in the away count, and a later end on another thread never goes through the queue." p07-ownership.md 621-622 [LT-4]: "that address is a kept `sharedref mut` link to the instance (`[LT-46]`)". p07-ownership.md 688 [LT-46]: "on two threads it is changed only under a lock, through `Atomic`, or by a reduction".

options.summary: `using` may not follow `thread_shared`: such a value always takes its block from the built-in manager.
options.code:
from std.sync import Atomic
import std.thread

class Stats:
    hits: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)

fn main():
    stats = thread_shared Stats()                         # its block from the built-in manager
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn() owns stats: stats.hits.fetch_add(1))
    println("done")
options.outcome: The example's `thread_shared Stats() using level` is E2114: "a `thread_shared` value takes its memory from the built-in manager, which every thread may give it back to; remove `using level`". This version compiles and prints done.

options.summary: Allowed when the manager kind may be used from any thread and has one instance. The value then keeps its making thread in its header.
options.code:
from std.sync import Atomic
import std.thread

class Stats:
    hits: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)

fn main():
    stats = thread_shared Stats() using System            # the platform's manager: one instance, any thread may give memory back to it
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn() owns stats: stats.hits.fetch_add(1))
    println("done")
options.outcome: The example's `using level` is refused, because an `Arena` is used by one thread (E7015, with that reason). `using System`, or any manager kind with one instance that implements `ThreadShared`, compiles and prints done. Such a value keeps its making thread in the 4 unused bytes of its header, since its block has no runtime chunk to read it from.

recommendation.reason: It keeps one way to find a shared value's making thread, the memory chunk that the two-count design chose, and adds no second header path. A mistake becomes a refusal at the line, not a race at run time. The program loses nothing it needs: its block can come from the built-in manager.
recommendation.checklist: 3, 5 (one place for the making thread), 8 (a mistake is a refusal, not a race), 13 (no special path for values made in a manager)

items.reason: [RC-1] lets a local be shared and stay one of the owners, and [RC-7] keeps its rights. [HEAP-3] puts the value in a block at the line that shares it. [BCK-4] ends views only at a storage end, a hand-over, a replacement or an end, and sharing is none of these. No rule says whether a view taken before that line survives it (grep 'becomes one of the owners', 'where it is made shared'). Whether `println(g)` compiles is the owner's question.
items.title: Does a view of a local still work after the local is made shared?
items.problem: A local struct can be made shared halfway through a function (`shop = Shop(stock=shares mut inv)`), and `inv` stays one of its owners with the rights it had. The specification says the value is put in a block of its own at the line that shares it, which moves it out of the function's frame. It does not say what happens to a view of it taken before that line: in C++ terms, `int& g = inv.gold;` followed by `std::make_shared<Inventory>(std::move(inv))`. So `println(g)` is either refused or reads where `inv` used to be.
items.example:
struct Inventory:
    gold: int
    items: Array[String]

class Shop:
    stock: shares mut Inventory

fn main():
    inv = Inventory(gold=5, items=[String("sword")])   # a local struct, inline in main's frame
    g = ref inv.gold                                    # a view of its gold, where inv is now
    shop = Shop(stock=shares mut inv)                   # inv is made shared: put in a block of its own
    println(g)                                          # does g still see inv's gold?
    inv.gold += 1                                       # inv keeps what it could do
    println(shop.stock.gold)
items.spec_today: p08-classes.md 106-108 [RC-1]: "`shares x`, `shares mut x` and `thread_shared x` are written before a new value, a local of this function (which becomes one of the owners) or a name that is already such an owner". p09-memory.md 61-62 [HEAP-3]: "any other value is put in a block where it is made shared (`count = shares mut Counter()`, `other = shares items`), one allocation". p08-classes.md 120-121 [RC-7]: "the name it was first shared from, which keeps what it could do". p18-implementation.md 185-186 [BCK-4]: "A place whose storage ends (scope exit, `StorageDead`, its owner handed over, replaced or ended) while a view of it is live is `E3060`". Sharing is none of these.

options.summary: Sharing a local moves it into its block at that line and ends every view into it.
options.code:
struct Inventory:
    gold: int
    items: Array[String]

class Shop:
    stock: shares mut Inventory

fn main():
    inv = Inventory(gold=5, items=[String("sword")])
    shop = Shop(stock=shares mut inv)        # inv is put in a block of its own here
    g = ref inv.gold                         # the view is taken after the move
    println(g)
    inv.gold += 1
    println(shop.stock.gold)
options.outcome: In the example, `println(g)` is E3060: "`shares mut inv` (line 11) puts `inv` in a block of its own, and `g` views it where it was (line 10) and is used on line 12; take `g = ref inv.gold` after line 11". This version compiles and prints 5, then 6.

options.summary: Views of a local survive its sharing. Where a view crosses the sharing line, the compiler gives the local its block earlier.
options.code:
struct Inventory:
    gold: int
    items: Array[String]

class Shop:
    stock: shares mut Inventory

fn main():
    inv = Inventory(gold=5, items=[String("sword")])
    g = ref inv.gold
    shop = Shop(stock=shares mut inv)
    println(g)
    inv.gold += 1
    println(shop.stock.gold)
options.outcome: The example compiles and prints 5, then 6. Where a view of `inv` is used across the line that shares it, `inv` is put in its block where it is declared: the same one allocation, made earlier. Everywhere else the block is made at the sharing line, as it is now.

recommendation.reason: Sharing does not change which inventory `g` views, so the program means what it says. The compiler does the placement unseen, and the cost is the same single allocation, made earlier only where a view needs it.
recommendation.checklist: 1, 2 (accepts a correct program), 3 (no run-time cost added), 4 (nothing written), 13 (one model: a shared local is one value for its whole life)

items.reason: I could not disprove it. [WK-11] lets any name make a link, "from a read-only p" included, and [GRM-44] lets a link be opened `ref mut`. [OWN-13]'s "An owner made from another may do no more than it" covers owners, and [FN-2a]'s E3027 covers `ref mut` before a place reached through a read-only name, but nothing covers a link that is opened `ref mut`. Inside `inspect` no rule is broken ([BRW-1] protects `e` only while it is still used), so today the program compiles. That runs against verdict 32: "what a function may do with a parameter is set by the word in front of its name". The evidence that the owner sees this as a hole is indirect (verdict 32 refused the same thing done with an owner), hence the lower confidence.
items.title: Can a function change a read-only parameter through a weakref link made from it?
items.problem: A plain parameter only reads what it names, and making an owner that may change it from such a name is refused. But any name may make a `weakref` link, and a link may be opened with `exists as ref mut`. So a function given a plain `e: Enemy` can write `w = weakref e` and change the enemy through the link, and nothing at the call says the caller's enemy changes. The specification has no rule tying what an opened link may do to the name it was made from.
items.example:
class Enemy:
    hp: int = 10

fn inspect(e: Enemy):                 # a plain parameter: inspect only reads the enemy
    w = weakref e                     # allowed: making a link changes nothing
    if w exists as ref mut x:         # opened as a name that may change the enemy
        x.hp = 0                      # changes the caller's enemy through the link

fn main():
    boss = Enemy()
    inspect(boss)                     # no word at the call says boss may change
    println(boss.hp)                  # 10 or 0?
items.spec_today: p08-classes.md 336-338 [WK-11]: "any name may make one (`up = weakref p` from a read-only `p`; `child.parent = weakref this` in a method that otherwise changes only `this.children`)". p03-grammar.md 272-273 [GRM-44]: "`if ui exists as ref mut me:` may change what it names". p07-ownership.md 144-146 [OWN-13]: "An owner made from another may do no more than it: `shares mut x` needs `x` to be a name that may change the value (`E3023` ...". p07-ownership.md 235-237 [BRW-15]: "A plain parameter, a plain loop, pattern or opened name, and a plain local that holds a view never change what they name or what it leads to".

options.summary: A link made from a name may do no more than that name: one made from a read-only name opens read-only.
options.outcome: In the example, `x.hp = 0` is E3023: "`x` is opened from `w`, a link made from `e` (line 5), and `e` only reads the caller's enemy; write `fn inspect(ref mut e: Enemy):` and call `inspect(ref mut boss)`". The compiler follows the link from where it was made, through locals, fields and calls, as it follows a view. `sharedref mut e` from a read-only `e` is refused the same way (E3027, as `ref mut e` is). A link read from a place the function may change opens as it does now. This version prints 0.

options.summary: Allowed: a link reaches the object, not the name. The specification says so and gives the reason.
options.outcome: Compiles and prints 0. The specification states it: a plain parameter never changes anything through its own name, but a link made from it may be opened `ref mut` like any link, so `inspect(boss)` may change `boss`. Every view the caller holds is still checked against what `inspect` does.

recommendation.reason: The word in front of a parameter sets what the function may do with it, and the language already refuses a changing owner made from a read-only name. A link made from it is the same idea and follows the same rule.
recommendation.checklist: 5, 6 (the nearest rule: an owner made from another may do no more than it), 11, 15 (a plain parameter means only what it says), 16 (the verdict that refused the owner-made way reaches the link-made way)

items.reason: The finder is right that IV.9 (p04 781-783), [TYP-45] (p04 413-415) and [IFC-5] list `dyn I` only as a parameter's type, a view's type or one of the held forms. But verdict 152 states this very program: "With `p: dyn Picker = Mine(items=[9]) if input() == "m" else Yours(items=[9])` and `show(p)`, a `Mine` prints `[9]`", and [LT-1] and [LT-48] carry it. Who owns the `Mine` follows from [BRW-19]/[EXP-4]: a temporary lives until the last use of every view made from it, and conversion 8 makes the `dyn` value a view read in place. So the program is decided, and the list of places where a `dyn I` may stand is missing the local.
items.decided_by: Verdict 152: the owner's own line `p: dyn Picker = Mine(items=[9]) if input() == "m" else Yours(items=[9])`, which prints `[9]` for a `Mine`. [BRW-19] and [EXP-4] decide the temporary.
items.lead_fix_text: In IV.9 (p04 781-783), [TYP-45]'s `dyn I` bullet (p04 413-415) and [IFC-5], list a local beside a parameter: "`dyn I` alone is a parameter's or a local's type, a read-only view of the value (`ref mut v: dyn I` may change it); a local given a value made on its line (`p: dyn Picker = Mine(items=[9]) if input() == "m" else Yours(items=[9])`) views a temporary, which lives until the local's last use and is ended then ([BRW-19], [EXP-4]); a value kept longer is held `owns dyn I`." The lines in [LT-1] and [LT-48] stay as they are. If verdict 163's `Box[dyn Renderer]` is ever quoted, it reads as `owns dyn Renderer` by [TYP-45]'s E1010 map.

items.reason: The closed list in [TYP-46] (p04 433-435) and [ALC-1] leaves out `String` and makes anything not on it E2114. Yet [ALC-1] (1) (p09 208-209) describes a `String` made in a manager, the E2114 row (p17a 83) describes `using` "after a type with no heap memory of its own", and [TXT-1] says a `String` owns a heap buffer. No verdict names `String`: 19, 24, 47 and 107 name `Array`, lists and values that grow. The two sides decide `text: String using Arena` opposite ways, so it is the owner's.
items.title: Can a `String` take its memory from an arena with `using`?
items.problem: A parser or level loader wants its token text in the same arena as its tokens: `text: String using Arena`. The list of types that `using` may follow names `Array`, `Map` and `Set` but not `String`, and anything else is `E2114`. Yet the same rule says a `String` made in an arena keeps the arena's address for its growth, and `E2114` itself is described as `using` on a type with no heap memory of its own, which a `String` has. The specification says both.
items.example:
struct Token:
    kind: int
    text: String using Arena                  # the token's text in the parse's arena

fn read_token(ref mut arena: Arena, src: StrView) -> Token:
    return Token(kind=1, text=String(src) using arena)   # the text's buffer taken from `arena`

fn main():
    arena = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)
    t = read_token(ref mut arena, "let")
    println(t.text)

options.outcome: Compiles and prints let. The text's buffer comes from `arena`, and its growth goes back to it. The `Token` lives no longer than `arena` (E3063 otherwise), as every value holding an arena-made value does.

options.summary: `String` keeps the built-in manager, and the arena sentence drops `String`.
options.outcome: In the example, `text: String using Arena` is E2114: "a `String` takes its memory from the built-in manager; remove `using`". This version prints let, with the text outside the arena.

recommendation.reason: A `String` is a growable buffer exactly as an `Array` is, and the specification already describes a `String` made in an arena. One rule covers every growable buffer, and a parser can keep its tokens and their text in one arena.
recommendation.checklist: 5 (one word, one meaning for every type), 6 (the nearest rule: `Array`, `Map` and `Set`), 7

items.reason: Verdicts 152, 162 and 163 added a run-time check that stops when a list changes while a view looks at it. Yet [EFF-9] (p10 69-70) and [DSJ-6] (p09 512-514) still call `assert_disjoint`/`check_disjoint` "the one run-time alias check there is", [EFF-12] forbids only their compare, and the cost table row (p10 315) gives `runtime` no check kind. Read literally, `@no_alias_checks` allows `runtime`; by what the attribute means, it forbids it. No verdict covers the pair.
items.title: Does `@no_alias_checks` allow a `runtime` parameter, which checks aliasing while running?
items.problem: `@no_alias_checks` on a function forbids run-time alias checks there, and the specification says `assert_disjoint` and `check_disjoint` are "the one run-time alias check there is". The `runtime` word, added since, stops the program when a list changes while a view looks at it. By what it does, that is an alias check, but it is given no check kind, so the specification does not say whether `@no_alias_checks` refuses it.
items.example:
interface Picker:
    fn pick(other: Array[int]) -> Span[int]

struct Mine:
    items: Array[int]

extend Mine implements Picker:
    fn pick(other: Array[int]) -> Span[int]:
        return this.items                     # a view of its own list

struct Yours:
    unused: int

extend Yours implements Picker:
    fn pick(other: Array[int]) -> Span[int]:
        return other                          # a view of the list it was handed

@no_alias_checks                              # "no run-time alias checks in this function"
fn show(p: runtime dyn Picker, ref mut xs: Array[int]):   # "check p's kind while running"
    r = p.pick(xs)
    xs.push(owns 3)                           # checks p's kind here: for a Yours, r looks at xs
    println(r)

fn main():
    xs = [1, 2]
    p: dyn Picker = Mine(items=[9]) if input() == "m" else Yours(unused=0)
    show(p, ref mut xs)

options.code:

items.title: How does a program take over an owner as its concrete class (a downcast that moves)?
items.problem: An owner typed as a base class (`owns u: Unit` holding a `Player`) can be tested with `is` or cast with `cast u as Player`. But the specification only says that a cast of a place is a place, and that a name bound from it is a read-only view. `return` hands a value over as `=` does, and `=` from a cast binds a view, so `return cast u as Player` either hands the player over or returns a view of a local that is about to end. There is no written way to get the owner as its kind, as Rust's `Box<dyn Any>::downcast` or C++'s `static_pointer_cast` do.
items.example:
open class Unit:
    name: String

class Player(Unit):
    score: int = 0

fn take_player(owns u: Unit) -> Player:   # the caller hands over a unit it knows is a player
    return cast u as Player               # the player handed over as a Player, or a view of `u`?

fn main():
    u: Unit = Player(name=String("ann"))  # one owner, typed as its base class (upcast)
    p = take_player(owns u)
    p.score += 10                         # p is main's own Player
    println(p.name, p.score)

items.reason: The grammar (p03 63) allows `unsafe` before any method, `override` included, and [UNS-12] makes the whole body unsafe code. [UNS-1] requires unsafe code to call an `unsafe fn`, while [DRP-1]/[DRP-8] run `drop` wherever the value ends, and [DSP-2]/[DSP-5] send a safe virtual call to any override. No rule refuses `unsafe fn drop()` or an `unsafe` override, and none says who vouches (grep 'unsafe fn drop', 'override.*unsafe': nothing). Verdicts 60, 118 and 119 do not reach this case.
items.title: May a class's `drop`, or an override of a safe method, be an `unsafe fn`?
items.problem: The grammar lets `unsafe` stand before any method, and the body of an `unsafe fn` is unsafe code as a whole, which invites `unsafe fn drop()` in a class that wraps a C handle. But an `unsafe fn` may be called only from unsafe code, while `drop` runs wherever the object ends: the end of a block in safe code, a list being cleared. Likewise, a safe virtual call may land in an `unsafe` override. No rule refuses either case or says who vouches for it.
items.example:
# SAFETY: these declarations match window.h
unsafe extern "C":
    safe fn create_window() -> *mut u8
    @safety("`w` came from `create_window` and is destroyed once")
    unsafe fn destroy_window(w: *mut u8)

class Window:
    handle: *mut u8

    @safety("`this.handle` came from `create_window` and is destroyed only here")
    unsafe fn drop():                        # the whole body is unsafe code
        destroy_window(this.handle)

fn main():
    w = Window(handle=create_window())       # a C window wrapped in an Ember object
    println("open")
    # w ends here, in safe code: its `unsafe fn drop` runs with no unsafe: block and no SAFETY note

Its body is unsafe code". p09-memory.md 266-268 [UNS-1]: "An `unsafe` context is required to: ... call an `unsafe fn`". p07-ownership.md 842-844 [DRP-1]: "`fn drop():` runs exactly once per value, at the end of its life ... Calling it explicitly is `E3070`". No rule names `unsafe` on `drop` or on an `override`.

items.reason: The specification settles this. [RC-4] (p08 189-190) says "The home count, and a count that is not `thread_shared`, keep the exact compare of `[RC-1]` and `[WK-11]`", and [RT-7] says the home count "is checked as a one-thread count is". [RC-1]'s parenthesis, "a `thread_shared` count stops at the lower limit", summarises the atomic counts that [RC-4] spells out. The add at the hand-over cannot roll anything over: the away count is a 64-bit field ([OBJ-1]'s table, p08 56: "away i64 ... the owners the other threads hold, times 8"), and the next +1 meets the half-range test and stops. [RT-7]'s 127 is the 8-bit test's limit for the atomic counts (half of 255), which agrees. At most the parenthesis could name the away and weak counts, and that is wording.

The case is not missing: [ARN-1] decides it (E3060). The problem is a contradiction in the rules' own terms. [ARN-1] (p09 102-106) says views "point into the arena's memory, not into its cursor", and that `scope()` "may reuse or free that memory". [ARN-6] (p09 140-141) says a scope "releases everything at the block's end, last in first out", that is, only what was taken from it. Memory taken before the scope is never reused under it, so the rule refuses a correct program for a reason that is untrue for that program. No verdict covers scopes. Changing this changes which programs compile, so it is the owner's; the severity is low.
items.title: Does opening an arena scope end views made from the arena before it?
items.problem: A parser keeps its tree in an arena and opens `frame.scope()` for scratch memory, which is given back last in first out when the block ends. The specification says a scope gives back only what was taken from it, but it also says that `scope()` may reuse or free the arena's memory, and so it ends every view into the arena. As a result, the tree's root, taken before the scope and never touched by it, cannot be used inside the scope or after it (`E3060`). The stated reason is untrue for the root, and a correct program is refused.
items.example:
@derive(Zeroable)
struct Tok:
    kind: int

struct Node:
    kind: int

fn parse(ref mut frame: Arena) -> int:
    root = ref mut frame.alloc(owns Node(kind=1))   # kept for the whole parse
    with s = frame.scope():                          # scratch memory, given back when the block ends
        toks = ref mut s.alloc_zeroed[Tok](64)       # taken from the scope, above root
        toks[0].kind = 2
        root.kind += toks[0].kind                    # E3060 today: the scope ended every view into `frame`
    return root.kind                                 # E3060 today, though the scope never touched root's bytes

fn main():
    frame = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)
    println(parse(ref mut frame))
items.spec_today: p09-memory.md 102-106 [ARN-1]: "the views point into the arena's memory, not into its cursor ... `reset()`, `scope()` (`[ARN-6]`) and the arena's end may reuse or free that memory: each ends every view into the arena, and a later use of one is `E3060`". p09-memory.md 140-142 [ARN-6]: "`with s = frame.scope():` allocates from `s` and releases everything at the block's end, last in first out. Using the parent while a scope is live is `E3096`".

options.summary: A scope ends only the views made from it.
options.code:

struct Node:
    kind: int

fn parse(ref mut frame: Arena) -> int:

options.outcome: Compiles and prints 3. The scope's end lowers the arena's pointer back to where the scope began, so `root`, which lies below it, stays valid. Reading or writing `root` is not using the parent; allocating from, resetting or scoping the parent while the scope is live stays E3096.

options.summary: As now: opening a scope ends every view into the arena.
options.code:
@derive(Zeroable)
struct Tok:
    kind: int

struct Node:
    kind: int

fn parse(ref mut frame: Arena) -> int:
    kind = 1                                         # kept in a local instead of the arena
    with s = frame.scope():
        toks = ref mut s.alloc_zeroed[Tok](64)
        toks[0].kind = 2
        kind += toks[0].kind
    root = ref mut frame.alloc(owns Node(kind=kind)) # made after the scope
    return root.kind

fn main():
    frame = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)
    println(parse(ref mut frame))
options.outcome: In the example, `root.kind += toks[0].kind` and `return root.kind` are E3060: "`frame.scope()` (line 11) ends every view into `frame`, and `root` (line 10) is used on line 14". This version prints 3, and the rule's stated reason is corrected to "one rule for reset, scope and end".

recommendation.reason: A scope gives back only what it took, last in first out, so memory taken before the scope is never reused under it. The rule then refuses only what is really wrong, and the layout every parser and frame allocator uses, a lasting tree plus scratch memory, works as written.

It touches Parts VII ([BRW-17], [DRP-8]), VIII ([EXC-3], [RC-5], [WK-17]), XII ([SIMD-3]: "the two have different types" gives noalias, so an unsound alias fact is possible too) and XVIII ([BCK-3], [BCK-7]). items.reason: LT-48 (p07 704-721, verdicts 152, 162, 163) adds a check that runs and stops the program when a view and a change overlap. No rule gives it an effect: the effect table's Panic(Explicit) row (p10 16) does not list it, EFF-9 (p10 65-71) and DSJ-6 (p09 512-513) still say assert_disjoint/check_disjoint are 'the one run-time alias check there is', and COST-6's table of stops (p10 355-372) has no row for it, although COST-3 has its cost row (p10 315). Whether @no_alias_checks or @nopanic(explicit) code may hold a `runtime` name changes which programs compile, and no verdict says.
items.title: Does a runtime parameter's check count as a written panic, an alias check, or both?
items.problem: A programmer writes `runtime` on a parameter, so the program checks a value's kind while running and stops if a change overlaps a view. The specification gives this stop no effect: it is not listed with the panics the programmer writes, nor with the run-time alias checks (the text still says assert_disjoint is the only one). So it is not said whether a function marked `@nopanic(explicit)` or `@no_alias_checks` that has a `runtime` parameter compiles.
items.example:
interface Renderer:
    fn draw(scratch: Array[u8]) -> Span[u8]

struct Gpu:
    pixels: Array[u8]

struct Software:
    unused: int

extend Gpu implements Renderer:
    fn draw(scratch: Array[u8]) -> Span[u8]:
        return this.pixels              # its own buffer

extend Software implements Renderer:
    fn draw(scratch: Array[u8]) -> Span[u8]:
        return scratch                  # gives back the buffer it was handed

@nopanic(explicit)                      # no panic the programmer writes
@no_alias_checks                        # no alias compare while running
fn present(r: runtime dyn Renderer, ref mut scratch: Array[u8]):
    frame = r.draw(scratch)             # for a Software, `frame` looks at `scratch`
    scratch.push(owns 1)                # the runtime check: stops here when `r` is a Software
    println(frame.len())

fn main():
    scratch: Array[u8] = [0]
    r: dyn Renderer = Gpu(pixels=[0, 0]) if input("gpu? ") == "y" else Software(unused=0)
    present(r, ref mut scratch)         # does `present` compile with its two contracts?

items.title: Can code with an unsafe block run at compile time?
items.problem: A programmer builds a lookup table at compile time with a function that writes it through a pointer inside an `unsafe:` block. One rule says compile time never calls a function that contains unsafe code, even far down its calls (so a library's own private unsafe code bars it too). Another rule says only unsafe pointer access outside the compiler's own memory is refused, so this table could be built.
items.example:
fn crc_of(n: u32) -> u32:                       # one CRC-32 table entry
    c = n
    for _ in 0..8:
        c = (c >> 1) ^ 0xEDB88320 if c & 1 == 1 else c >> 1
    return c

fn crc_table() -> [u32; 256]:
    t: [u32; 256] = [0; 256]
    unsafe:
        # SAFETY: p points at t's 256 entries and i stays below 256
        p = t.as_mut_ptr()                      # a pointer into the table
        for i in 0..256:
            p.add(i).write(crc_of(i as u32))    # writes entry i through the pointer
    return t

const CRC: [u32; 256] = comptime(crc_table())   # built while compiling: allowed?

fn checksum(data: Span[u8]) -> u32:             # a packet parser's checksum
    c: u32 = 0xFFFFFFFF
    for b in data:
        c = CRC[((c ^ b as u32) & 0xFF) as int] ^ (c >> 8)
    return c ^ 0xFFFFFFFF

fn main():
    println(checksum(b"hello"))

options.summary: Unsafe code runs at compile time; each pointer access is checked as it runs
options.code: const CRC: [u32; 256] = comptime(crc_table())
options.outcome: Compiles: the table is built while compiling. A pointer access outside the compiler's own memory (an address made from a number, a C pointer) is E6010 naming the chain of calls. `Unsafe` leaves CT-1's list; a library function with a private `unsafe:` block can be called at compile time.

options.summary: Unsafe code never runs at compile time
options.code: const CRC: [u32; 256] = comptime(crc_table())
options.outcome: E6010: "`crc_table` runs `unsafe` code (line 9), which compile time does not run; write the entries by index: `t[i] = crc_of(i as u32)`". Every function that reaches an `unsafe:` block, a library's own included, is refused at compile time; CT-2's 'outside the evaluator's heap' goes.

recommendation.reason: The compiler's evaluator sees every pointer it runs, so it can refuse a bad access instead of refusing all unsafe code; this accepts correct programs, keeps the unsafe block's writer the one who vouches, and stops a library's private unsafe code from silently barring its callers.
recommendation.checklist: 2, 3, 6 (CT-2's per-operation rule kept), 7, 13 (no hidden bar from a library's internals), 15

It cannot be spawn or join in general, since THR-21's reduction of scoped tasks is not Nondet (p10 260-261). Nothing elsewhere assigns it (every Nondet mention checked). items.title: Which line makes a function nondeterministic when threads race for a lock?
items.problem: A lockstep game server starts two threads that each add a player's input to one list under a lock, then returns the list from a `@deterministic` function. The list is [1, 2] or [2, 1] depending on which thread gets the lock first. The specification says 'thread completion order' is nondeterministic but never says which operation carries it, so it does not say which line is refused.
items.example:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

static INPUT_LOCK: Lock = Lock()
static mut INPUTS: Array[int] guarded by INPUT_LOCK = []   # this turn's inputs, in arrival order

fn receive(player: int):
    with INPUT_LOCK:
        INPUTS.push(owns player)         # the order the threads get here decides the list

@deterministic
fn gather_turn() -> Array[int]:
    a = thread.spawn(owns fn(): receive(1))
    b = thread.spawn(owns fn(): receive(2))
    a.join()
    b.join()
    with INPUT_LOCK:
        return copy of INPUTS            # [1, 2] or [2, 1]

fn main():
    println(gather_turn())
items.spec_today: p10 253-257 (DET-2): "`Nondet` is introduced by exactly: ... the wall clock, the monotonic clock, the system random source, thread and job completion order; ...". p10 260-261: "A reduction of scoped tasks, combined in spawn order, is not `Nondet` either (`[THR-21]`)." p10 245-246 (DET-1): "`@deterministic` ... `Nondet` MUST NOT appear in its effect set (`E4070`, naming the operation and the chain)."

options.summary: Named operations carry it: a contested lock, a shared channel's receive, try_lock, a used atomic result
options.code:
with INPUT_LOCK:
    INPUTS.push(owns player)
options.outcome: `with INPUT_LOCK:` in `receive` is Nondet because another thread may take the same lock; `gather_turn` is E4070 at line 13, naming `receive` and the lock. Also Nondet: `recv`/`try_recv` on a channel more than one thread sends to, `try_lock`, and an atomic read-modify-write whose result is used. Starting and joining a thread are not.

options.summary: Threads touching one place carry it, worked out from what each function changes
options.code: b = thread.spawn(owns fn(): receive(2))
options.outcome: E4070 at line 13: "`receive` (started on lines 12 and 13) adds to `INPUTS` from two threads at once, so the list's order depends on which runs first". The rule: starting a thread or job whose function changes a place (under a lock, an Atomic, a channel) that another running thread, or the starter before its join, also reads or changes is Nondet; a lock only one thread takes is not, and reductions of scoped tasks stay as they are.

recommendation.reason: B names the real cause (two threads touching one place) with one rule for locks, atomics and channels, decided when compiling from what the compiler already works out about every function, the way it already refuses two tasks changing one place; A also refuses a lock that only one thread ever takes.

The std.math vector and quaternion methods (STD-28) call these with no stated effect. J6-09 is the same question (which float operations are Nondet) and is merged here. No verdict.

The specification says only that a 'transcendental' platform function is nondeterministic, without a list: by the word's meaning, cube root is allowed although C libraries give different last bits for it, and SIMD estimates are allowed although CPUs from different makers give different results.

items.reason: Part decided: the owner ruled that a function from a variable given to a standard-library function is lent (verdict 150, ODR-240, FN-2a p05 132-134, STD-19 p15 315-317), and that the program's own `owns` parameters take `owns` at the call (verdict 147); that split is the owner's and is not reopened here. Still open: std's `push` keeps what it is given and takes `owns` at the call (verdict 149: "`push` too ... `names.push(p.name)` is an error"), while verdict 150 lends a function from a variable to std. For `handlers.push(beep)` the two verdicts give different answers, and a list cannot hold a lent function past the call. ODR-240's 'std's callable-taking functions' does not say whether push on a list of functions is one.
items.title: Does handlers.push(beep) hand over a function kept in a variable?
items.problem: A GUI program keeps a click handler in a variable and adds it to a button's list of handlers with the standard `push`. One ruling says a function from a variable given to a standard-library function is only lent; another says `push` takes over what it is given and needs `owns` at the call. A list keeps its elements after the call, so the two cannot both hold, and the specification does not say which one wins.
items.spec_today: p05 132-134 (FN-2a): "A function from a variable given to a standard-library function that takes one is lent and takes no word: after `xs.iter().for_each(h)`, `h` is the caller's still (`[STD-19]`)." p05 119-121 (FN-2a): "`take(owns xs)` for `fn take(owns xs: Array[int]):`, whatever is given ... `names.push(owns p.name)` a part". p15 305-306 (STD-19): "**A function is taken as a type parameter**, by the adapters that apply one and the consumers alike". p15 311-312: "the shared type, `owns f: fn(Item)`, is legal too, and is what keeps functions of different kinds in one list (`handlers: Array[fn()]`)".

options.summary: push keeps it, so it is handed over like any value; lending stays for functions given as a function parameter
options.code:
b.handlers.push(owns beep)              # beep is the list's now
b.handlers.push(owns copy of beep)      # or keep beep and give the list a copy
options.outcome: `b.handlers.push(beep)` is an error: "`push` keeps what it is given; hand `beep` over: `push(owns beep)`, or keep it: `push(owns copy of beep)`". With `owns beep`, a later `beep()` is E3040; with `owns copy of beep`, it prints "beep" and the loop prints "beep". A function from a variable is still lent, with no word, to a standard function that takes a function as its function parameter (`for_each(h)`, `map(h)`, `retain(keep)`).

options.summary: Lent, and the list holds a view of it
options.code: b.handlers.push(beep)
options.outcome: Compiles; the list holds a view of `beep` and may not outlive it (as a list of `StrView`s may not outlive their text): returning or storing `b` past `beep`'s scope is E3063. `beep()` prints "beep".

recommendation.reason: A list owns its elements, so its `push` hands over a function as it does every other value, with `owns` written at the call; lending stays exactly where the library already takes a function as a function parameter (STD-19), so no line keeps a value silently.
recommendation.checklist: 1, 4 (the word at the call says it), 5, 6 (push's existing rule), 9, 11

if "trudy" in banned:

items.reason: TYP-21 (p04 741-742; spec 1841-1842) settles that String's `+` is not `Add` ("`String`'s `+` takes its left operand over, `[TXT-11]`"), so the 'outside Add' part is refuted. Still open: TXT-11 (p15 163-164) hands the left operand over with no word on the line, while every other hand-over is written with `owns` (FN-2a, the owner's rule that a word in the line says what each name is), and every other operator reads both operands in place (TYP-21). So `println(first)` after `first + " Lovelace"` is E3040 with no word to point at, and `return name + "!"` on a read-only parameter is refused with no stated reason. No verdict speaks of operators.
items.title: Should String + read its left side, or hand it over with a word?
items.problem: A programmer builds a name with `full = first + " Lovelace"`. Today `+` on a String silently takes `first` over, so a later `println(first)` is an error although no word on the line says `first` was handed over, and `+` on a read-only parameter is refused. Every other operator in the language only reads its operands.
items.example:
fn greet(name: String) -> String:
    return name + "!"                  # `name` only reads the caller's string: may `+` take it over?

fn main():
    first = String("Ada")
    full = first + " Lovelace"         # no word says `first` is handed over
    println(full)
    println(first)                     # E3040, or "Ada"?
    println(greet(full))
items.spec_today: p15 163-164 (TXT-11): "`a + b` for `a: String, b: StrView` takes `a` over and returns it extended; `s += t` appends." Spec 1831-1832 (TYP-21): "Operators desugar to these interfaces for non-scalar operands; `a + b` calls `Add.add(a, b)` with both operands read in place." Spec 1841-1842: "`bool`, `char` and `String` implement none of them (`String`'s `+` takes its left operand over, `[TXT-11]`)." p05 115-116 (FN-2a): "A call says ... `owns` before one it takes over".

options.summary: `+` reads both sides and makes a new String
options.code:
full = first + " Lovelace"
return name + "!"
options.outcome: Both compile; prints "Ada Lovelace", "Ada", "Ada Lovelace!". One allocation, as an f-string makes; adding in place stays `s += t`. String then implements `Add` like other types, and the exception in the operator rule goes.

options.summary: `+` takes its left side over, written with `owns`
options.code: full = owns first + " Lovelace"
options.outcome: Compiles and reuses `first`'s buffer; `first + " Lovelace"` without `owns` is an error giving this line; `println(first)` after it is E3040; `greet` must take `owns name: String` and be called `greet(owns full)`.

options.summary: As today: taken over with no word
options.code: full = first + " Lovelace"
options.outcome: Compiles; `println(first)` is E3040; `return name + "!"` is refused because a read-only parameter cannot be handed over.

recommendation.reason: A makes `+` mean the same for every type (operands read in place), needs no hidden hand-over, and costs what C++'s `a + b` on two named strings costs; the in-place append is already spelled `s += t`.
recommendation.checklist: 4 (no hidden hand-over), 5, 6 (the operator rule without an exception), 7, 11, 13

items.title: What does a @ser(skip) field hold after a save file is read back?
items.problem: A game marks some fields of its save file `@ser(skip)`, so they are never written. When the save is read back, those fields are missing from the data. The specification says what a missing field takes only under `@ser(default)` or `@ser(since=N)`, and that any other missing field is an error, so it does not say what a skipped field holds, or whether a skipped field with no default compiles.

items.reason: thread.spawn needs its result `R` to be Send (THR-10, p11 175-176). A thread's result must be safe to send to another thread, and by the specification's rules AnyError is not, because it can hold any error, including one that holds a one-thread owner. The specification never says so, and this ordinary program is refused.

J6-07 B rewrites DET-2's 'completion order' as a rule over what threads change (Part XI's summary, EFF-24/EFF-26); it must not touch THR-21's reductions. J6-12 A narrows the lending rule in FN-2a and STD-19 (Part V/XV) to std functions that take a function as a function parameter; it does not reopen verdict 150 for those, or verdict 147 for the program's own functions. The finder's wider point, that one `owns f: F` declaration lends in std and takes over in a program's own code, is the owner's own split (verdicts 147 and 150) and was not raised as a gap, but the critic may want the owner to see it beside J6-12. items.reason: Nothing settles it. RC-4 point 3 puts check points at every loop's back edge and before every blocking call; RC-4 point 5 and WK-3 run a queued value's drop there. No rule counts those drops in the making thread's summary (EFF-24 counts what the code calls), none keeps check points out of a lock's `with` block, a walk or a live view, and THR-19 promises that every wait for a held lock is refused when compiling. THR-20 counts the drop only on the other thread. The check-point placement was a lead choice (decisions.md section 6, RC-4 point 3: 'the owner may overturn any'), not an owner verdict. Verdict 101 says only that the making thread deletes the value 'at its next check point'.
items.title: Where may a queued thread_shared value's drop run: inside a held lock or a walk?
items.problem: When another thread lets go of the last owner of a `thread_shared` object that travelled to it inside another object, the object goes back to the thread that made it, and that thread runs its `drop` at its next check point: a loop's back edge or a blocking call. That point can sit inside a `with lock:` block that the drop also takes, or inside a walk of a list that the drop pushes to. The specification does not say whether this compiles, and if it does, nothing stops the drop from hanging on the lock or changing the walked list.
items.example:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

class Pool:                                   # a connection pool: a free list behind a lock (std::mutex + std::vector)
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:                                   # one connection
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():                                # gives its id back to the pool
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Batch:                                  # a plain object, handed to the worker whole
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)])   # the Conn is made on main
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len())   # the Conn travels inside b; the worker ends its last owner
    for frame in 0..1000:                     # the server's main loop
        with pool.lock:                       # main holds the pool's lock
            for id in pool.free:              # this walk's back edge is a check point: Conn's drop may run HERE
                println(id)                   # ... and would wait for the lock main holds, and push to the walked list
    println(h.join())
items.spec_today: RC-4 point 3 (p08-classes.md 169-172): "Check points. The compiler places them: at every loop's back edge, before every call that may block the thread (waiting for a lock, `join`, a channel's receive, a sleep) and when the thread ends." items.title: When does a value queued to an idle job worker or a C thread get its drop?
items.problem: A job worker makes a `thread_shared` object that reaches the main thread inside another object, and main lets go of its last owner, so the object goes back to the worker to be ended at the worker's next check point. The worker is now idle, waiting for work inside the runtime, where the compiler placed no check point. The same happens to an object made in a callback on a thread C owns, once that thread has gone back into C. The specification does not say when such an object's `drop` runs, or whether it ever does.
items.example:
import std.jobs

class Texture:                            # a GPU texture a worker loaded
    id: int
    fn drop():
        println("texture", this.id, "freed")   # in an engine: hand the GPU memory back

class Bundle:                             # a plain object, combined into main's list
    textures: Array[thread_shared Texture] = []

fn load_all(ids: Span[int]) -> Array[Bundle]:
    out: Array[Bundle] = []
    with s = jobs.scope():
        for id in ids:
            s.submit(owns fn() copy of id: out.push(owns Bundle(textures=[thread_shared Texture(id=id)])))   # each Texture is made on a worker
    return out

fn render_frame(n: int):
    println("frame", n)

fn main():
    bundles = load_all([1, 2])
    bundles.clear()                       # main ends the last owners: each Texture goes back to the worker that made it
    frame = 0
    while true:                           # the game runs on; the workers wait for work and run no Ember code
        render_frame(frame)
        frame += 1

items.title: May a type that is not safe to read from two threads be made thread_shared?
items.problem: A class holds an `RwLock` of a `Cell`. Several threads may hold the read lock at once, and a `Cell` may be changed through a read-only name, so two threads could set it together. Writing `thread_shared` before such an object is checked only for `Send` and for direct changes, never for 'several threads may read it at once', and a function any thread may run may hold any `thread_shared` owner. So the program below passes every rule written, and two threads change one `Cell` at the same time.
items.example:
import std.thread
from std.sync import RwLock

class FrameStats:                                  # read by the render thread and the UI thread
    draws: RwLock[Cell[int]] = RwLock(Cell(0))     # a Cell: changed through a read-only name, meant for one thread

fn count_draw(stats: thread_shared FrameStats):
    with g = stats.draws.read():                   # a READ guard: several threads may hold one at once
        g.set(g.get() + 1)                         # changes the Cell under the read lock

fn main():
    stats = thread_shared FrameStats()             # FrameStats is Send, but not ThreadShared: refused?
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared stats: count_draw(stats))
    count_draw(stats)                              # both threads set the Cell at once
    h.join()
    with g = stats.draws.read():
        println(g.get())                           # 2, or 1 when one add is lost

items.title: May a scoped task end shares owners, whose count has no atomics?
items.problem: A scoped task clears a list of `shares mut` owners on another thread, which subtracts from each object's owner count with an ordinary, non-atomic subtract. At the same moment the parent makes another owner of one of those objects, adding to the same count. The specification forbids a task to make a `shares` owner, but says nothing about ending one. It forbids a task to make or end a `weakref` link to a one-thread object, but says nothing about ending an object that such links point at, which also writes its header.

import std.thread

class Enemy:
    hp: int = 10

class Level:
    enemies: Array[shares mut Enemy] = []    # each enemy has several owners, counted without atomics (std::shared_ptr's count, but not atomic)

class Hud:
    target: Option[shares mut Enemy] = None

fn main():
    boss = shares mut Enemy()
    level = Level(enemies=[shares mut boss])
    hud = Hud()
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): level.enemies.clear())   # the task, on another thread: -1 on boss's count
        hud.target = Some(shares mut boss)             # the parent, at the same moment: +1 on that count
    println(boss.hp)

So a program's wrapper of a thread-safe C handle can be vouched `Send` but never `ThreadShared`. It cannot be a `static` (STA-1, E7002), cannot be read by scoped tasks (`ref T` is `Send` only for a `ThreadShared` T, THR-8), and cannot usefully be `thread_shared`. The only way out is a `Mutex` around it, an Ember lock on top of C's own. ODR-111 (p26 399, a delegation ruling, not the owner's) had allowed `Send|Sync`; when `Sync` was renamed `ThreadShared`, the second was dropped without a verdict. JOB.md has no verdict on vouching `ThreadShared`.
items.title: Can a program vouch that its wrapper of a thread-safe C object is ThreadShared?
items.problem: A program wraps a C logger that takes its own lock inside, so any thread may call it at once. The author can vouch with `unsafe extend Logger implements Send:` that it may move to another thread, but has no way to vouch that several threads may use it at once. Writing `ThreadShared` by hand is an error. So scoped tasks cannot read it, and it cannot be a `static`, unless every call goes through an Ember `Mutex` that the C library does not need.
items.example:
import std.thread
from std.ffi import c_int

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("call it once, at start-up")
    unsafe fn logger_open() -> *mut void
    @safety("`logger` came from logger_open; the C library takes its own lock, so any thread may call it")
    unsafe fn logger_write(logger: *mut void, event: c_int)

struct Logger:                                  # wraps a thread-safe C logger (like a spdlog logger)
    raw: *mut void

    fn write(event: c_int):
        # SAFETY: raw came from logger_open, and the C logger locks inside
        unsafe:
            logger_write(this.raw, event)

# SAFETY: the C logger may be used from any thread
unsafe extend Logger implements Send:

fn open_logger() -> Logger:
    # SAFETY: called once, at start-up
    unsafe:
        return Logger(raw=logger_open())

fn main():
    lg = open_logger()
    events: Array[c_int] = [1, 2, 3]
    with scope = thread.scope():
        for e in events:
            scope.spawn(owns fn() copy of e: lg.write(e))   # each task reads `lg`: needs Logger ThreadShared, which it can never be

PAR-3's `reduce=[best: max]` exists only for loops. A scoped task has no place to declare one. So a listed reduction has no spelling that compiles. Searched THR-11, THR-21, PAR-3, the E7007 row, the glossary's 'reduction', grep for 'max=' and 'max(', and JOB.md verdicts 77 and 92.
items.title: How does a scoped task keep the largest value it saw?
items.problem: The specification lists `max` and `min` as reductions a task may make, alongside `total += e`. Ember has no `max=` operator, so the natural line is `best = max(best, t.len())`. But that is a plain assignment that reads the current value, which the same rule sends to 'needs a lock'. The listed reduction has no form that compiles.
items.example:
import std.thread

fn longest(lines: Array[String]) -> int:      # the longest line of a text file, split across tasks
    best = 0
    with scope = thread.scope():
        for t in lines:
            scope.spawn(owns fn() ref t: best = max(best, t.len()))   # a max reduction, or E7007?
    return best

fn main():
    println(longest([String("ember"), String("is fast"), String("c")]))
items.spec_today: THR-21 (p11-concurrency.md 408-409): "A task's `total += e` (and `-=`, `*=`, `|=`, `&=`, `^=`, `max`, `min`, `push`, `extend`, `add`, `m[k] op= e`) ... is a reduction". THR-21 (p11 424-425): "A plain assignment from a task (`a.target.hp = 5`) and a task that reads the current value (`if stats.total < 10: stats.total += x`) need a lock (`E7007`)." PAR-3 (p11 477): "`@parallel(reduce=[total: +, best: max])` declares variables combined after the loop".

options.outcome: Compiles and prints 7. `best = max(best, t.len()) + 1`, or `if best < 3:` in a task, is refused (E7007).

items.reason: PAR-2 (p11 455-456) says the body 'follows the rules of a scoped task' (THR-21: an undeclared `total += e` is a reduction, decimals included, per verdict 92). Yet in a range loop every written place must be indexed `i + k` and be a MutSpan or SoA column (clause c, p11 456-461), and a by-element loop 'writes nothing else but declared reductions' (p11 461-462). PAR-3 (p11 480-481) says a float reduction 'must be declared', which implies an integer one need not. E7010's message offers an `Atomic` as a fix (p11 469-470), but an Atomic is a written place with no index, which clause (c) refuses. Each of `count += 1`, `total += x` and an Atomic gets two answers. decisions.md's PAR-3 row covers only overflow.
items.title: Must a @parallel loop declare its running totals, when scoped tasks need not?
items.problem: A `@parallel` loop adds up masses into `total` and counts into `count`. The specification says the loop body follows a scoped task's rules, where an undeclared `total += x` is a running total combined at the end. It also says every place a range loop writes must be an indexed element, and that a float total must be declared in `@parallel(reduce=...)`. So the loop below gets two answers, and so does an `Atomic` changed in the body, which an error message itself suggests.
items.example:
fn total_mass(masses: Span[float]) -> float:    # a physics step: the mass of every body
    total = 0.0
    count = 0
    @parallel
    for i in 0..masses.len():
        total += masses[i]          # a float total, not declared
        count += 1                  # a whole-number total, not declared
    println(count)
    return total

fn main():
    println(total_mass([1.0, 2.0, 3.5]))

In a loop over a range, for each place `P` written in the body ... (c) `P` is the elements of a `MutSpan` or an `SoA` column the loop uses". PAR-2 (p11 461-462): "A loop walked by element hands each chunk its own elements through the loop's `ref mut` name, and writes nothing else but declared reductions (`[PAR-3]`)". PAR-3 (p11 480-481): "for floats it can differ from the serial left-to-right sum, which is why a float reduction must be declared." THR-21 (p11 408-412): a task's undeclared `total += e` "is a reduction". PAR-2 (p11 469-470): "where an `Atomic`, `chunks_mut` or `@parallel(reduce=…)` makes the loop compile, the message gives that line."

options.outcome: Compiles and prints 3, then 6.5, the same on every machine. A float total may differ from the serial sum in the last digit, as the owner accepted for tasks.

options.outcome: The program as written does not compile; with the declaration it prints 3, then 6.5. A scoped task's `total += x` stays undeclared.

recommendation.reason: The rule already says a parallel body follows a scoped task's rules, and the owner accepted undeclared decimal totals for tasks. One rule for the same line in both places, with nothing said twice.
recommendation.checklist: 5 (one rule wherever the same thing happens; 'same rule for every loop'), 2 (accepts the correct loop), 3 (nothing added while running), 11 (one spelling of a reduction, so `reduce=` goes)

items.title: May a @parallel loop over a range write the elements of an Array?
items.problem: The most common parallel loop writes `pixels[i]` of an image held in an `Array`. The rule lists the places such a loop may write as 'the elements of a `MutSpan` or an `SoA` column', and an `Array` is neither, although walking the same `Array` element by element in parallel is allowed. The specification does not say whether the loop below compiles or must first take a `MutSpan` of the array.
