Then `a` and `b` are two `ref mut` names of one component. The outcome is already decided: BRW-1 (p07 251-254) allows exactly one name that may change a place, verdict 98 refuses two changeable elements not proved apart when compiling, and verdict 100 refuses ECS clashes when compiling. Only the rule saying where the refusal falls is missing.
items.decided_by: BRW-1 ("through exactly one name that may change it ... checked when compiling"), verdict 98 (two changeable elements not known to differ are refused when compiling) and verdict 100 (ECS clashes are refused when compiling, never checked while running).
items.lead_fix_text: In ECS-4 (p12-dod.md 218-220), after "so they never name one place", add: "A `view_mut` whose listed types repeat, written out (`reg.view_mut[Position, Position]()`) or made so by a generic function's instance (`swap_into[Position, Position]`), is refused at the line where the types are known (`E3022`, naming the repeated type and, for an instance, the generic line that lists it twice), since two of its items would be one component: `[BRW-1]`." A `view` that only reads, with a repeated type, stays allowed.

items.reason: SOA-1 (p12 35-36) splits a `@soa(flatten)` field into one column per field of its own (`ps.pos.x`). SOA-2 (p12 37) defines `ps.f` as 'the column of field `f` ... a `MutSpan[F]`', and SOA-6 (p12 51-52) defines `ps[i].f` as 'a place in column `f`'. A flattened field has no column of its own, so neither rule says what `ps.pos`, `ps[i].pos` or `ps[i].pos = v` are. Searched SOA-1 to SOA-7, SIMD-3 (c), the attribute table, and HR-13.
items.title: What is ps.pos when pos is split into x, y, z columns?
items.problem: In a struct of arrays, a field marked `@soa(flatten)` is stored as one column per field of its own, `ps.pos.x`, `ps.pos.y` and `ps.pos.z`. The specification defines `ps.pos` as the column of `pos`, a `MutSpan[Vec3]`, and `ps[i].pos` as a place in that column, but a flattened field has no such column. It does not say whether `ps.pos` compiles, or what reading and writing `ps[0].pos` do.
items.example:
from std.math import Vec3

struct Particle:
    @soa(flatten)
    pos: Vec3                     # stored as three float columns: ps.pos.x, ps.pos.y, ps.pos.z
    vel: Vec3                     # stored as one Vec3 column

fn integrate(ref mut pos: MutSpan[Vec3], vel: Span[Vec3], dt: f32):
    for i in 0..pos.len():
        pos[i] += vel[i] * dt

fn main():
    ps = SoA[Particle].with_capacity(1024)
    ps.push(owns Particle(pos=Vec3.ZERO, vel=Vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)))
    integrate(ref mut ps.pos, ps.vel, 0.016)   # pos has no Vec3 column: does this compile?
    ps[0].pos = Vec3.ZERO                       # one place, or three?
    println(ps.pos.x[0])
items.spec_today: SOA-1 (p12-dod.md 35-36): "A field marked `@soa(flatten)` whose type is a struct is split into one column per field of its own (`ps.pos.x`); otherwise a struct field is one column." SOA-2 (p12 37): "`ps.f` names the column of field `f`: a view of that column's elements, a `MutSpan[F]`". SOA-6 (p12 51-52): "A proxy's field `ps[i].f` is a place in column `f` at index `i`; reading or writing it touches that column only, and no `T` is assembled."

options.summary: `ps.pos` is no column; `ps[i].pos` gathers and scatters its columns
options.code:
integrate(ref mut ps.pos, ps.vel, 0.016)
# refused: "`pos` is split into the columns `ps.pos.x`, `ps.pos.y` and `ps.pos.z` (`@soa(flatten)`,
#  line 4), so there is no column of `Vec3`; pass the columns: `ps.pos.x`, ..."
ps[0].pos = Vec3.ZERO        # accepted: writes ps.pos.x[0], ps.pos.y[0], ps.pos.z[0]
options.outcome: The `integrate` line does not compile. `ps[0].pos` reads the three columns into a `Vec3`, and `ps[0].pos = v` writes v's three fields into them, as `ps[i] = v` scatters a whole value.

options.summary: `ps.pos` is a view of its columns together, a new view type
options.code:
fn integrate(ref mut pos: SoASpan[Vec3], vel: Span[Vec3], dt: f32):   # a new type: Vec3s stored as columns
    for i in 0..pos.len():
        pos[i] += vel[i] * dt

integrate(ref mut ps.pos, ps.vel, 0.016)
options.outcome: Compiles with the new view type. A function taking `MutSpan[Vec3]` still cannot take `ps.pos`.

recommendation.reason: It adds no new type: the field's own columns already exist, and an element's field behaves as an element does (gather on read, scatter on write). B adds a view kind for one attribute.
recommendation.checklist: 5 (`ps[i].pos` behaves as `ps[i]` does), 7 (no special type for one attribute), 9 (the message names the columns to use), 13 (no extra path)

items.reason: PAR-2b (p11 473-476) and SIMD-5 (p12 123-124) read through 'each call to a function `[CG-C-3]` places in the inline header', and HR-9a (p20 99-101) keeps every reloadable function out of that header. So `@parallel` acceptance (E7010) and `@simd(assert)` (E4020) change with `[build] reload`. PHIL-13 (p01 87-90) has already decided the outcome: no profile or manifest key changes 'whether it is accepted'. So does PRF-1 (p17 313-314): 'Every profile accepts the same programs'. The text that keys the analysis on header membership is what is wrong. The same wording also ties the analysis to the C backend's header, which an LLVM-backend build does not have.
items.decided_by: PHIL-13 ("No build profile, compiler flag, manifest key or optimisation level changes ... whether it is accepted") and PRF-1 ("Every profile accepts the same programs"), together with HR-44 (every fact a compile-time safety decision rests on is recorded and compared at a reload).
items.lead_fix_text: In PAR-2b (p11-concurrency.md 473-474) and SIMD-5 (p12-dod.md 123-124), replace "each call to a function `[CG-C-3]` places in the inline header" with "each call to a function that meets `[CG-C-3]`'s criteria (`@inline`, an operator on a type of at most 64 bytes, the listed accessors, or at most 40 statements and no foreign call), whether or not this build places it in the inline header (a reloadable function in a hot-reload build, `[HR-9a]`, or a build on the LLVM backend)". In HR-44 add that a proof that read through a reloadable callee is one of the recorded facts, so a reload that changes the callee so the proof no longer holds is refused in plan (`E9030`), naming the loop and the callee.

items.reason: HR-16 (p20 168-170) gives `migrate_from` 'a read-only view of the old instance', so an owned field that is not `Clone` (an open socket) can be neither handed over nor copied, though the annex promises to keep 'open resources' (p20 5-6). HR-2a (p20 31-33) has reclaim free the old version 'field by field without the type's own drop' and end only 'removed fields', and for a `migrate_from` type, which 'replaces field-wise migration', it does not say which old fields count as removed. If they are not ended, `shares old.target` leaves one count too many and the old socket is never closed. If they are, nothing could have been carried over. Searched HR-2, HR-2a, the HR-14 table, HR-15, HR-16 and HR-34 to HR-43.
items.title: How does migrate_from keep an open socket, and what happens to old fields?
items.problem: A server's `Session` holds an open socket and one owner of a player, and an edit changes another of its fields, so the type declares `migrate_from` to build the new session from the old one. That function only gets a read-only view of the old session, so it cannot hand the socket on, and a copy would close it twice. The specification also does not say whether the old session's fields are ended after the migration (their `drop` run, their owner counts lowered) or just freed.
items.example:
from std.hot import ReloadError

struct Socket:                                  # an open connection, one owner (like a unique_ptr to a socket)
    fd: int
    fn drop():
        println("socket", this.fd, "closed")

struct Health:
    value: int

class Player:
    name: String

class Session:                                  # the edit: `hp: int` became `hp: Health`
    sock: Socket
    target: shares Player                       # one of the player's owners
    hp: Health

    static fn migrate_from(old: OldSession) -> Result[Session, ReloadError]:
        # `old` is a read-only view: `sock=old.sock` hands over from a view, and Socket is not Clone
        return Ok(Session(sock=???, target=shares old.target, hp=Health(value=old.hp)))

static mut SESSIONS: Array[Session] = []        # live sessions, kept across reloads

@unsafe(export("on_connect"))
fn on_connect(fd: int):                         # the C host calls this, and ember_reload_poll() between frames
    p = shares Player(name=String("ana"))
    SESSIONS.push(owns Session(sock=Socket(fd=fd), target=shares p, hp=Health(value=10)))
items.spec_today: HR-16 (p20-annex-b.md 168-170): "`static fn migrate_from(old: OldSelf) -> Result[Self, ReloadError]` replaces field-wise migration for its type. ... `old` is a read-only view of the old instance." HR-2a (p20 30-33): "Prepare ... runs every `migrate_from` against a read-only view of the old instance ... Reclaim frees each migrated instance's old version field by field without the type's own `drop`, since the instance lives on in its new form, and ends removed fields, running their `drop`." HR-2 (p20 24-25): "A failure in plan or prepare leaves the process running the old image, with no instance changed, handed over or ended". Annex B intro (p20 5-6): "keeping existing objects, statics and open resources".

options.summary: `migrate_from` takes the old instance with `owns`; what it leaves is ended at reclaim
options.code:
static fn migrate_from(owns old: OldSession) -> Result[Session, ReloadError]:
        return Ok(Session(sock=owns old.sock, target=owns old.target, hp=Health(value=old.hp)))
# what `old` still owns after the call is ended in reclaim (drops run, counts lowered),
# as an `owns` parameter's leftovers are; if prepare fails, nothing of `old` is ended or taken
options.outcome: Compiles. After the reload the session keeps socket 7 open, with the same player owner and no extra count, and nothing is printed. A field not taken (say `target`, if the function made `shares old.target` instead) is ended at reclaim, its count lowered.

options.summary: Keep the read-only view; such a type cannot declare migrate_from
options.code:
static fn migrate_from(old: OldSession) -> Result[Session, ReloadError]:
        ...
# refused when compiling: "`Session` owns `sock`, a `Socket` that is not `Clone`, which a
#  read-only `old` cannot hand on; restart to change `hp`"; the old instance's fields are all
#  ended at reclaim
options.outcome: The type with the socket does not compile with `migrate_from`, so the edit needs a restart, which closes every connection. A type with only copyable fields migrates, and its old fields are ended at reclaim.

recommendation.reason: It reuses the word the language already has for 'this function takes the value over', and keeps the annex's promise to keep open resources. Reclaim then ends exactly what nobody took, as any `owns` parameter's leftovers are.
recommendation.checklist: 2 (the correct migration compiles), 5 (`owns` means the same here as everywhere), 11 (the existing spelling of handing over), 13 (no special path: leftovers ended as for any `owns` parameter)

items.reason: HR-12 (p20 120-122) registers only 'class instances' and gives reload header sizes for the 8- and 12-byte headers only. Since 0.9.15, RC-1 (p08 103-104) puts any shared value, a struct included, in 'a block of its own with the header of `[OBJ-1]`', and OBJ-1 gives a `thread_shared` value a 32-byte header that HR-12 never mentions. HR-13 (p20 125-126) migrates value data 'through its container', but a struct in its own shared block has no container, and HR-15 (p20 157-162) rewrites owners 'in live instances and registered containers'. HR-13b refuses only data behind raw pointers or foreign memory. So a changed struct reached only through a `shares` block is neither migrated nor listed as refused, against HR-1's 'all live object state preserved'.
items.title: Does a reload migrate a struct that lives in a shared block?
items.problem: A game shares a `Stats` struct between the game and the HUD with `shares mut Stats()`, so it lives in a counted block of its own, not inside a class object or a list. While the game runs, the programmer adds a field to `Stats`. The specification registers and migrates class objects and the values inside lists, and says nothing about a struct in a shared block. So the reload may migrate it, refuse, or leave the old layout under the new code.
items.spec_today: HR-12 (p20-annex-b.md 120-122): "In a reloadable build, class instances are registered in a live-instance list, which adds 16 bytes to the object header of `[OBJ-1]` (24 bytes instead of 8, and 28 instead of 12 for an object `weakref` links may reach)". HR-13 (p20 125-126): "Value-typed data (structs in arrays, `SoA` columns, ECS storage, arena contents) is migrated through its container, which registers itself". HR-15 (p20 161-162): "in live instances and registered containers, in statics, and inside tuples, `owns` blocks and function values' state held by any of these". RC-1 (p08-classes.md 103-104): "A value made shared lives in a block of its own with the header of `[OBJ-1]` (a class object already does)". HR-1 (p20 9-10): "with all live object state preserved".

# in a reload build every `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared` and `owns` block is registered as a
# class object is, with 16 bytes more in its header (a `thread_shared` value's: 32 + 16 = 48)
options.outcome: The reload applies: the Stats block migrates, `hits` keeps its count and `misses` starts at 0. Release builds are unchanged.

#  reload cannot find; restart to change it"
options.outcome: The reload is refused and the old code keeps running. Adding a field to any struct that is ever shared needs a restart.

recommendation.reason: One model for every block that lives on its own: it keeps HR-1's promise, and costs 16 bytes per block only in reload builds, as class objects already pay. B turns an everyday edit into a restart.
recommendation.checklist: 2 (the edit applies), 5 (one rule for every block with an OBJ-1 header), 7 (general: every shared kind), 13 (no unregistered side path)

items.reason: HR-24 (p20 262-265) calls this case a refusal ('is then refused'), yet detects it in prepare and says 'the reload is discarded'. HR-15b (p20 167) says every refusal is decided in plan, and HR-41's matrix has no row for it. The outcome the program sees is the same either way: the old image keeps running, with a report. HR-24's own last sentence (detected in prepare, discarded) and HR-15b decide which word is right. What plan does across the waiting polls is the runtime's, not a language question.
items.decided_by: HR-15b ("Every refusal is decided in plan, before prepare runs") and HR-24's own "This is detected in prepare, so the reload is discarded and the old image keeps running".
items.lead_fix_text: In HR-24 (p20-annex-b.md 263) write "... waits at most `frames_in_flight + 1` polls and is then discarded (a prepare failure, `[HR-2]`), naming the resource; each poll while it waits runs plan again". Add to HR-41's matrix the row: "an object in use by an in-flight GPU frame does not fit and is still in flight after `frames_in_flight + 1` polls | prepare | discarded; old image keeps running (`[HR-24]`)".

items.reason: HR-11 (p20 116-118) lists the words a field's type is written with but not `guarded by`. HR-44's facts are what functions change, read, end and lock, not which lock a field needs. So an edit adding `guarded by lock` to a field changes neither the schema nor any fact, and code not rebuilt (a frame below a checkpoint, another package) keeps using the field without the lock: the data race THR-13 rules out. Only one answer is safe. HR-44's own scope ('Every rule that decides when compiling whether a line is safe ... a lock this thread holds and a call that may take it') and THR-13's guarantee already require the reload to compare it.
items.decided_by: THR-13 (the data-race guarantee in Safe Ember) and HR-44's stated scope ("Every rule that decides when compiling whether a line is safe ... The image records these facts").
items.lead_fix_text: In HR-11 (p20-annex-b.md 116-118), add to a field's schema the lock it is `guarded by` (none, or the lock's name), so adding, removing or changing it is a change of the field. In HR-44 add 'which lock each field needs' to the recorded facts, so a reload that changes it while code the reload does not rebuild uses the field (a frame below a checkpoint, a suspended generator, another package) is refused in plan (`E9030`), naming the field, its new lock and the code that uses it without that lock.

items.reason: GPU-2 (p22 27-30) settles a frame that never began and a frame ended twice, but not a frame that ends without `end_frame`, from an early `return` or `?`. `Frame` is not `@must_drop` (THR-6, p11 350: only `Scope` and `JobScope`), and Annex D gives `Frame` no `drop`, so the device's state after such an exit (a swapchain image acquired, a recording open) is undecided. Searched all of Annex D, THR-6, ALC-1 and GPU-3.
items.title: What happens when a GPU frame ends without end_frame, on an error?
items.problem: A renderer begins a frame, and an error while creating a texture leaves the function through `?` before `end_frame` is called. The frame has one owner, so it simply ends there. The specification refuses ending a frame twice or ending one that never began, but does not say what ending a frame without `end_frame` does: whether it compiles, and what happens to the acquired swapchain image and the open recording.
items.spec_today: GPU-2 (p22-annex-d.md 27-30): "A `Frame` has one owner and is not `Copy`, and `end_frame(owns frame: Frame)` takes it over (`device.end_frame(owns frame)` ends the name `frame`), so ending a frame that never began, or ending one twice, is refused when compiling." THR-6 (p11-concurrency.md 350): "The standard library applies it [`@must_drop`] to `Scope` and `JobScope` only." GPU-3 (p22 31-33): "`frame.arena()` ... lives as long as the `Frame`".

options.summary: A Frame's own drop closes the frame and submits nothing
options.code:
# the program above, unchanged
# `Frame` has a drop: it ends the frame as `end_frame` does (gives the swapchain image back, frees
# the frame's memory) but discards the recording
options.outcome: Compiles. On the error nothing is drawn this frame, the error is returned, and the next `begin_frame` works as usual.

options.summary: Ending a frame without end_frame stops the program
options.code:
# the program above, unchanged
# `Frame`'s drop stops the program: "panic: a Frame ended without end_frame (render, line 8)"
options.outcome: Compiles. On the error the program stops at the `?` line, naming the frame.

recommendation.reason: It is how every one-owner resource in the language behaves on an early exit (the C++ RAII guard, `std::lock_guard`): the `?` stays an ordinary error path, and the device is left in a usable state. B turns a handled error into a crash.
recommendation.checklist: 1 (the error is returned, as the program says), 2 (accepts the correct program), 7 (no ceiling: every early exit), 13 (an ordinary drop, no special path)

items.reason: PAR-2 (p11 454-455) names `break`, `return`, `yield` and an outer `continue`, but not `?`. THR-5 (p11 380) names `?` beside `return`, which shows the spec treats them as separate words. But ERR-2 (p13 50-52) defines `?` as an early return ('evaluates to the `Ok` payload, or returns `Err(F.from(err))`'), and p13's introduction (line 8) says 'every place a function can return early is marked by `?` or `return`'. PAR-2's rule against `return` (iterations must be independent, with no exit from the function) therefore covers `?`. Only the word is missing from the list.
items.decided_by: PAR-2's "The body MUST NOT contain `break`, `return`, ..." (iterations are independent and none leaves the function), with ERR-2's definition of `?` as a return of the error.
items.lead_fix_text: In PAR-2 (p11-concurrency.md 454-455) write "The body MUST NOT contain `break`, `return`, `?`, `yield`, or a `continue` naming an outer loop", with E7010's help for `?`: "`?` on line 4 would return from `parse_all` in the middle of the parallel loop; keep each result instead: write `out[i] = parse_int(lines[i])` into an `Array[Result[int, ParseError]]` and check them after the loop".

jobs.notes:
Patterns and cross-part notes for the phase-3 critic:
(1) J7-01 and J7-02 both come from where check points sit (RC-4 point 3, Part VIII). That placement was a lead choice (decisions.md section 6, 'the owner may overturn any'), not owner verdict 101. My recommendations fit together: J7-01 B (the queue is emptied only at check points where nothing held clashes with a queued drop) and J7-02 A (also when a worker goes idle and when a host thread returns to C). Together they say a queued drop runs only at points where the thread holds no lock, walks no list and keeps no clashing view. A smaller question remains, which I did not raise as an ODR: RC-4 point 3 puts a check point 'when the thread ends', and THR-16 says no drop runs once `main` returns. Whether values queued to main are ended before the process exits is not said; the Part VIII checker may have it.
(2) J7-03 A and J7-06 A both touch the marker rules of Part IV (TYP-43 and its table, lines 577-594) and THR-8/THR-9. J7-03 A requires `ThreadShared` at the line that makes a value `thread_shared`. J7-06 A lets `unsafe extend T implements ThreadShared:` lift TYP-43's E2040 for `ThreadShared` (ODR-111's old `Send|Sync`). They agree: vouching is how a raw-pointer wrapper then becomes `thread_shared`. J7-07 (a lead fix) puts the same conditions on `Sender[T]`/`Receiver[T]`.
(3) J7-08 A, J7-09 A and J7-10 A form one reduction rule for scoped tasks and `@parallel`: neutral starting values, `-=` totalling what is taken away, mixed operators refused, `best = max(best, e)` as the max spelling, and undeclared totals in loops as in tasks. J7-10 A withdraws `@parallel(reduce=...)`. SIMD-5 (Part XII, p12 132) names `@parallel(reduce=…)` as the permission for a float reduction in a vectorised loop, so the critic must reconcile SIMD-5 (permission from `@fastmath`, or from the undeclared `@parallel` reduction). PAR-3's chunk-order rule (PAR-5) is unchanged. If the owner picks J7-10 B instead, J7-09 A is for tasks only and `reduce=[best: max]` stays the loop spelling.
(4) J7-04 A extends THR-11's sentence. RC-7 and WK-11 (Part VIII) defer to §XI.3, so the Part VIII checker may see the same hole from the other side.
(5) J7-05 (a lead fix) is in RC-1 (Part VIII); the Part VIII checker may report it too: merge.
(6) J7-14 (a lead fix) ties PAR-2b/SIMD-5 to CG-C-3's criteria instead of the inline header. That also makes C-backend and LLVM-backend builds accept the same loops (PHIL-13), and it touches Part XVIII's CG-C-3/CG-C-3a wording.
(7) J7-15 A changes HR-16's signature to `owns old` and HR-2a's reclaim (leftovers ended, the type's own drop still not run). J7-16 A changes HR-12's header sizes (a thread_shared block 48 bytes in reload builds), which touches OBJ-1 (Part VIII) and COST-3.
(8) J7-12, J7-17, J7-18 and J7-20 are lead fixes where only one safe or consistent answer exists; each names the rule that decides it.
I left out, as the finder did: verdict 100's `owns dyn AnyPool` against ECS-2's `owns dyn AnyStorage` (a naming difference), and the finder's unchecked notes (SIMD-7 with memory-mapped files, ECS-8's signal timing, `Ring[T, N]` against the run-time `frames_in_flight()`, HR-3 with other threads inside Ember code). I did not check them in depth and add no item for them.

jobs.name: C and C++ interoperation (Part XVI, Annex C)

items.reason: The spec's only hand declaration of a C function that keeps a callback (FFI-52, p16-ffi.md 489-499) breaks FFI-10 in three ways. It is a `safe fn` with raw `*mut void` parameters, which FFI-10 lines 82-84 refuse. It writes no result, yet `setup` returns its value as `Retained[ForeignCallback]`. It is called with one argument where two are declared. FFI-10 says how a `count(n)` length leaves the callable signature (lines 85-92, ODR-074), and nothing says the same for `user_data`. FFI-11's ownership row (line 290) gives a callback no Ember type, only "`callback(retained)` (`[FFI-21]`)". FFI-21 (lines 403-405) moves the function into a block C keeps, which is a hand-over, and verdicts 147 and 158 put `owns` at the call for a hand-over. Neither verdict covers a foreign callback parameter, because the parameter is never written as `owns`. No rule, verdict or ODR settles any of this.
items.title: How is a C function that keeps an Ember callback declared and called?
items.problem: A game gives a C library a function that C keeps and runs later, through a function-pointer and user-data pair. The specification's own declaration of such a function writes raw `*mut void` parameters on a `safe fn`, which the hand-declaration rule refuses. It also writes no result, although the caller returns a token from it, and its call passes one argument where two are declared. The specification does not say what the callback parameter's Ember type is, whether the user-data pointer leaves the call as a counted length does, or whether the call writes `owns` before a function C takes over.
items.spec_today: FFI-10 (p16-ffi.md 79-84): "A `safe fn` writes the safe Ember types and the words in front of its parameters' names (`ref mut`, `owns`) produced by those words ... A raw `*T` can be declared for an unsafe call, but complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter or result safe to expose; `safe fn` with one is `E5002`." FFI-10 (85-87): "On a hand-declared `safe fn` with `count(n)`, `n` is written as an integer scalar parameter at its C ABI position (ODR-074). The contract marks it as an ABI witness: it is absent from the callable Ember signature". FFI-11 ownership row (290): "for a callback, `callback(retained)` (`[FFI-21]`)" (no type given). FFI-21 (402-405): "the function value, its code and its state, is moved into a block of its own, and C is given the trampoline as the function pointer and the block's tagged number as the user data." FFI-21 (415): "`retained` returns a `Retained[ForeignCallback]` token". FFI-52 example (492-499): `safe fn register_cb(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)` ... `return register_cb(fn() owns game: game.add_point())`.

options.summary: The declaration writes the Ember side: `owns cb: fn()`, the user-data pointer as a hidden witness (like a counted length), and the token as its result. The call says `owns`, as it does for every argument to an `owns` parameter.
options.outcome: Compiles. `register_cb(fn() owns game: ...)` without `owns` is the error that asks for `owns`, as `take(xs)` is. Under `threads(any)` the parameter is `owns cb: thread_shared fn()`. Calling it with two arguments is the error for too many arguments.

options.summary: The same declaration with a plain parameter `cb: fn()`. The call takes no word, because the capture list already says what C keeps.
options.outcome: Compiles. A function is handed over here with no word at the call, unlike every other `owns` hand-over.

recommendation.reason: C keeps the function, so it is handed over, and the language already writes a hand-over as `owns` on the parameter and at the call, a function written in the call included. The user-data witness is written exactly as the counted-length witness is.
recommendation.checklist: 2 (callback APIs become declarable), 4 (hand-over written, plumbing hidden), 5 and 11 (`owns` and the ABI-witness form reused), 16 (the call-site `owns` verdicts reach foreign calls)

items.reason: Verdict 147: "An argument for an `owns` parameter says `owns` at the call, whatever is passed: with `fn take(owns xs: Array[int])`, `take(owns xs)` hands `xs` over and `take(xs)` is an error". FFI-39c's parameter is "contracted `owns` in the overlay", which FFI-11 (p16-ffi.md 290) maps to an `owns x: owns T` parameter. FFI-54 already writes `widget_take(owns first)` (line 553). FFI-39c (p21-annex-c.md 134) still writes the bare `panel.add_child(b)`. Verdicts 159 (constructors) and 160 (`shares`/`weakref` made in the call) do not apply to it, and decisions.md N41's exemption covers only compiler-made calls.
items.decided_by: Verdict 147 (an argument for an `owns` parameter says `owns` at the call, whatever is passed); FFI-54's `widget_take(owns first)` already follows it.
items.lead_fix_text: In FFI-39c (p21-annex-c.md line 134), write "the argument is handed over (`panel.add_child(owns b)`: `b` ends, upcast to the C++ base)" in place of `panel.add_child(b)`. The bare form then gets verdict 147's error, for example "`add_child` takes `b` over (its contract says `owns`); say so at the call: `panel.add_child(owns b)`". Check that E5060's message, which gives both lines, writes the hand-over the same way.

items.reason: FFI-21 (p16-ffi.md 415-417) gives the token and E5041 only to `retained`: "with `once` the trampoline ends the block after the first call". FFI-23 (541-542) defines the token as what "a registering call returns for a callback C keeps", and the glossary (p24-appx-f.md 29) and FFI-52 (454, "not yet unregistered") count a `once` callback as kept. So the rules do not say whether a `once` registration returns a token, needs `destroys(f)`, or what ending such a token after the run does (calling C's unregister for a request C already finished). The finder's second case (`atexit`, a capture-free function with no user data) is settled: FFI-21's first sentence (line 400) lets a C function-pointer parameter take a capture-free Ember function as an `extern "C" fn` with no `callback(...)` word, and FFI-52 (457-458) counts "every Ember function given to C as an `extern "C" fn` value" as runnable. Only the `once` question is left.
items.title: Does a one-shot C callback give a token, and must it name an unregister function?
items.problem: Async C APIs (libuv-style file reads, HTTP requests) take a callback that C runs exactly once and then drops. Some can cancel the request and many cannot. The specification gives a token and requires an unregister function only for callbacks C keeps (`retained`). For a one-shot callback (`once`) it says only that the block ends after the first call, so it does not say what the registering call returns, whether an unregister function is required, or what ending a token after the callback has run does.
items.example:
from std.ffi import CStrView

class Loader:
    loaded: i32 = 0

unsafe extern "C":
    # C calls `cb` once, with `req`, when the read finishes or fails; the library has no cancel function
    @ffi(param(cb, callback(once, user_data=req), threads(creator)))
    safe fn fs_read_async(path: CStrView, owns cb: fn(i32), req: *mut void)   # result: nothing, or a token? E5041 for no `destroys`?
    safe fn run_loop()                                                       # runs finished requests' callbacks

fn main():
    loader = shares mut Loader()
    fs_read_async(c"save.dat", owns fn(n: i32) shares mut loader: loader.loaded += n)
    run_loop()
    println(loader.loaded)
items.spec_today: FFI-21 (p16-ffi.md 408-409): "With `callback(retained)` or `callback(once)` C keeps the function after the call"; (415-417): "`retained` returns a `Retained[ForeignCallback]` token (`[FFI-23]`) whose end unregisters the callback through the declared `destroys(f)` (`E5041` if none is declared), and with `once` the trampoline ends the block after the first call." FFI-23 (541-542): "`Retained[ForeignCallback]` is the token a registering call returns for a callback C keeps". FFI-53 (522-523): "a `callback(once)` slot carries a used-up mark". Glossary (p24-appx-f.md 29): "kept callback ... (`callback(retained)` or `callback(once)`)".

options.summary: `once` is like `retained`: it returns a token and needs `destroys(f)`. Ending the token before the run unregisters, and ending it after the run does nothing.
options.outcome: Compiles when the library has a cancel function. The declaration in the example (no cancel function) is E5041, so a library without one cannot be declared safe.

options.summary: `once` never gives a token and never needs `destroys(f)`. The block ends when C makes the one call.
options.outcome: The example compiles and prints the bytes read. A library that can cancel cannot pass that on to Ember: with `destroys(f)` written, the word is refused or ignored.

options.summary: A token exactly when `destroys(f)` is written. Without it, the behaviour is B. With it, the behaviour is A: ending the token before the run cancels, and after the run does nothing (the used-up mark).
options.outcome: Both declarations compile. The example prints the bytes read, and `http_get`'s token cancels the request if it ends before the callback has run.

recommendation.reason: The declaration means only what it says: a written `destroys` gives a token, and no `destroys` gives none. Both real kinds of one-shot API become safe. Nothing runs twice, because the used-up mark is checked when the token ends.
recommendation.checklist: 2 (accepts both API kinds), 7 (general), 15 (meaning from what is written), 3 (the existing used-up mark, no new run-time cost)

items.reason: TYP-26 (p04-types.md 867-868): "There is no overloading: two functions of one name in one scope are `E1030`". FFI-48 (p21-annex-c.md 90) refuses only overloads that differ in return type, which implies that the others import, but no rule says how. FFI-39b (128-129) picks a base constructor "by arity and argument types" for `super.init` only. FFI-17 (10-12) generates "one thunk per imported function, method, constructor", so a class with two constructors gets two `new`. GRM-35's `overlay_fn` (p16-ffi.md 260) and FFI-12 (322-323) match entries by name, count and parameter names, so FFI-48's own fix, "rename one in the overlay", cannot name one overload. No verdict covers this. C++ overloads, constructors above all, are in nearly every C++ header.
items.title: How do C++ overloaded functions and constructors import into Ember?
items.problem: Almost every C++ class has overloaded methods or several constructors, and Ember itself has no overloading. The specification refuses only overloads that differ in return type (which C++ cannot declare anyway). It does not say what Ember name or names the ordinary overloads get, how a call picks one, or how an overlay entry names one of them.
items.spec_today: TYP-26 (p04-types.md 867-868): "There is no overloading: two functions of one name in one scope are `E1030`, except operator-interface implementations and `extend` blocks for different types." FFI-48 row (p21-annex-c.md 90): "overloads differing only in return type | Ember has no return-type overloading | rename one in the overlay". FFI-39b (128-129): "`super.init(…)` selects the C++ base constructor by arity and argument types". FFI-12 (p16-ffi.md 322-323): "An overlay entry whose name, parameter count or parameter names do not match the header is `E5010`". GRM-35 (260): `overlay_fn := ["unsafe"] "fn" IDENT "(" [overlay_param ...] ")"`.

options.summary: One Ember name for each C++ name. The call picks the overload by the arguments' types, as C++ does and as `super.init` already does. An overlay entry names one overload by its parameter count and names.
options.outcome: Compiles and calls the overload C++ would call. A call that no overload fits, or that two fit equally, is an error naming the candidates.

options.summary: Each overload imports under its own name, built from its C++ parameter types.
options.code:
r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new_int_int(1280, 720)
    r.draw_Mesh(mesh)
    r.draw_Sprite(hud)
options.outcome: Compiles. Each overload is a separate Ember function. The names come from types the program never wrote, and they change when the header renames a type.

options.summary: An overload set imports only through an overlay that renames each overload. Without that, every overload is skipped with a warning that gives the overlay lines.
options.code:
unsafe overlay cpp "renderer.hpp":
    class Renderer:
        rename new(width, height) as sized
        rename draw(mesh) as draw_mesh
        rename draw(sprite) as draw_sprite
options.outcome: Without the overlay, `r.draw(mesh)` is the "skipped: overloaded" diagnostic. With it, `r.draw_mesh(mesh)` compiles.

recommendation.reason: It keeps what the C++ header means and works with no overlay. It reuses the selection Ember already does for `super.init`, and Ember's own no-overloading rule only fails to describe C++ names, so the exception says why.
recommendation.checklist: 2 (ordinary C++ imports), 4 (no names to invent), 6 (an exception only where the general rule is untrue for C++, with the reason), 11 (FFI-39b's selection reused), 13 (no hidden renaming)

items.reason: FFI-2 (p16-ffi.md 40-41) and verdict 125 ("C++ too, same rule ... members included") keep every header member with no overlay entry unsafe to call. FFI-42 (p21-annex-c.md 188-189) maps `operator[]` to `Index`/`IndexMut`, whose methods `index`/`index_mut` (p04-types.md 666-671) are ordinary safe methods behind `x[i]`. GRM-35's `overlay_fn := ["unsafe"] "fn" IDENT ...` has no form for an operator member, so no entry can assert the operator safe or mark it `@ffi(const)` (verdict 132). Whether `g[3]` on an imported class compiles outside `unsafe` is not stated, and if it does not, the syntax to make it safe is missing (OWNER-DIRECTION checklist 12).
items.title: How does an overlay name a C++ operator[] so that indexing can be safe?
items.problem: An imported C++ grid or buffer class with `operator[]` becomes indexable in Ember (`g[i]`). Every imported member stays unsafe to call until an overlay entry vouches for it. But an overlay entry is `fn NAME(...)`, and no NAME refers to `operator[]`. So the specification does not say whether `g[3]` needs `unsafe`, and it leaves no way to vouch for the operator.
items.spec_today: FFI-42 (p21-annex-c.md 188-189): "Overloaded operators map to Ember operator interfaces where one exists (`operator[]` to `Index`/`IndexMut`, ...)". FFI-2 (p16-ffi.md 40-41): "A header function with no overlay entry therefore stays unsafe to call." GRM-35 (259-260): `overlay_class := "class" IDENT ":" ... {{attribute} overlay_fn}`, `overlay_fn := ["unsafe"] "fn" IDENT "(" ...`. Index (p04-types.md 668, 671): `fn index(i: Idx) -> ref Output`, `fn index_mut(i: Idx) -> ref mut Output`.

options.summary: An overlay entry names an operator member by the Ember method it becomes (`index`, `index_mut`). With no entry, `g[3]` is unsafe code, as any header member is.
options.outcome: With the entries, `g[3]` compiles outside `unsafe`, and the entry vouches that C++ never reads out of bounds. Without them, `g[3]` is the unsafe-call error, whose help gives these lines.

options.summary: An overlay entry names an operator by its C++ spelling, in quotes.
options.outcome: Same result as A. The overlay gets a second kind of name that appears nowhere else in Ember.

recommendation.reason: The operator already becomes Ember's `index`/`index_mut`, so the overlay uses the name Ember gives it. The missing syntax is added instead of leaving operators always unsafe, and FFI-2's rule holds for operators unchanged.
recommendation.checklist: 11 (Ember's own method names), 12 (syntax added, no exemption), 5 (one rule for every member), 15

items.reason: FFI-2a (p16-ffi.md 45): "In result position a pointer's lifetime is never derived." FFI-17a's span row (p21-annex-c.md 58): "a result needs a lifetime word". FFI-40 (162-163) instead derives a member's `T&` result as "a `ref mut T` view into the object" (LT-1 rule 1). For an Ember method that rule is backed by reading the body (verdict 137), but C++ has no body to read, and a C++ member that returns into a reference parameter (`Node& first_child(Node& parent)`) then counts as pointing into the wrong object. For free functions LT-1's rules 2 and 3 apply, and a `const T&` parameter of a `Copy` type imports as a plain `x: T`, which is no source parameter (p07-ownership.md 528-529), so the result points into nothing. The `string_view` and fixed-extent span rows say nothing about results. A call is safe only with an overlay entry (FFI-2), and an entry may write `-> from(parent)`, but whether an entry without a lifetime word is accepted, and what it then means, is exactly what the two rules disagree on.
items.title: Must a C++ function returning a reference say where the reference points?
items.problem: A C++ method returning `Node&` imports as a view, and the specification takes that view to point into the object the method was called on, with nothing written. That is false for a C++ method that returns a reference into one of its parameters. The same specification says a C pointer result's lifetime is never derived, and that a `std::span` result needs a lifetime word, so the two rules disagree on whether an overlay entry must say where a returned reference points.
items.spec_today: FFI-2a (p16-ffi.md 45): "In **result** position a pointer's lifetime is never derived." FFI-11 lifetime row (293): "`from(this)`, `from(p)`, `from(static)` | a view into the receiver, into `p`, or into what lives for the whole program". FFI-17a (p21-annex-c.md 58): "`std::span<T>` ... zero-copy; a result needs a lifetime word (`[FFI-11]`)". FFI-40 (162-163): "a `T&` result is a `ref mut T` view into the object and a `const T&` result a `ref T` one (`[LT-1]`)." LT-1 (p07-ownership.md 538, 544-545): "1. if it is a method, the result points into `this`" ... "The three rules decide a call where there is no code to read: ... a function with no Ember body."

options.summary: As today: a C++ reference result needs no word. A method's points into its object and a free function's follows the three rules, with a `const T&` parameter counted as a source when the result is a reference. An entry returning into a parameter writes `-> from(parent)`.
options.code:
#     class Scene:
#         fn root()                              # into the scene
#         fn first_child(parent) -> from(parent)  # must be remembered; leaving it out is accepted
options.outcome: With `-> from(parent)`, `level = sc.Scene.new()` while `child` is used is refused. Without it, the example compiles and reads freed memory, because the entry's assertion was wrong and nothing asked for the word.

options.summary: A C++ reference or view result needs a lifetime word in its overlay entry, as a `std::span` result and a C pointer result already do. `[[clang::lifetimebound]]` supplies it as an asserted fact.
options.code:
#     class Scene:
#         fn new()
#         fn root() -> from(this)
#         fn first_child(parent) -> from(parent)
options.outcome: The entry `fn first_child(parent)` with no word is the error naming the missing fact and giving this line. With the words, `level = sc.Scene.new()` while `child` is used is refused (the view of `level` is still in use).

recommendation.reason: It is one rule for every foreign result that points somewhere (C pointers, `std::span`, C++ references). An entry's meaning then comes only from what it says, and a forgotten word is a refusal, not a read of freed memory. The cost is one word per entry that returns a reference.
recommendation.checklist: 5 and 6 (one rule with FFI-2a and FFI-17a), 8 (a forgotten mark is refused), 15 (no fallback to an unwritten fact), 2

items.reason: FFI-8's static row (p16-ffi.md 186): a foreign global's read "needs `unsafe` unless `@ffi(immutable)` asserts a `const` C object and an unchanged value (ODR-082) ... a safe read also requires `T: needs ThreadShared`". GRM-35's overlay grammar (256-258) has no item for a variable, so a global from an imported C header can never be given `@ffi(immutable)` and is always read in `unsafe`. FFI-41 (p21-annex-c.md 181) makes a C++ namespace or static-member variable safe to read "unless it is `const` and holds no pointer", with no assertion and no `ThreadShared` check. It also ignores FFI-40a's own warning that `const` is no guarantee for a class with a `mutable` member. The owner's answer behind FFI-41 (tasks/90/owner-questions.md Q4) says only that it "reads and writes like a global", and the rule replacing ODR-163 makes pointer-holding variables `unsafe`. Neither decides the `const` exemption.
items.title: Is reading a foreign `const` global safe, the same way for C and C++?
items.problem: A game reads a constant such as `MAX_PLAYERS` from a library header. A C++ `extern const int` is safe to read with nothing written. The same declaration in a C header is always read in `unsafe`, because the assertion that would make it safe can only be written on a hand declaration. The C++ rule also ignores `mutable` members, which a `const` C++ object's own methods may change, and asks for no thread check.

fn main():
    println(lp.game.MAX_PLAYERS)    # compiles
    println(lc.MAX_PLAYERS)         # compiles: the C header says `const`
    println(lp.game.STATS.hits)     # unsafe-read error: `Stats` has a `mutable` member

items.reason: FFI-10 (p16-ffi.md 59-61) accepts a `safe fn` when "every parameter and result is a scalar, a `@layout(c)` value type, or a pointer whose contract is complete", and lines 82-84 refuse a raw pointer even with complete facts. Wrapped in a `@layout(c)` struct, the same raw pointer passes the list. Contract words attach only to parameters, and FFI-30a (210-212) bars an overlay from touching fields, so nothing can state a field pointer's count or lifetime. Safe code can fill such a field with any address (`ref_to_ptr` is safe, p04-types.md 340-342, ODR-075). FFI-56 (596-598) uses the same list for `@ffi(safe)` typedefs. The spec's own XVI.4 overlay asserts `vkCreateBuffer(pCreateInfo: borrowed one)` safe, and its create-info struct holds `pQueueFamilyIndices` and `pNext`. No verdict covers this.
items.title: May a safe C call take a struct that holds raw pointers?
items.problem: A safe C function may not take a raw pointer, because the compiler cannot check what C does through it. The same pointer inside a `@layout(c)` struct (a buffer description, a Vulkan create-info) passes the rule, although nothing can state its length or lifetime. Safe Ember code can then fill the struct with any address and length, and C writes through it.
items.example:
@layout(c)
struct PixelBuf:
    data: *mut u8      # C writes `len` bytes here
    len: usize

unsafe extern "C":
    @ffi(no_callbacks)
    safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)    # accepted by the parameter list today

fn main():
    x: u8 = 7
    clear_pixels(PixelBuf(data=ref_to_ptr(ref mut x), len=4096))   # every line is safe code; C writes 4,096 bytes over one
    println(x)

FFI-30a (210-211): "An overlay changes the signatures, safety and names of *functions* ...; it never changes a type's identity, layout or fields". FFI-56 (596-598): "`@ffi(safe)` on the typedef's entry ... when every parameter and result is a scalar or a `@layout(c)` value type". IV.5 (p04-types.md 340-341): "Creating one from a reference is safe (ODR-075): `ref_to_ptr(r: T) -> *T`".

options.summary: A `@layout(c)` type that holds a raw pointer, by value or behind a contracted pointer, counts as a raw pointer. A `safe fn` (or an `@ffi(safe)` typedef) taking one is refused. The safe interface is an ordinary wrapper that builds the struct from a checked view inside `unsafe:`.
options.outcome: `safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)` is E5002, naming the field `data`. The wrapper compiles, and safe callers can only clear bytes they own. The XVI.4 example's `vkCreateBuffer` becomes an `unsafe fn` entry with `@safety`, or gets a wrapper.

options.summary: As today. `safe fn` is the declarer's promise and also covers the struct's pointer fields.
options.outcome: The example compiles, and C overwrites 4,095 bytes past `x` (memory corruption in safe code). `ember tcb` lists the assertion.

recommendation.reason: A raw pointer is refused on a safe C call whether it travels alone or in a struct, and C's view of the memory comes from a span the compiler checked. This keeps Rust-level safety with no run-time cost.
recommendation.checklist: 5 and 6 (one rule for raw pointers, no struct-shaped way around it), 8, 2 (correct programs keep a safe wrapper), 7

items.reason: FFI-31b (p16-ffi.md 651) lets an exported signature carry `CStrView` and `extern "C" fn`. CStrView has a non-null niche (ODR-080's `Option[CStrView]` is how null is said). The `@unsafe(export)` `# SAFETY:` note vouches only for the symbol name (FFI-26, 629-634). FFI-56 (590-596) makes every function pointer "that comes from C ... an argument C passes to a callback" an `unsafe extern "C" fn`, because "nothing tells the compiler what the function it points to does". An export's parameter comes from C in exactly that way. E5054 (652-656) refuses `char` because "C may pass any `uint32_t`", and the same reason applies to a null `const char*`. No rule or verdict says how an export's C-supplied parameters are typed.
items.title: What may an exported function trust about the arguments its C host passes?
items.problem: A game module exports `game_log(msg, done)`, which the host calls with a C string and a completion function. Ember lets the export declare a non-null string view and a safe function pointer, so its body reads the string and calls the pointer in safe code. The host may pass NULL, or any address. The specification already treats a function pointer that arrives from C as unsafe to call, and refuses `char` because C may pass a value it cannot hold, but neither rule reaches an export's own parameters.
items.example:
from std.ffi import CStrView

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `game_log`
@unsafe(export("game_log"))
pub extern "C" fn game_log(msg: CStrView, done: extern "C" fn(i32)) -> i32:
    match msg.to_str():          # reads bytes at `msg`: the host may pass NULL
        Ok(text):
            println(text)
            done(1)              # a safe call through whatever address the host passed
        Err(_):
            done(0)
    return 0
items.spec_today: FFI-31b (p16-ffi.md 651): "`@layout(c)` values, scalars, opaque handles, `CStrView` and `extern "C" fn` may." FFI-56 (590-596): "A function pointer that comes from C — a field of an imported struct, a typedef, a result, an `extern static`, an argument C passes to a callback — imports as `unsafe extern "C" fn(…)` ... nothing tells the compiler what the function it points to does with its arguments". FFI-31b (652-654): "`char` may not appear in a foreign signature, an export's or a hand declaration's ... (`E5054`) ...: C may pass any `uint32_t`". FFI-26 (629-634): the `# SAFETY:` note says "why nothing else defines that name".

options.summary: What C passes to an export follows the rules for what C hands back: a function pointer is `unsafe extern "C" fn`, called in `unsafe:`, and a C string is `Option[CStrView]`, where NULL is `None`.
options.code:
@unsafe(export("game_log"))
pub extern "C" fn game_log(msg: Option[CStrView], done: unsafe extern "C" fn(i32)) -> i32:
    if msg exists as m:
        match m.to_str():
            Ok(text):
                println(text)
                # SAFETY: the host's `done` takes one int and runs no Ember code
                unsafe:
                    done(1)
            Err(_):
                return 1
    return 0
options.outcome: This compiles. The example as written is refused: `done: extern "C" fn(i32)` and `msg: CStrView` each get the error giving these types. A NULL from the host becomes `None`, not a crash.

options.summary: As today. The types the export writes are the host's promise, and the `# SAFETY:` note above `@unsafe(export(...))` vouches for every argument as well as the symbol name.
options.outcome: The example compiles. A host that passes NULL makes Ember read address 0.

recommendation.reason: A value arriving from C gets the same type whichever way it arrives (a callback's argument, a struct field, an export's parameter), and a value C may send that the Ember type cannot hold is refused, as `char` already is. The NULL test is one compare.
recommendation.checklist: 5 and 6 (one rule with FFI-56 and E5054), 8, 3 (one compare), 11 (`Option[CStrView]` and `unsafe extern "C" fn` reused)

items.reason: FFI-33 (p16-ffi.md 666-677): under `creator` a `static mut` an export reaches must be `guarded by` a lock (E7012), and `creator` is "the thread of the first successful `ember_rt_init`" (or `ember_module_init`), with "initialization after shutdown establish[ing] a new creator". FFI-33c (681-683): under `main` the wrapper checks "that the calling thread is the one that initialised the module ... in exchange the body may use thread-confined state, the module's `static mut`s among it". The two checks name the same thread, yet one permits the `static mut` and the other refuses it. The only difference the text implies, re-initialisation on another thread, is stated for `creator` and not for `main`. STA-1 (p05-declarations.md 478) ties a `static mut` to "the main thread", and for a library module that thread is undefined except by FFI-33c. No verdict covers this.
items.title: May an export marked `creator` change a module variable, as one marked `main` may?
items.problem: A plugin module exports `bump()`, which changes a module variable. Marked `threads main` it compiles, and marked `threads creator` it is refused unless the variable is behind a lock. Both are checked at run time against the thread that initialised the module. The specification gives no reason for the difference, and does not say whether `main` moves to a new thread when the host shuts the module down and initialises it again elsewhere, as `creator` does.
items.example:
#! threads creator
static mut HITS: int = 0

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `bump`
@unsafe(export("bump"))
pub extern "C" fn bump() -> i32:
    HITS += 1        # E7012 under `creator`; accepted with `#! threads main`
    return 0
items.spec_today: FFI-33 (p16-ffi.md 663-666): "a `static mut` it reaches is `guarded by` a lock it holds there (`E7012` ...). The same holds under `creator`." (670-675): "For a static library or executable using a private runtime, this is the thread of the first successful `ember_rt_init`. For a `cdylib`, it is the thread of that module's successful `ember_module_init` ... initialization after shutdown establishes a new creator." FFI-33c (681-683): "Under `threads = main`, the exported wrapper checks, in every profile, that the calling thread is the one that initialised the module, and panics otherwise; in exchange the body may use thread-confined state, the module's `static mut`s among it." STA-1 (p05-declarations.md 478-479): a `static mut` "is reached only by the main thread and its scoped tasks unless it is `guarded by` a static `Lock`".

options.summary: Keep the difference and give its reason. An export's `main` is the first thread that ever initialised the module, fixed for the process, and initialising again on another thread panics. The module's `static mut`s live on that thread. `creator` may move after a re-initialisation, so a `static mut` it reaches needs a lock.
options.outcome: Under `main` this compiles. Under `creator` it is E7012, whose message gives the reason: a later initialisation may run on another thread. A host that re-initialises a `main` module on another thread gets a panic naming both threads.

options.summary: One thread for both words: the thread of the current initialisation. The module's `static mut`s get their first values again at each initialisation, and under either word an export may change them with no lock.
options.outcome: Compiles under both words, and a re-initialisation starts `HITS` at 0 again. For exports `main` and `creator` then mean the same thing.

recommendation.reason: It keeps both written rules and states the one fact that makes them differ, so `main` keeps a meaning of its own. A forgotten lock under `creator` stays a compile-time refusal.
recommendation.checklist: 6 (the exception says why), 5 (each word one meaning), 3 (the existing one-compare check), 8

items.reason: FFI-51 (p16-ffi.md 133-141) requires `unsafe import c` for an import that "compiles C into the program ... runs C code that nothing checks, a constructor in it even before `main`". It exempts "an import of a header alone" because "its functions run only when they are called". For C++, FFI-3 and FFI-17 (p21-annex-c.md 8-12) compile a thunk translation unit that includes the header with the project's compiler. That unit instantiates the header's inline variables and namespace-scope objects, whose dynamic initialisers run before `main` uncalled, which is exactly FFI-51's reason. Header-only libraries (CXX-1) compile all their code this way. The annex never mentions `unsafe import cpp`, TCB-4 (p21-annex-c.md 213) lists only `unsafe import c`, and no verdict covers it.
items.title: Does `import cpp` need `unsafe`, given that the header's code runs before `main`?
items.problem: `unsafe import c` is required when an import compiles C into the program, because that code runs unchecked, before `main` too. A C header alone is exempt, because its functions run only when called. A C++ import always compiles the header into the program (Ember's glue code includes it), and a C++ header can define objects whose initialisers run before `main`. The specification does not say whether `import cpp` needs `unsafe` and a `# SAFETY:` note.
items.spec_today: FFI-51 (p16-ffi.md 133-141): "An import that compiles C into the program ... runs C code that nothing checks, a constructor in it even before `main`, so it is written `unsafe import c`, with a `# SAFETY:` note above it ... An import of a header alone needs no word: its functions run only when they are called, and those calls are fenced by `[FFI-2]`." FFI-3 (p21-annex-c.md 8-9): "The importer generates `extern "C"` thunks, compiled by the project's own C++ compiler with the project's flags". FFI-17 (10-12): "parses the header ... and generates one thunk per imported function". TCB-4 (213): lists "`unsafe import c` (`[FFI-51]`)".

options.summary: Every C++ import is written `unsafe import cpp` with a `# SAFETY:` note, because Ember always compiles the header into the program.
options.code:
# SAFETY: config.hpp is ours; load_default_path only reads config/default.txt
unsafe import cpp "config.hpp" with (project="engine") as cfg
options.outcome: This compiles. The plain `import cpp` is E3100, with the line above as its help. `ember tcb` lists the import.

options.summary: `unsafe import cpp` only when the header defines something that runs uncalled (a namespace-scope, inline or static-member variable with a dynamic initialiser). The importer finds these in the header.
options.code:
# SAFETY: config.hpp is ours; load_default_path only reads config/default.txt
unsafe import cpp "config.hpp" with (project="engine") as cfg
import cpp "vec3.hpp" with (project="engine") as v3     # no dynamic initialiser: no word
options.outcome: `config.hpp` without `unsafe` is E3100 naming `g_default_path`, and `vec3.hpp` needs nothing. A header that includes `<iostream>` (whose standard library defines a static initialiser object) needs `unsafe` too.

options.summary: As today: a C++ header needs no word, as a C header does not.
options.code: import cpp "config.hpp" with (project="engine") as cfg
options.outcome: Compiles, and `load_default_path()` runs before `main` with nothing written about it.

recommendation.reason: By FFI-51's own test, a C++ import compiles code into the program, and C++ code can run before `main` from nearly any header (`<iostream>` included), so a per-header test would hold for almost every import. One word on every C++ import says plainly that its code is vouched for.
recommendation.checklist: 5 and 6 (FFI-51's rule wherever code is compiled in), 13 (no special detection path), 2, 11 (`unsafe import` reused)

items.reason: Verdict 114 fix 3: "an object given to C under a `retained` contract never moves; for it a link at the hand-over stops the program", carried in FFI-35a (p16-ffi.md 363-365) and THR-2 (p11-concurrency.md 122-125, whose message shows a safe `register(names)` on line 4). FFI-11's ownership row (290) gives `retained` on any non-callback pointer "no safe type ... the call stays `unsafe`, with a raw pointer". FFI-23 (545-547) says an Ember value C keeps goes only by `owns` or `into_raw()`, and both end the Ember name, so nothing on this thread could later hand the object to another thread. `Retained.pin` (ODR-156, in the appendix's history) was removed (verdict 91's correction). The spec defines no spelling that gives C a class object's address while Ember keeps the owner, and THR-2's example cannot be written. Because verdict 114 decides the stop, the open question is the spelling (which programs compile), not the behaviour.
items.title: How does code give C an object's address while Ember keeps owning it?
items.problem: A physics library keeps a pointer to each body it simulates, while the game keeps owning the body. The owner decided that such an object never moves: handing it to another thread while a `weakref` on this thread points at it stops the program. But the specification leaves no way to write that call. A `retained` pointer gets no safe type, and the two ways to give C an object, `owns` and `into_raw()`, both end the program's name for it.
items.example:
from std.ffi import ObjectPtr

class Body:
    mass: f32 = 1.0

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`p` stays alive until `world_remove(p)` is called")
    @ffi(param(p, retained, one))
    unsafe fn world_add(p: ObjectPtr[Body])        # the physics world keeps `p`
    @safety("`p` was given to `world_add`")
    unsafe fn world_remove(p: ObjectPtr[Body])

fn main():
    body = Body()
    w = weakref body
    # SAFETY: `world_remove` is called before `body` ends
    unsafe:
        world_add(???)           # no spelling gives the address and keeps `body`
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns body: body.mass)   # the decided rule: stops, since C keeps the address and `w` points at it
    println(h.join())
items.spec_today: FFI-35a (p16-ffi.md 363-365): "A class object given to a `retained` parameter is marked in its header as kept by C and never moves: handed to another thread while a `weakref` link on this thread points at it, it stops the program (`[THR-2]`, verdict 114)." FFI-11 ownership row (290): "on any other pointer no safe type, since C keeps Ember memory only when it is handed over (`owns`) or given with `into_raw()` (`[FFI-23]`, `[FFI-54]`): the call stays `unsafe`, with a raw pointer". FFI-54 (555-557): "`w.into_raw()` gives the address ... and stops Ember freeing it ...; the name ends." THR-2 (p11-concurrency.md 123-124): "C keeps its address (`register(names)`, line 4)".

options.summary: In `unsafe:`, `ref_to_ptr(body)` gives a class object's address as an `ObjectPtr[Body]` without ending `body`. Passing it to a parameter contracted `retained` marks the object as kept by C, so the decided stop applies.
options.code:
# SAFETY: `world_remove` is called before `body` ends
    unsafe:
        world_add(ref_to_ptr(body))
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns body: body.mass)
options.outcome: This compiles. At run time the spawn stops with THR-2's message (`w` points at it and C keeps its address). With `w = None` first, the body goes to the thread and stays at the same address.

options.summary: There is no such way. An object C keeps goes only by `owns` or `into_raw()`, which end the name, so it can never be handed to a thread, and the stop and the mark are removed as unreachable.
options.code:
# SAFETY: the world keeps the body and never frees it
    unsafe:
        world_add(body.into_raw())
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns body: body.mass)
options.outcome: The spawn line is the use-after-hand-over error (`body` ended at `into_raw()`). The owner's decided stop never happens.

recommendation.reason: It gives the decided rule a program it applies to, using the language's existing safe address-of spelling, and keeps the unsafe call vouched for. B would quietly remove a stop the owner chose.
recommendation.checklist: 11 (`ref_to_ptr` and `ObjectPtr` reused), 2 (the common engine pattern compiles), 10 (keeps the owner's decided behaviour), 8

items.reason: FFI-54 (p16-ffi.md 555-561) and verdict 91 let `into_raw()` give C an `owns T`'s `*mut T` or a class object's `ObjectPtr[C]`, and say a mistake "leaks it or frees it twice". No operation takes such a value back. `adopt` (FFI-36a, 386-389) reads the destructor from `@ffi(destroys(f))` on a foreign `type T`, which an Ember class has none of. `ObjectPtr[C]` (FFI-23, 548-550) is defined only as a `Copy`, comparable address. So an Ember object given to C as user data (the GLFW `glfwSetWindowUserPointer` pattern) can never be ended. JOB.md and decisions.md have no `from_raw`.
items.title: How does Ember take back an object it gave C with into_raw()?
items.problem: A game gives a C windowing library a pointer to its `Game` object as user data, and gets it back at shutdown. `into_raw()` gives C the address and stops Ember freeing the object. The specification defines no way to turn that address back into an owner, so the object's `drop` never runs and its memory is never freed.
items.example:
from std.ffi import ObjectPtr

class Game:
    score: i32 = 0

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`p` stays valid until `take_user_pointer` gives it back")
    unsafe fn set_user_pointer(p: ObjectPtr[Game])
    @safety("a pointer was set and not taken back yet")
    unsafe fn take_user_pointer() -> ObjectPtr[Game]

fn main():
    game = Game()
    # SAFETY: the window keeps the address until `take_user_pointer` hands it back
    unsafe:
        set_user_pointer(game.into_raw())
    # ... the frame loop runs ...
    # SAFETY: the pointer C hands back is the one `into_raw()` gave
    unsafe:
        p = take_user_pointer()
        # no operation turns `p` back into an owner: the game is never ended
items.spec_today: FFI-54 (p16-ffi.md 555-561): "`w.into_raw()` gives the address of a value Ember holds alone ..., an `owns T` (as a `*mut T` ...) or a class object with one owner (as an `ObjectPtr[C]`), and stops Ember freeing it ... a mistake leaks it or frees it twice". FFI-36a (386-389): "`std.ffi.adopt[T](h) -> owns T` is an `unsafe fn` that takes ownership of a foreign object, reading its destructor from the contract of `T`'s declaration, `@ffi(destroys(f))` on `type T`". FFI-23 (548-550): "An `ObjectPtr[C]` is the address of a class object, which `into_raw()` gives ...: `Copy`, equal when it is the address of the same object."

options.summary: `adopt`, in `unsafe:`, also takes back what `into_raw()` gave: an `ObjectPtr[C]` gives the class object's owner, and the `*mut T` of an `owns T` gives the `owns T`. Ember then ends it as usual.
options.code:
# SAFETY: the pointer C hands back is the one `into_raw()` gave
    unsafe:
        back = std.ffi.adopt[Game](take_user_pointer())
    println(back.score)      # `back` ends at the end of `main`, running Game's drop
options.outcome: Compiles. It prints 0 and frees the game at the end of `main`. Taking the same address back twice is caught as adopting one object twice is (a panic naming both sites).

options.summary: A separate built-in on the type, Rust's spelling.
options.code:
unsafe:
        back = Game.from_raw(take_user_pointer())
options.outcome: Same as A. The language gets a second word for taking ownership of an address.

options.summary: There is no way back: what `into_raw()` gives is C's for good.
options.code:
unsafe:
        p = take_user_pointer()
options.outcome: Compiles. The game is never ended (a leak, which the `debug` leak report lists), and any object kept as user data leaks.

recommendation.reason: `adopt` already means "take ownership of an object C hands back, in unsafe code", so taking back what `into_raw()` gave reuses that one word, and its existing twice-adopted check applies.
recommendation.checklist: 11 (`adopt` reused, no second word), 2 (the user-data pattern frees its object), 5, 7
