No rule gives its meaning: what Ember type it produces, whether it is `Copy`, or whether a parameter of a handle type is a pointer contract. The spec's own overlay writes `vkCreateBuffer(device: borrowed, ...)` and `vkCmdSetViewport(commandBuffer: borrowed, ...)` (239-245) with no count word, which FFI-11a (310) makes E5012 unless `handle` changes that. In Vulkan, `VkDevice` is a pointer typedef, and the non-dispatchable handles such as `VkBuffer` are 64-bit integers on 32-bit targets. No verdict or ODR (ODR-247 only refuses `handle` on a function) defines it.
items.title: What does `@ffi(handle)` make a C type, and does a handle parameter need pointer words?
items.problem: Vulkan, Win32 and most C graphics APIs pass objects as handles, opaque values typedef'd to a pointer or a 64-bit number. The specification's own Vulkan overlay marks `VkDevice` `@ffi(handle)` and then writes `device: borrowed` with no element count, which the specification refuses for any pointer. Nothing says what `@ffi(handle)` means: whether the type is a copyable value, how it is passed, or which words its parameters take.
items.spec_today: FFI-1 (p16-ffi.md 31-32): "`threads(creator)` and `handle` are words of a type's or a result's contract, not a function's: on a function each is a contract error (`E5002`)." FFI-11 (301-302): "Other contract words: ... `handle`; ..." (no meaning given). FFI-11a (310): "A pointer contract with no count word is `E5012`". XVI.4 example (239-245): `fn vkCreateBuffer(device: borrowed, pCreateInfo: borrowed one, ...)`, `fn vkCmdSetViewport(commandBuffer: borrowed, ...)`. Glossary (p24-appx-f.md 27): "a C object's `@ffi(handle)`; never a class object".

options.summary: `@ffi(handle)` makes the type an opaque `Copy` value with the C type's representation (a pointer or a number). It is passed and returned by value and never dereferenced, and a parameter of a handle type takes no pointer words.
options.outcome: Compiles, and `copy_of_device = device` copies the handle. `device: borrowed` on a handle parameter is E5002, "a handle is passed by value and takes no pointer words". The XVI.4 example drops `borrowed` on `device` and `commandBuffer`.

options.summary: `@ffi(handle)` is an opaque type behind a pointer. Its parameters keep pointer contracts, a count included.
options.code: fn vkDestroyBuffer(device: borrowed one, buffer, pAllocator: nullable borrowed one)
options.outcome: Compiles once every handle parameter says `borrowed one`. A handle is not `Copy`, and `VkBuffer` (a number on 32-bit targets) cannot be described this way.

recommendation.reason: It matches what a handle is in C and in the glossary (a token naming something elsewhere, passed by value), it covers handles that are numbers, and it makes the specification's own Vulkan overlay compile with one rule.
recommendation.checklist: 2, 5 (one meaning for `handle` whatever its C representation), 7, 15 (the word says what the type is)

items.reason: Verdict 121 moved the header's fingerprint out of the overlay line into `ember.overlays` ("The overlay line's `with (header_hash = ...)` ... goes"). GRM-35 (p16-ffi.md 254) still has every overlay name a header (`overlay ("c" | "cpp") STRING`), FFI-17 (p21-annex-c.md 12-13) writes `overlay cpp "Header.hpp":`, and the `import c ... with (overlay = ...)` line names a header too. GRM-35 (274-275) also says the header is recorded "never in the overlay". FFI-30c (222-223) applies another package's overlay "only to the header it was written for". With three places naming the header, nothing says which one wins or what happens when the overlay's line names a header other than the one imported.
items.title: What happens when an overlay's first line names a different header from the import?
items.problem: An overlay file begins `unsafe overlay c "SDL.h":`, and a program applies it to an import of `SDL2/SDL_video.h`. The specification names the header in three places: the overlay's first line, the import, and Ember's record file. It does not say which one counts, or whether a mismatch is an error.
items.example:
# overlays/sdl.em
unsafe overlay c "SDL.h":
    @ffi(no_callbacks)
    safe fn SDL_Quit()

# main.em
import c "SDL2/SDL_video.h" with (overlay = "overlays/sdl.em") as sdl   # the overlay says SDL.h: applied, refused, or ignored?

fn main():
    sdl.SDL_Quit()
items.spec_today: GRM-35 (p16-ffi.md 254): `overlay_decl := ["unsafe"] "overlay" ("c" | "cpp") STRING`; (274-275): "Ember records the header each overlay was written for in `ember.overlays`, never in the overlay (`[FFI-55]`)." FFI-55 (337-338): `file = "overlays/sdl.em"`, `header = "SDL.h"`. FFI-30c (222-223): "An overlay of another package is applied only to the header it was written for".

options.summary: The overlay's first line says which header it describes. It must name the header the import names (and the record's), and a different one is an error.
options.code: import c "SDL.h" with (overlay = "overlays/sdl.em") as sdl
options.outcome: This compiles. The example is E5010, "`overlays/sdl.em` is written for `SDL.h`, and this import is of `SDL2/SDL_video.h`".

options.summary: The overlay's first line names no header, `unsafe overlay c:`. The import names it and the record keeps it.
options.code:
# overlays/sdl.em
unsafe overlay c:
    @ffi(no_callbacks)
    safe fn SDL_Quit()
options.outcome: The example's import applies the overlay to `SDL2/SDL_video.h`, and the record's fingerprints catch any declaration that differs.

recommendation.reason: The overlay file keeps saying, in readable words, which header it is about, and a mismatch is refused instead of silently applied. Only the fingerprint stays out of the file, as decided.
recommendation.checklist: 2 (written meaning stays in the line), 8 (a mismatch is refused), 9, 10 (does not reopen the decided fingerprint)

items.reason: FFI-36 (p21-annex-c.md 118-120) turns a C++ raw-pointer result into an `owns T` "ended through the contract's destructor". FFI-36a (p16-ffi.md 386-389) reads that destructor from `@ffi(destroys(f))` on `type T`. A C++ class imported with no overlay has no such word. FFI-32 (74-80) ends a by-value opaque result "by the class's destructor", and FFI-17a's `std::unique_ptr` row (63) ends one "through the deleter", but nothing says whether a C++ class's own destructor (with `delete`) counts as "the contract's destructor" for `adopt`, or whether `adopt` is refused without a `destroys(f)`. JOB.md has no verdict on this.
items.title: What ends a C++ object that Ember adopts from a raw pointer?
items.problem: A C++ factory returns `Enemy*`, a new object the caller must delete. Ember's `adopt` turns such a pointer into an owner "ended through the contract's destructor", but a C++ class imported without an overlay names no destructor function. The specification does not say whether the owner's end runs C++'s `delete` (the class's own destructor), or whether `adopt` is refused until an overlay names a function.
items.spec_today: FFI-36 (p21-annex-c.md 118-120): "A C++ function returning a raw pointer with no ownership contract yields `*mut T`; `ffi.adopt[T](p)` (`unsafe`) turns it into an `owns T` ended through the contract's destructor." FFI-36a (p16-ffi.md 386-388): "reading its destructor from the contract of `T`'s declaration, `@ffi(destroys(f))` on `type T`". FFI-32 (p21-annex-c.md 77-80): "A function returning an opaque class by value gives an `owns T` ... ended by the class's destructor; an abstract class, or one without a public destructor, is refused". FFI-17a (63): "`std::unique_ptr<T>` | `owns T`, ended through the deleter".

options.summary: For an imported C++ class with no `destroys(f)`, the adopted owner's end runs C++'s `delete` (its destructor and its memory release) through a generated thunk, as `std::unique_ptr`'s default deleter does. A class with no public destructor is refused.
options.code: return adopt[f.Enemy](p)
options.outcome: Compiles. `e`'s end runs `delete` on the enemy. An overlay's `@ffi(destroys(free_enemy))` replaces `delete` for an object made some other way.

options.summary: `adopt` needs a `destroys(f)` stated in the overlay, for C++ as for C.
options.outcome: The example without the overlay is E5002, naming the missing `destroys`. C++ classes need a free function to be written for them.

recommendation.reason: `delete` is what a C++ class's own declaration says ends it, and Ember already uses that for by-value results and `unique_ptr`. So `adopt` follows the same rule with nothing extra to write, and an overlay can still say otherwise.
recommendation.checklist: 5 and 6 (one rule with FFI-32 and FFI-17a), 4, 2

items.reason: FFI-24 (p21-annex-c.md 97-101) decides every imported C++ function: a function whose declaration is non-throwing returns `T`, and "Every other function returns `Result[T, CppError]`". Templates import only as explicit instantiations (FFI-17b, 18-19), and Clang evaluates every `noexcept(expr)` of an instantiated declaration, so the finder's example (`noexcept(Traits<T>::safe)` for `integrate<Body>`) is derived as either `T` or `Result`. No program is left undecided. E5061 (FFI-43, 112) is a diagnostic with no case left, and which error codes exist is the lead's housekeeping, not a language gap. Note for the lead: retire E5061 or name the case it covers.

FFI-53 (p16-ffi.md 515-520, 532-533) gives the callback table 48 slot bits (16 on a 32-bit target) and retires a slot whose generation is used up, "as `[HND-3]` retires a `Pool` slot". HND-3 (p09-memory.md 414-415) says what a full pool does ("`insert` panics and `try_insert` returns `Err(CapacityError.Full)`"). FFI-53 says nothing about a full callback table, and a registering `safe fn` has no error result to carry it. A 32-bit target reaches the limit at 65,536 live callbacks. No verdict covers this.
items.title: What happens when a program registers more C callbacks than the table holds?
items.problem: Each callback C keeps takes a slot in a table whose size is fixed by the bits of the number C is given: 65,536 slots on a 32-bit target. A worn-out slot is retired for good. The specification says what a full `Pool` does (it panics), but not what a registration does when no callback slot is free.
items.spec_today: FFI-53 (p16-ffi.md 516-520): "the callback's slot in a table that never moves in the low 48 bits and the slot's generation in the top 16 ... On a 32-bit target the slot is the low 16 bits and the generation the top 16"; (532-533): "A slot whose generation reaches its last value is retired and never reused, as `[HND-3]` retires a `Pool` slot". HND-3 (p09-memory.md 414-415): "When every slot is retired or live, `insert` panics and `try_insert` returns `Err(CapacityError.Full)`."

options.summary: The registering call panics when no slot is free, with a message naming the line and the table's size, as a full `Pool`'s `insert` does.
options.code: tokens.push(owns on_click(owns fn() shares mut hud: hud.clicks += 1))
options.outcome: On a 32-bit target the program stops at the 65,537th registration ("no callback slot is free: 65,536 callbacks C keeps are registered (line 15)"). On 64-bit it prints 70000.

options.summary: A registering call whose callback C keeps returns `Result[Retained[ForeignCallback], CapacityError]`, and the program handles a full table.
options.code: tokens.push(owns on_click(owns fn() shares mut hud: hud.clicks += 1)?)
options.outcome: Every kept-callback registration must handle the error, including on 64-bit, where the table cannot fill.

recommendation.reason: It is the rule the language already has for a full table of generational slots. It costs nothing per call, and it does not make every registration handle an error that 64-bit targets cannot reach.
recommendation.checklist: 5 and 6 (one rule with HND-3), 3, 7 (the limit is stated, not hidden)

jobs.notes:
Patterns: (1) Part XVI's C rules are not applied to Annex C's C++ imports, or the reverse: result lifetimes (J8-06: FFI-2a against FFI-40), const globals (J8-07), `unsafe import` (J8-11), the destructor `adopt` uses (J8-16), and what arrives from C (J8-09: FFI-56 and E5054 against FFI-31b). (2) The hand-declaration surface (FFI-10) is defined for counts, nullable spans and strings (ODR-074..080) but not for callbacks or user data (J8-01) or handles (J8-14). (3) The overlay grammar (GRM-35) cannot name C++ overloads (J8-04) or operators (J8-05).

For the phase-3 consistency critic:
- J8-01's recommendation A (a kept callback is written `owns cb: fn()` and called with `owns fn() ...`) extends verdicts 147 and 158 to foreign callback parameters. It must agree with Part VI/VII's call-word rules (FN-2a, OWN-9, STD-19) and with verdict 150 (a function from a variable passed to a std function is borrowed). A `callback(borrowed)` parameter stays `cb: fn()` with no word. J8-03 and J8-18 use the same spelling in their examples; if J8-01 goes another way, rewrite their declarations and calls to match. J8-01 also changes the E7004 message in FFI-21 (lines 412-414) and the FFI-52 example, which must then write the `owns` and the result type.
- J8-06 recommendation B (every C++ reference or view result needs `from(...)` in its overlay entry) touches FFI-40's last sentence and LT-1's \"no code to read\" clause (p07-ownership.md 544-545) as far as C++ goes. It does not change Ember methods. It must agree with any Part VII reviewer's reading of verdict 137.
- J8-08 recommendation A (a `@layout(c)` type with a raw pointer field counts as a raw pointer for `safe fn` and `@ffi(safe)`) makes the XVI.4 flagship overlay's `vkCreateBuffer` entry (p16-ffi.md 239-241) wrong. It must become `unsafe fn` with `@safety`, or gain an `extend` wrapper. This interacts with J8-14 (the same overlay's `device: borrowed`).
- J8-07 recommendation A drops the C rule that requires `@ffi(immutable)` for imported headers (ODR-082 stays for hand declarations) and adds FFI-40a's `mutable` test to FFI-41. It must agree with STA-1 and ODR-163 (a pointer-holding global, read only in `unsafe`, need not be `ThreadShared`).
- J8-09 recommendation A changes which types FFI-31b allows in an export (`Option[CStrView]`, `unsafe extern \"C\" fn`). Check it against `@export_table` fields (FFI-26), which are `extern \"C\" fn` Ember values going out, not values coming in, so they are unaffected.
- J8-12 recommendation A gives `ref_to_ptr` of a class object the type `ObjectPtr[C]` (IV.5, p04-types.md 340-342, defines it only for `ref T` to `*T`). A Part IV reviewer should confirm that it does not clash with how class handles are typed.
- J8-13 recommendation A widens `adopt` (FFI-36a) to take back what `into_raw()` gave. It should agree with J8-16's answer on what ends an adopted C++ object.
Settled, not raised: J8-03's `atexit` half (FFI-21's first sentence plus FFI-52's last clause: a capture-free function needs no `callback(...)` word). J8-17 (E5061 is dead code, the lead's to retire). J8-02 is a one-line lead fix under verdict 147.
